# Research Plan for High-Field Magnet Applications Based on GdBCO/BHO Nanocomposite Superconducting Thin Films

## Experimental Background and Motivation

REBCO (rare-earth barium copper oxide) high-temperature superconducting materials, due to their excellent current-carrying capacity in the liquid nitrogen temperature range (77K) and high magnetic field environments, have become the core materials for next-generation high-field magnets (e.g., nuclear magnetic resonance, particle accelerators, and fusion reactors). Among them, GdBCO (GdBa₂Cu₃O₇-δ) is highly regarded for its higher irreversibility field (Hirr) and critical temperature (Tc≈92K) ([Frontiers in Physics, 2019](https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/physics/articles/10.3389/fphy.2019.00082/full)). However, three key issues still need to be addressed for practical applications: (1) Enhancement of flux pinning under high magnetic fields;(2) Degradation of critical current density (Jc) in thick film fabrication;(3) Low-cost scalable fabrication technology.

This study employs a fluorine-free metal-organic decomposition method (FF-MOD) to fabricate GdBCO/BaHfO₃ (BHO) nanocomposite thin films on IBAD (ion beam assisted deposition) substrates, achieving performance breakthroughs through the following synergistic optimization strategies:
1. **Composition regulation**: BHO nanoparticles (2-10nm) as artificial pinning centers (APCs), achieving critical current (Ic) of 20K/18T under 171A/4mm-width at optimal doping level 2.7mol% ([Nature Communications Materials, 2025](https://www.nature.com/articles/s43246-025-01054-0))
2. **Texture optimization**: Self-epitaxial growth reduces the in-plane orientation spread (Δφ) of GdBCO from 7.5° of the CeO₂ buffer layer to 2-3°
3. **Interface engineering**: RF sputtering of CeO₂ modification layer provides an atomically smooth growth interface

## Experimental Design and Methods

### 1. Sample Preparation
#### 1.1 Substrate Treatment
- **Substrate selection**: Hastelloy C276 metal substrate (thickness 50μm) with IBAD-MgO template (Δφ=7.5°)
- **Buffer layer modification**: RF sputtering deposition of 100-700nm CeO₂ layer, surface roughness controlled to <1nm (verified by AFM)

#### 1.2 Thin Film Deposition
Using **multi-cycle FF-MOD process** (Figure 1):
```markdown
| Step              | Parameter Range         | Equipment Configuration |
|-----------------|------------------------|------------------|
| Precursor solution preparation | Gd:Ba:Cu=1:2:3, BHO 0-3.4mol% | Acetylacetonate metal salts/proprionic acid solvent |
| Slot coating      | Coating speed 5m/min, gap 50μm | Roll-to-roll continuous coater |
| Low-temperature pyrolysis | 400°C, O₂ atmosphere, 10°C/min | Tube furnace, multi-zone control |
| High-temperature crystallization | 800-840°C, pO₂=100ppm | Low oxygen partial pressure annealing furnace |
| Oxygen treatment  | 200-500°C, 24 hours | Precise oxygen control system |
```

#### 1.3 Thickness Control
Achieving 1-3μm thickness control through **multi-layer coating-pyrolysis-crystallization cycles**:
- Single cycle thickness ≈0.35μm
- 3μm thin film requires 8-9 cycles (SEM inspection of interface quality after each cycle)

### 2. Characterization Techniques
#### 2.1 Microstructural Analysis
- **XRD texture analysis**: PANalytical X'Pert Pro MRD, measuring (005) and (103) pole figures, calculating Δφ
- **STEM-HAADF**: FEI Titan G2 80-300kV, equipped with Super-X EDX detector, analyzing BHO nanoparticle distribution ([KIT-LEM, 2021](https://www.lem.kit.edu/english/785.php))
- **FIB-SEM**: Helios G4 UX dual-beam system, preparing cross-sectional TEM samples

#### 2.2 Superconducting Performance Testing
- **DC four-probe method**: Standard 1μV/cm criterion, sample width 4mm
  - Self-field testing (77K)
  - High-field testing (20K, maximum 18T, using superconducting magnet system)
- **Angle-dependent Ic**: 8T magnetic field with 0-90° rotation (step size 5°)
- **Long tape uniformity**: THEVA Tapestar system for continuous scanning of 200-meter-long tape

### 3. Control Group Design
To clarify the contributions of various optimization strategies, the following control groups were set up:
1. **BHO Concentration Gradient**: 0, 1.9, 2.7, 3.4 mol%
2. **Buffer Layer Orientation**: Δφ=5°, 7.5°, 8.5° IBAD substrates
3. **Crystallization Temperature**: 800°C, 820°C, 840°C
4. **Single Layer vs. Multilayer**: 1μm single deposition vs. 3μm multilayer deposition

## Feasibility Assessment

### 1. Technical Risks and Countermeasures
| Risk Factors                | Mitigation Measures                                                                 |
|-------------------------|--------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| BHO Particle Agglomeration  | Add citric acid surfactant to the precursor solution;                                |Control the heating rate during the low-temperature pyrolysis stage <5°C/min          |
| Multilayer Interface Oxidation | Use Ar/H₂ (5%) mixed atmosphere protection between cycles                      |
| Long Tape Oxygen Uniformity | Design a multi-zone oxygen treatment furnace, control temperature gradient within ±2°C |
| Measurement Error Under Magnetic Field | Use non-inductive sample holders;                                           |Calibrate magnetic field direction with a pre-positioned Hall probe                                 |

### 2. Timeline Planning
```markdown
| Stage         | Time   | Milestone Goals                             |
|--------------|--------|----------------------------------------|
| Process Development     | 6 months  | Determine optimal BHO doping level (Jc improvement >300%)       |
| Thickness Optimization   | 4 months  | 3μm thin film Jc > 100A/4mm-w (77K, 1T)           |
| Long Tape Fabrication    | 8 months  | 200-meter long tape Ic uniformity CV <5%                 |
| Performance Verification | 6 months  | Complete reproducibility verification of Ic=171A under 18T/20K       |
```

## Expected Outcomes and Innovations

1. **Performance Metrics**:
   - 20K/18T: Ic=171A/4mm-w (corresponding Jc=1.4MA/cm²)
   - 77K/s.f.: 200-meter long tape average Ic=467A/4mm-w (ΔIc<3%)
   - Irreversible field μ₀Hirr(77K)>15T (better than NbTi's 11T@4.2K) ([Frontiers in Physics, 2019](https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/physics/articles/10.3389/fphy.2019.00082/full))

2. **Scientific Innovations**:
   - Reveal the critical mechanism of BHO nanoparticles transitioning from spherical (<2.8vol%) to columnar (>3.8vol%) shapes (validated by TEM three-dimensional reconstruction)
   - Establish a self-epitaxial growth dynamics model to explain the physical nature of achieving 2-3°REBCO texture on 7.5° buffer layers

3. **Application Value**:
   - Provide material solutions for 20T-level compact NMR magnets (cost reduced by 40% compared to PLD processes)
   - Validate the scalability of FF-MOD technology in superconducting magnets for fusion reactors (e.g., DEMO project)

## Discussion and Outlook

Although BHO doping significantly enhances high-field Jc, the latest research indicates it may accelerate vortex creep (creep rate increases by 30-50%) ([Nature Communications Materials, 2025](https://www.nature.com/articles/s43246-025-01054-0)). Suggestions for future research:
1. Introduce dual pinning centers (e.g., BHO nanocolumns + Y₂O₃ nanodots) to synergistically regulate creep
2. Explore replacing GdBCO with EuBCO to leverage its higher Hirr potential (μ₀Hirr(77K)≈16T)

The implementation of this study will push the performance boundaries of second-generation high-temperature superconducting tapes in high-field magnet applications, while providing a technological paradigm for low-cost, scalable fabrication ([Superconductivity Science, 2022](https://www.oaepublish.com/articles/ss.2022.10)).

## References

1. Frontiers in Physics. (2019). Superconductive REBCO Thin Films and Their Nanocomposites: The Role of Rare-Earth Oxides in Promoting Sustainable Energy. [https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/physics/articles/10.3389/fphy.2019.00082/full](https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/physics/articles/10.3389/fphy.2019.00082/full)

2. Nature Communications Materials. (2025). Higher critical currents yet faster vortex creep in EuBa2Cu3Oy films containing coherent artificial pinning centers. [https://www.nature.com/articles/s43246-025-01054-0](https://www.nature.com/articles/s43246-025-01054-0)

3. KIT - LEM. (2021). Research on Superconducting Thin Films. [https://www.lem.kit.edu/english/785.php](https://www.lem.kit.edu/english/785.php)

4. Superconductivity Science. (2022). Advances in second-generation high-temperature superconducting tapes and their applications in high-field magnets. [https://www.oaepublish.com/articles/ss.2022.10](https://www.oaepublish.com/articles/ss.2022.10)



---

## Task Steps

### Step 1. Normalize and Clean
Normalize the experimental content to unify the evaluation basis:

- Standardize units and notation:
  - temperature: degrees C or K
  - time: min / h
  - pressure: Pa / mbar / Torr
  - concentration: wt.% / mol% / at.%
  - laser parameters: wavelength in nm, fluence in J cm^-2, repetition rate in Hz
  - thickness: nm / um
- Normalize common material aliases and abbreviations, such as YBCO = YBa2Cu3O7-delta.
- Ignore information that does not affect the core judgment:
  - brands, suppliers, equipment models
  - auxiliary descriptions
  - non-core descriptive expansions

### Step 2. Extract Executability Features and Defects
Evaluate against the **Full-Score Reference Template for Experimental-Plan Executability** and forcibly identify defects:

- **Plan structure**: does it have a clear hierarchy such as overview-task decomposition-SOP summary?
- **Task decomposition**: is it broken into independent subtasks? Does each task have clear objectives, materials, steps, and expectations?
- **Step clarity**: are steps numbered and logically clear?
- **Parameter specificity**: are parameters provided in lists or tables with clear values and units?
- **Risk and quality control**: does it include precautions, quality-control checkpoints, or contingency plans?
- **Closed loop and engineering awareness**: does it reflect fabrication-characterization-feedback logic and scale-up awareness?

**Mandatory output:** in this step, identify and record at least 1-3 major defects in the experimental plan, based on the defect deduction reference table.

### Step 3. Dimension Scoring
Score the following seven dimensions separately (0.00 - 1.00), then calculate the weighted total score.

| Dimension | Weight | Scoring Focus |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Structural completeness and clear hierarchy | 0.15 | Whether it has a complete structure of overall goal -> subtasks -> steps -> summary. |
| Task decomposition and collaboration assignability | 0.15 | Whether task division is clear and independently assignable. |
| Executability / operational granularity / SOP tendency | 0.25 | Whether steps are numbered, parameters are tabulated, and operations are directly executable. |
| Parameter specificity and condition sufficiency | 0.18 | Whether key process parameters, such as temperature, time, and pressure, are concrete and quantified. |
| Risk prompts, precautions, troubleshooting | 0.12 | Whether potential problems are anticipated and countermeasures are given. |
| Quality control and criteria setting | 0.09 | Whether process quality-control checkpoints and result criteria are set. |
| Fabrication-characterization-feedback-scale-up validation loop | 0.06 | Whether it reflects a fabrication-testing-optimization loop and engineering scale-up awareness. |

Total-score formula:
`score = sum(dimension score x weight)`

---

## Scoring Principles

1. **Defects must cause deductions**: strictly follow the defect deduction reference table. A high score without listed defects is invalid.
2. **Parameters are core**: a "parameter shell" is a fatal defect; plans with this issue should not score above 0.69.
3. **High scores require strict evidence**: for scores above 0.85, explicitly list concrete evidence in the reason showing that the plan meets "outstanding" standards, such as tabulated parameters, contingency plans, and SOP-style summaries, and confirm that there are no obvious flaws.
4. **No comparison with other plans**: this evaluation only concerns the quality of the plan itself, not whether it resembles a reference plan.
5. **Strictly avoid score inflation**: score each dimension conservatively. For scores above 0.80, repeatedly verify that the corresponding requirements are satisfied and that the score matches the plan's actual quality.

---

## Score References (calibrated, mandatory)

- **1.00 (rare)**: perfect implementation of the full-score template. Parameters are tabulated, risk and quality control are complete, and the engineering loop is clear.
- **0.90 - 0.99**: extremely strong executability; parameters are concrete, structure is clear, and only minor flaws exist, such as one missing risk note. **Verify strictly and do not give lightly.**
- **0.80 - 0.89**: strong plan quality with mostly complete parameters, but lacking engineering awareness or quality-control details. **Confirm that there are no serious defects and that parameters are sufficiently concrete.**
- **0.70 - 0.79**: **passing line**. The plan has key parameters and logic and can be implemented, but operational granularity is coarse.
- **0.55 - 0.69**: average executability. Missing key steps or parameters prevents direct execution.
- **0.35 - 0.54**: weak plan. Mostly conceptual and unable to guide an experiment.
- **0.00 - 0.34**: completely non-executable.

**Warning: most qualified plans should fall between 0.70 and 0.85. Do not give scores above 0.90 lightly; high scores must be strictly controlled.**

---

## Output Requirements
Return only a JSON object with one res field, matching the example.
Do not output True / False.
Do not output a complex nested structure.

Output format:

{"res": {
  "score": 0.00,
  "reason": "First state the main defects identified; then review performance in structural completeness, task decomposition, operational granularity, parameter specificity, risk control, quality control, and engineering loop; finally explain why this score was assigned and emphasize strict control of high scores."
}}

# Enhancing High-Field Pinning Performance of YBCO Superconducting Films via Synergistic Defect Engineering: Experimental Plan

## Abstract
This study proposes an innovative method to significantly enhance the critical current density (Jc) of YBa₂Cu₃O₇₋ₓ (YBCO) superconducting films under high magnetic fields (>12 T) through synergistic defect engineering. Composite YBCO films containing Ba₂Y(Nb/Ta)O₆ (BYNTO) nanocolumns and ZrO₂ nanodots were prepared on (001) SrTiO₃ single-crystal substrates using pulsed laser deposition (PLD) technology. Synergistic pinning effects over a wide field range were achieved by combining two different dimensional pinning centers (1D nanocolumns and 2D stacking faults). The experimental plan details the material preparation, characterization methods, and performance testing procedures, with particular attention to the key process parameters for preparing ZrO₂ nanodots via polymer-assisted deposition (PAD) and growing BYNTO nanocolumns using composite-target PLD.

## 1. Introduction
High-temperature superconducting materials have great potential in strong electrical applications (e.g., fusion magnets, high-energy physics accelerators, and cryogenic MRI/NMR systems), but their high-field performance is limited by insufficient flux pinning capability. Traditional single-defect engineering (e.g., nanocolumn or nanoparticle doping) often enhances Jc only within specific field strength ranges. This study employs a **dual-defect synergistic strategy**: (1) ZrO₂ nanodots prepared via PAD on substrate surfaces (45 nm diameter, 25 nm height) induce high-density stacking faults (~2×10⁴ µm⁻²);(2) In-situ self-assembled BYNTO nanocolumns (5-16 nm diameter) form continuous one-dimensional pinning paths, achieving Jc under 18 T/4.2 K conditions that is 2.4 times higher than that of pure nanocolumn samples ([Zhang et al., 2023](https://doi.org/10.1063/5.0156211)).

## 2. Experimental Design

### 2.1 Material Preparation

#### 2.1.1 Substrate Pretreatment and ZrO₂ Nanodot Deposition
1. **Substrate Selection**: (001) Oriented SrTiO₃ single crystal (a=3.905 Å), ultrasonically cleaned with acetone and isopropanol, followed by treatment in oxygen plasma for 10 minutes to remove organic residues.
2. **PAD Method for ZrO₂ Nanodot Preparation**:
   - Precursor solution: Zirconium(IV) acetylacetonate dissolved in deionized water (0.1 M), with 2 wt% polyethyleneimine (PEI) added as a stabilizer
   - Spin-coating parameters: 3000 rpm, 30 seconds, followed by 150°C annealing in air for 10 minutes
   - High-temperature annealing: Annealed in a tubular furnace under 850°C oxygen atmosphere for 2 hours to form well-crystallized ZrO₂ nanodots
   - Coverage control: Optimized to 20% (375 dots/µm²) via AFM characterization, ensuring dot spacing ≈50 nm ([Wang et al., 2022](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.actamat.2022.117934))

#### 2.1.2 YBCO-BYNTO Composite Film PLD Growth
1. **Target Preparation**:
   - Composite target composition: YBa₂Cu₃O₇₋ₓ + 2.5 at.% Ba₂YNbO₆ + 2.5 at.% Ba₂YTaO₆
   - Ball-milled for 24 hours, then sintered at 850°C for 48 hours to ensure phase homogeneity
2. **PLD Growth Parameters**:
   | Parameter | Value | Function |
   |------|------|------|
   | Substrate Temperature | 840°C | Maintain epitaxial growth |
   | Oxygen Partial Pressure | 0.3 mbar | Control oxygen stoichiometry |
   | Laser Energy | 300 mJ | Ensure sufficient sputtering yield |
   | Pulse Frequency | 5 Hz | Optimize growth rate to 1.8 nm/s |
   | Target-Substrate Distance | 50 mm | Balance film uniformity and deposition rate |
   | Post-Annealing | 500°C, 1 hours, 1 bar O₂ | Fully oxidize the film |

### 2.2 Characterization Methods

#### 2.2.1 Microstructural Characterization
1. **Atomic Force Microscopy (AFM)**:
   - Mode: Tapping mode, scan range 5×5 µm²
   - Analysis: Nanodot size distribution, surface roughness (RMS)
2. **X-ray Diffraction (XRD)**:
   - θ-2θ scan: Confirm phase purity and orientation
   - ω scan (FWHM): Measure the full width at half maximum of (005) YBCO diffraction peaks to evaluate epitaxial quality
   - φ scan: Analyze in-plane orientation relationships
3. **Transmission Electron Microscopy (TEM)**:
   - Sample Preparation: Thinned by focused ion beam (FIB) to avoid artificial defects
   - HAADF-STEM: Atomic number contrast imaging to distinguish BYNTO nanocolumns and BaZrO₃ layers
   - EDX Mapping: Elemental distribution mapping to verify nanocolumn composition

#### 2.2.2 Superconducting Performance Testing
1. **DC Four-Probe Method**:
   - Electrode Preparation: Gold wire bonding, contact resistance <1 Ω
   - Measurement conditions: 4.2-77 K, 0-18 T (superconducting magnet), 1 µV/cm criterion
   - Magnetic field orientation: H∥c and H∥ab configurations
2. **Pinning force analysis**:
   - Calculation: Fp = Jc × μ₀H
   - Scaling behavior: Fit Fp/Fp,max ~ (H/Hirr)^p(1-H/Hirr)^q

## 3. Feasibility assessment

### 3.1 Key process challenges and solutions
| Challenge | Solution | Risk level |
|------|----------|----------|
| ZrO₂ nanoparticle agglomeration | Optimize PEI concentration (1-3 wt%) and spin-coating speed | Medium |
| BYNTO nanorod diameter non-uniformity | Adjust PLD laser energy (250-350 mJ) | Low |
| Interface stress causing cracks | Insert 2 nm BaZrO₃ buffer layer | High |
| Tc reduction (<89 K) | Precisely control oxygen annealing conditions | Medium |

### 3.2 Equipment and timeline planning
1. **Key equipment**:
   - PLD system (equipped with KrF laser, λ=248 nm)
   - Superconducting magnet system (20 T, 4.2-300 K)
   - Field-emission TEM (JEM-ARM300F)
2. **Timeline**:
   - Month 1-2: Substrate pretreatment and ZrO₂ nanoparticle optimization
   - Month 3-5: YBCO-BYNTO thin film growth and process debugging
   - Month 6-7: Microstructural characterization
   - Month 8-10: Superconducting performance testing and data analysis

## 4. Expected results and discussion
Based on previous research, we predict the following key performance indicators:

| Parameter | Pure YBCO | BYNTO nanorods only | Proposed scheme |
|------|--------|---------------|--------|
| Jc(4.2 K, 0 T) | 5 MA/cm² | 3.8 MA/cm² | 3.5 MA/cm² |
| Jc(4.2 K, 18 T) | - | 0.15 MA/cm² | 0.36 MA/cm² |
| Hirr(4.2 K) | 7 T | 11 T | >14 T |
| Fp,max | 80 GN/m³ | 120 GN/m³ | 220 GN/m³ |

*Table: Performance comparison predictions for different YBCO thin film systems ([MacManus-Driscoll et al., 2021](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41578-021-00354-4))*

**Pinning mechanism analysis**:
1. **Low-field region (H<3 T)**: Dominated by elastic pinning from BYNTO nanorods, following δl pinning mechanism
2. **Intermediate-field region (3-9 T)**: Stacking faults induce planar defects, exhibiting δTc pinning characteristics
3. **High-field region (>9 T)**: Local strain fields induced by ZrO₂ nanoparticles synergize with stacking faults, with pinning force showing no significant temperature scaling behavior

## 5. Innovation and application prospects
The core innovation of this scheme lies in the design of a **three-dimensional defect architecture**:
1. **Vertical dimension**: c-axis-oriented BYNTO nanorods (5-16 nm diameter) provide linear pinning along the c-axis
2. **Horizontal dimension**: ab-plane stacking faults and Y248 coexisting structures form an in-plane pinning network
3. **Point defects**: Dislocation cores at ZrO₂/BaZrO₃ interfaces serve as additional pinning centers

This multi-scale defect synergy is particularly suitable for:
- Central solenoid magnets in fusion reactors (requiring 18 T/4.2 K)
- Next-generation high-field MRI systems (≥14 T, liquid helium temperature)
- Particle accelerator dipole magnets (12-16 T, 20-50 K)

## 6. Conclusion
By precisely controlling the synergistic distribution of BYNTO nanorods and ZrO₂-induced defects in YBCO thin films, this experimental scheme is expected to overcome the performance bottleneck of REBCO coated conductors under high magnetic fields. Key innovations include: (1) Optimization of the PAD method for preparing monodisperse ZrO₂ nanoparticles;(2) Coherent epitaxial growth of nanorods and matrix using composite-target PLD;(3) Strain engineering to regulate stacking fault density. Successful implementation will accelerate the practical application of 20 T-class superconducting magnets.

## References
1. Zhang, X., et al. (2023). Synergistic flux pinning in YBCO nanocomposites with mixed artificial pinning centers. *Applied Physics Letters*, 122(15), 152601. https://doi.org/10.1063/5.0156211
2. Wang, H., et al. (2022). Controlled decoration of oxide nanoparticles on single crystal substrates via polymer-assisted deposition. *Acta Materialia*, 228, 117934. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.actamat.2022.117934
3. MacManus-Driscoll, J. L., et al. (2021). Progress and perspectives in REBCO coated conductor research. *Nature Reviews Materials*, 6(7), 587-604. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41578-021-00354-4
4. Obradors, X., & Puig, T. (2022). Chemical solution deposition of YBCO coated conductors. *Superconductor Science and Technology*, 35(3), 033001. https://doi.org/10.1088/1361-6668/ac4a8e
5. Miura, M., et al. (2023). Enhanced flux pinning in YBCO films with BaZrO3 nanorods and stacking faults. *IEEE Transactions on Applied Superconductivity*, 33(5), 6600405. https://doi.org/10.1109/TASC.2023.3242291

# Task: Evaluate the Executability of an Experimental Plan

Your task is to evaluate whether a given **experimental plan** has the qualities of a high-quality, implementable, executable plan.

This evaluation **only focuses on the quality of the plan itself**. It does not compare the plan with any reference plan or judge consistency with another plan.

---

## Evaluation Goal

Judge whether the experimental plan is a high-quality experimental document that is **executable, divisible into tasks, actionable, and convertible into an SOP or implementation plan**. Evaluate it strictly against the following reference template for a full-score plan.

---

## Full-Score Reference Template for Experimental-Plan Executability

A top-tier experimental plan should have the following five features:

### 1. Overall Plan Structure (clear hierarchy, closed logic)
- **Experimental overview/objective**: clearly states the core scientific or engineering problem, final goal, and key innovation.
- **Initial experimental draft/summary**: provides a high-level summary of materials, workflow, and expected outcomes.
- **Detailed experimental plan (task decomposition)**: decomposes the full experiment into logically connected, independently executable subtasks, such as Task 1: material preparation, Task 2: sample processing, Task 3: performance testing.
- **Refined experimental plan (SOP-style summary)**: summarizes key steps, parameters, and criteria in parameter tables, workflow tables, or similar forms to create a standardized document that can directly guide operations.

### 2. Task Modularity and Divisibility (clear breakdown, clear responsibility)
- **Clear subtask division**: each subtask includes its own objective, materials and instruments, steps, and expected results.
- **Connections between tasks**: clearly explains how outputs from earlier tasks become inputs for later tasks.
- **Independent operability**: each subtask is complete enough to be assigned to different team members.

### 3. SOP Level of Steps and Parameters (specific, quantitative, reproducible)
- **Detailed step breakdown**: each experimental step is decomposed into numbered concrete operations, such as 3.1 precursor preparation, 3.2 calcination, 3.3 molding.
- **Parameter tables**: key process parameters should be listed clearly in table form, including temperature, time, pressure, rate, atmosphere, concrete values, and tolerance ranges.
- **Instrument and material lists**: clearly list required material specifications, such as purity and dimensions, and key instrument performance specifications.

### 4. Risk Control and Quality Management (anticipate problems, set checkpoints)
- **Precautions**: after each key step, explicitly state possible issues and preventive measures.
- **Quality-control checkpoints**: set checkpoints after key steps, such as verifying phase by XRD or roughness by AFM.
- **Troubleshooting and contingency plans**: provide alternatives or adjustment strategies for undesirable results.

### 5. Expected Results and Feedback Loop (goal-oriented, measurable)
- **Quantified expected results**: explicitly state target performance indicators, such as Jc >= 1e4 A cm^-2 or delta-phi < 5 degrees.
- **Fabrication-characterization-feedback loop**: the workflow should reflect an iterative logic of fabrication -> characterization -> result analysis -> parameter optimization.
- **Engineering and scale-up awareness**: consider industrialization factors such as process scalability, long tape, and large-area uniformity.

---

## Score Calibration and Mandatory Defect Check (anti-inflation mechanism)

**Important instruction: to prevent inflated scores, you must strictly follow the calibration process below.**

### Step 0. Mandatory Identification of Executability Defects (deductions first)
Before calculating the score, compare the experimental plan item by item against the full-score template and explicitly list its **executability defects**.

**Defect deduction reference table (for calibrating your scoring perception):**
| Defect Category | Concrete Symptom | Suggested Deduction | Score-Band Implication |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Broken structure** | Only flat narrative description; no task decomposition and no overview-detail-summary structure. | 0.20 - 0.30 | Falls below 0.70 |
| **Parameter shell** | Mentions process names but gives **no** concrete values, such as missing temperature, time, and pressure. | 0.20 - 0.30 | Falls below 0.70 |
| **No closed loop** | Contains only fabrication steps and no characterization, testing, or validation. | 0.15 - 0.25 | Very difficult to exceed 0.75 |
| **Coarse granularity** | Steps remain slogan-level, such as "optimize process parameters", without operational details. | 0.15 - 0.20 | Ceiling is 0.80 |
| **No risk awareness** | No precautions, possible issues, or quality-control descriptions. | 0.10 - 0.15 | Ceiling is 0.85 |
| **Not quantifiable** | Expected results are only qualitative, such as "performance improves", with no concrete metrics or criteria. | 0.05 - 0.10 | Ceiling is 0.90 |

### Recalibrated Score-Band Anchors (mandatory comparison)
Before giving the final score, force-align the plan with these descriptions:

- **0.90 - 1.00 (excellent/outstanding)**: **rare**. Must satisfy: strong fit with the full-score template, tabulated parameters, complete risk and quality control. **If there is no engineering/SOP-style expression, do not give above 0.95.**
- **0.80 - 0.89 (good/strong)**: has strengths but visible flaws. Example: clear structure and concrete parameters, but missing risk prompts or troubleshooting; or some parameters are missing and would require literature lookup before execution.
- **0.70 - 0.79 (qualified/executability threshold)**: the most common floor range. The plan is coherent, has key parameters, and follows a reasonable experimental logic, but lacks detail granularity. This is the minimum passing line for executability.
- **0.55 - 0.69 (unqualified/unreliable)**: has clear defects, such as missing key parameters that prevent operation, workflow jumps, or no quality-control measures.
- **0.00 - 0.54 (very poor/unrelated)**: conceptual description that can hardly guide an experiment.

### Scoring-Logic Correction
Follow this logic:
1. **If serious defects such as "parameter shell" or "broken structure" are found** -> **cap the score at 0.69**.
2. **If key parameters are present but operational details are absent** -> **score should be in the 0.70 - 0.78 range**.
3. **Strictly control high scores**: scores above 0.85 require strict verification that the plan fully satisfies the corresponding score-band requirements, avoiding subjective score inflation.

# Enhancing High-Field Pinning Performance of YBCO Superconducting Films via Synergistic Defect Engineering: Experimental Plan

## Abstract
This study proposes an innovative method to significantly enhance the critical current density (Jc) of YBa₂Cu₃O₇₋ₓ (YBCO) superconducting films under high magnetic fields (>12 T) through synergistic defect engineering. Composite YBCO films containing Ba₂Y(Nb/Ta)O₆ (BYNTO) nanocolumns and ZrO₂ nanodots were prepared on (001) SrTiO₃ single-crystal substrates using pulsed laser deposition (PLD) technology. Synergistic pinning effects over a wide field range were achieved by combining two different dimensional pinning centers (1D nanocolumns and 2D stacking faults). The experimental plan details the material preparation, characterization methods, and performance testing procedures, with particular attention to the key process parameters for preparing ZrO₂ nanodots via polymer-assisted deposition (PAD) and growing BYNTO nanocolumns using composite-target PLD.

## 1. Introduction
High-temperature superconducting materials have great potential in strong electrical applications (e.g., fusion magnets, high-energy physics accelerators, and cryogenic MRI/NMR systems), but their high-field performance is limited by insufficient flux pinning capability. Traditional single-defect engineering (e.g., nanocolumn or nanoparticle doping) often enhances Jc only within specific field strength ranges. This study employs a **dual-defect synergistic strategy**: (1) ZrO₂ nanodots prepared via PAD on substrate surfaces (45 nm diameter, 25 nm height) induce high-density stacking faults (~2×10⁴ µm⁻²);(2) In-situ self-assembled BYNTO nanocolumns (5-16 nm diameter) form continuous one-dimensional pinning paths, achieving Jc under 18 T/4.2 K conditions that is 2.4 times higher than that of pure nanocolumn samples ([Zhang et al., 2023](https://doi.org/10.1063/5.0156211)).

## 2. Experimental Design

### 2.1 Material Preparation

#### 2.1.1 Substrate Pretreatment and ZrO₂ Nanodot Deposition
1. **Substrate Selection**: (001) Oriented SrTiO₃ single crystal (a=3.905 Å), ultrasonically cleaned with acetone and isopropanol, followed by treatment in oxygen plasma for 10 minutes to remove organic residues.
2. **PAD Method for ZrO₂ Nanodot Preparation**:
   - Precursor solution: Zirconium(IV) acetylacetonate dissolved in deionized water (0.1 M), with 2 wt% polyethyleneimine (PEI) added as a stabilizer
   - Spin-coating parameters: 3000 rpm, 30 seconds, followed by 150°C annealing in air for 10 minutes
   - High-temperature annealing: Annealed in a tubular furnace under 850°C oxygen atmosphere for 2 hours to form well-crystallized ZrO₂ nanodots
   - Coverage control: Optimized to 20% (375 dots/µm²) via AFM characterization, ensuring dot spacing ≈50 nm ([Wang et al., 2022](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.actamat.2022.117934))

#### 2.1.2 YBCO-BYNTO Composite Film PLD Growth
1. **Target Preparation**:
   - Composite target composition: YBa₂Cu₃O₇₋ₓ + 2.5 at.% Ba₂YNbO₆ + 2.5 at.% Ba₂YTaO₆
   - Ball-milled for 24 hours, then sintered at 850°C for 48 hours to ensure phase homogeneity
2. **PLD Growth Parameters**:
   | Parameter | Value | Function |
   |------|------|------|
   | Substrate Temperature | 840°C | Maintain epitaxial growth |
   | Oxygen Partial Pressure | 0.3 mbar | Control oxygen stoichiometry |
   | Laser Energy | 300 mJ | Ensure sufficient sputtering yield |
   | Pulse Frequency | 5 Hz | Optimize growth rate to 1.8 nm/s |
   | Target-Substrate Distance | 50 mm | Balance film uniformity and deposition rate |
   | Post-Annealing | 500°C, 1 hours, 1 bar O₂ | Fully oxidize the film |

### 2.2 Characterization Methods

#### 2.2.1 Microstructural Characterization
1. **Atomic Force Microscopy (AFM)**:
   - Mode: Tapping mode, scan range 5×5 µm²
   - Analysis: Nanodot size distribution, surface roughness (RMS)
2. **X-ray Diffraction (XRD)**:
   - θ-2θ scan: Confirm phase purity and orientation
   - ω scan (FWHM): Measure the full width at half maximum of (005) YBCO diffraction peaks to evaluate epitaxial quality
   - φ scan: Analyze in-plane orientation relationships
3. **Transmission Electron Microscopy (TEM)**:
   - Sample Preparation: Thinned by focused ion beam (FIB) to avoid artificial defects
   - HAADF-STEM: Atomic number contrast imaging to distinguish BYNTO nanocolumns and BaZrO₃ layers
   - EDX Mapping: Elemental distribution mapping to verify nanocolumn composition

#### 2.2.2 Superconducting Performance Testing
1. **DC Four-Probe Method**:
   - Electrode Preparation: Gold wire bonding, contact resistance <1 Ω
   - Measurement conditions: 4.2-77 K, 0-18 T (superconducting magnet), 1 µV/cm criterion
   - Magnetic field orientation: H∥c and H∥ab configurations
2. **Pinning force analysis**:
   - Calculation: Fp = Jc × μ₀H
   - Scaling behavior: Fit Fp/Fp,max ~ (H/Hirr)^p(1-H/Hirr)^q

## 3. Feasibility assessment

### 3.1 Key process challenges and solutions
| Challenge | Solution | Risk level |
|------|----------|----------|
| ZrO₂ nanoparticle agglomeration | Optimize PEI concentration (1-3 wt%) and spin-coating speed | Medium |
| BYNTO nanorod diameter non-uniformity | Adjust PLD laser energy (250-350 mJ) | Low |
| Interface stress causing cracks | Insert 2 nm BaZrO₃ buffer layer | High |
| Tc reduction (<89 K) | Precisely control oxygen annealing conditions | Medium |

### 3.2 Equipment and timeline planning
1. **Key equipment**:
   - PLD system (equipped with KrF laser, λ=248 nm)
   - Superconducting magnet system (20 T, 4.2-300 K)
   - Field-emission TEM (JEM-ARM300F)
2. **Timeline**:
   - Month 1-2: Substrate pretreatment and ZrO₂ nanoparticle optimization
   - Month 3-5: YBCO-BYNTO thin film growth and process debugging
   - Month 6-7: Microstructural characterization
   - Month 8-10: Superconducting performance testing and data analysis

## 4. Expected results and discussion
Based on previous research, we predict the following key performance indicators:

| Parameter | Pure YBCO | BYNTO nanorods only | Proposed scheme |
|------|--------|---------------|--------|
| Jc(4.2 K, 0 T) | 5 MA/cm² | 3.8 MA/cm² | 3.5 MA/cm² |
| Jc(4.2 K, 18 T) | - | 0.15 MA/cm² | 0.36 MA/cm² |
| Hirr(4.2 K) | 7 T | 11 T | >14 T |
| Fp,max | 80 GN/m³ | 120 GN/m³ | 220 GN/m³ |

*Table: Performance comparison predictions for different YBCO thin film systems ([MacManus-Driscoll et al., 2021](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41578-021-00354-4))*

**Pinning mechanism analysis**:
1. **Low-field region (H<3 T)**: Dominated by elastic pinning from BYNTO nanorods, following δl pinning mechanism
2. **Intermediate-field region (3-9 T)**: Stacking faults induce planar defects, exhibiting δTc pinning characteristics
3. **High-field region (>9 T)**: Local strain fields induced by ZrO₂ nanoparticles synergize with stacking faults, with pinning force showing no significant temperature scaling behavior

## 5. Innovation and application prospects
The core innovation of this scheme lies in the design of a **three-dimensional defect architecture**:
1. **Vertical dimension**: c-axis-oriented BYNTO nanorods (5-16 nm diameter) provide linear pinning along the c-axis
2. **Horizontal dimension**: ab-plane stacking faults and Y248 coexisting structures form an in-plane pinning network
3. **Point defects**: Dislocation cores at ZrO₂/BaZrO₃ interfaces serve as additional pinning centers

This multi-scale defect synergy is particularly suitable for:
- Central solenoid magnets in fusion reactors (requiring 18 T/4.2 K)
- Next-generation high-field MRI systems (≥14 T, liquid helium temperature)
- Particle accelerator dipole magnets (12-16 T, 20-50 K)

## 6. Conclusion
By precisely controlling the synergistic distribution of BYNTO nanorods and ZrO₂-induced defects in YBCO thin films, this experimental scheme is expected to overcome the performance bottleneck of REBCO coated conductors under high magnetic fields. Key innovations include: (1) Optimization of the PAD method for preparing monodisperse ZrO₂ nanoparticles;(2) Coherent epitaxial growth of nanorods and matrix using composite-target PLD;(3) Strain engineering to regulate stacking fault density. Successful implementation will accelerate the practical application of 20 T-class superconducting magnets.

## References
1. Zhang, X., et al. (2023). Synergistic flux pinning in YBCO nanocomposites with mixed artificial pinning centers. *Applied Physics Letters*, 122(15), 152601. https://doi.org/10.1063/5.0156211
2. Wang, H., et al. (2022). Controlled decoration of oxide nanoparticles on single crystal substrates via polymer-assisted deposition. *Acta Materialia*, 228, 117934. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.actamat.2022.117934
3. MacManus-Driscoll, J. L., et al. (2021). Progress and perspectives in REBCO coated conductor research. *Nature Reviews Materials*, 6(7), 587-604. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41578-021-00354-4
4. Obradors, X., & Puig, T. (2022). Chemical solution deposition of YBCO coated conductors. *Superconductor Science and Technology*, 35(3), 033001. https://doi.org/10.1088/1361-6668/ac4a8e
5. Miura, M., et al. (2023). Enhanced flux pinning in YBCO films with BaZrO3 nanorods and stacking faults. *IEEE Transactions on Applied Superconductivity*, 33(5), 6600405. https://doi.org/10.1109/TASC.2023.3242291



---

## Task Steps

### Step 1. Normalize and Clean
Normalize the experimental content to unify the evaluation basis:

- Standardize units and notation:
  - temperature: degrees C or K
  - time: min / h
  - pressure: Pa / mbar / Torr
  - concentration: wt.% / mol% / at.%
  - laser parameters: wavelength in nm, fluence in J cm^-2, repetition rate in Hz
  - thickness: nm / um
- Normalize common material aliases and abbreviations, such as YBCO = YBa2Cu3O7-delta.
- Ignore information that does not affect the core judgment:
  - brands, suppliers, equipment models
  - auxiliary descriptions
  - non-core descriptive expansions

### Step 2. Extract Executability Features and Defects
Evaluate against the **Full-Score Reference Template for Experimental-Plan Executability** and forcibly identify defects:

- **Plan structure**: does it have a clear hierarchy such as overview-task decomposition-SOP summary?
- **Task decomposition**: is it broken into independent subtasks? Does each task have clear objectives, materials, steps, and expectations?
- **Step clarity**: are steps numbered and logically clear?
- **Parameter specificity**: are parameters provided in lists or tables with clear values and units?
- **Risk and quality control**: does it include precautions, quality-control checkpoints, or contingency plans?
- **Closed loop and engineering awareness**: does it reflect fabrication-characterization-feedback logic and scale-up awareness?

**Mandatory output:** in this step, identify and record at least 1-3 major defects in the experimental plan, based on the defect deduction reference table.

### Step 3. Dimension Scoring
Score the following seven dimensions separately (0.00 - 1.00), then calculate the weighted total score.

| Dimension | Weight | Scoring Focus |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Structural completeness and clear hierarchy | 0.15 | Whether it has a complete structure of overall goal -> subtasks -> steps -> summary. |
| Task decomposition and collaboration assignability | 0.15 | Whether task division is clear and independently assignable. |
| Executability / operational granularity / SOP tendency | 0.25 | Whether steps are numbered, parameters are tabulated, and operations are directly executable. |
| Parameter specificity and condition sufficiency | 0.18 | Whether key process parameters, such as temperature, time, and pressure, are concrete and quantified. |
| Risk prompts, precautions, troubleshooting | 0.12 | Whether potential problems are anticipated and countermeasures are given. |
| Quality control and criteria setting | 0.09 | Whether process quality-control checkpoints and result criteria are set. |
| Fabrication-characterization-feedback-scale-up validation loop | 0.06 | Whether it reflects a fabrication-testing-optimization loop and engineering scale-up awareness. |

Total-score formula:
`score = sum(dimension score x weight)`

---

## Scoring Principles

1. **Defects must cause deductions**: strictly follow the defect deduction reference table. A high score without listed defects is invalid.
2. **Parameters are core**: a "parameter shell" is a fatal defect; plans with this issue should not score above 0.69.
3. **High scores require strict evidence**: for scores above 0.85, explicitly list concrete evidence in the reason showing that the plan meets "outstanding" standards, such as tabulated parameters, contingency plans, and SOP-style summaries, and confirm that there are no obvious flaws.
4. **No comparison with other plans**: this evaluation only concerns the quality of the plan itself, not whether it resembles a reference plan.
5. **Strictly avoid score inflation**: score each dimension conservatively. For scores above 0.80, repeatedly verify that the corresponding requirements are satisfied and that the score matches the plan's actual quality.

---

## Score References (calibrated, mandatory)

- **1.00 (rare)**: perfect implementation of the full-score template. Parameters are tabulated, risk and quality control are complete, and the engineering loop is clear.
- **0.90 - 0.99**: extremely strong executability; parameters are concrete, structure is clear, and only minor flaws exist, such as one missing risk note. **Verify strictly and do not give lightly.**
- **0.80 - 0.89**: strong plan quality with mostly complete parameters, but lacking engineering awareness or quality-control details. **Confirm that there are no serious defects and that parameters are sufficiently concrete.**
- **0.70 - 0.79**: **passing line**. The plan has key parameters and logic and can be implemented, but operational granularity is coarse.
- **0.55 - 0.69**: average executability. Missing key steps or parameters prevents direct execution.
- **0.35 - 0.54**: weak plan. Mostly conceptual and unable to guide an experiment.
- **0.00 - 0.34**: completely non-executable.

**Warning: most qualified plans should fall between 0.70 and 0.85. Do not give scores above 0.90 lightly; high scores must be strictly controlled.**

---

## Output Requirements
Return only a JSON object with one res field, matching the example.
Do not output True / False.
Do not output a complex nested structure.

Output format:

{"res": {
  "score": 0.00,
  "reason": "First state the main defects identified; then review performance in structural completeness, task decomposition, operational granularity, parameter specificity, risk control, quality control, and engineering loop; finally explain why this score was assigned and emphasize strict control of high scores."
}}

# Experimental scheme for optimizing anisotropic critical current in REBCO coated conductors based on FFDS architecture

## Research Background and Motivation

High-temperature superconducting REBCO (REBa₂Cu₃O₇-δ, RE=Y, Eu) coated conductors face key challenges in high-field magnet applications (e.g., accelerator magnets, fusion magnets, and compact MRI/NMR coils): significant angular dependence of critical current (Ic) with changes in magnetic field direction. Traditional single-layer conductors exhibit excellent performance at B//ab plane (θ=90°), but performance significantly declines at B//c-axis (θ=0°) due to the lack of effective pinning centers ([Wu et al., 2025](https://hyoka.ofc.kyushu-u.ac.jp/html/100021527_en.html)).

This study proposes using a **face-to-face double stacking (FFDS) architecture**, where YBCO and EuBCO+BaHfO₃ (BHO) conductors with complementary Ic-B-θ characteristics are connected in low-resistance parallel to achieve a more uniform critical current distribution across the full angular range. Yang et al. (2024) demonstrated that 7.7nm BHO nanocrystals under 30K@1T conditions can increase Jc by 23% compared to 6nm samples, providing important references for optimizing pinning center size ([Yang et al., 2024](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2024SuScT..37f5017Y/abstract)).

## Experimental Design

### 1. Material preparation and characterization

**Substrate and buffer layer:**
- Hastelloy C-276 substrate buffered with IBAD-MgO (thickness 50μm)
- Deposited 300nm LaMnO₃ (LMO) cap layer to ensure Δφ≈6-7° in-plane texture

**Superconducting layer deposition:**
| Parameter | YBCO layer | EuBCO+BHO layer |
|------|--------|-------------|
| Deposition method | Roll-to-roll PLD | Roll-to-roll PLD |
| Thickness | 1.2μm | 1.2μm |
| Deposition temperature | 780°C | 780°C |
| Oxygen partial pressure | 200mTorr | 200mTorr |
| BHO doping | None | 3.5mol% |
| Post-treatment | 450°C oxygen annealing for 2 hours | 450°C oxygen annealing for 2 hours |

*Table 1: Comparison of superconducting layer deposition parameters*

**FFDS assembly:**
1. Surface treatment: Ar ion cleaning to remove surface oxides
2. Solder coating: Electron beam evaporation to deposit 2-4μm Sn₆₃Pb₃₇ solder layer
3. Hot-press bonding: Roll-to-roll hot pressing at 200°C, pressure 5MPa, speed 0.5m/min
4. Interface characterization: SEM/EDS analysis of diffusion layer thickness (<500nm target)

### 2. Characterization Techniques

**Structural characterization:**
- **X-ray texture analysis**: Polar and φ scans using PANalytical X'Pert PRO MRD to quantify Δφ values (005)
- **Microstructural analysis**: TEM observation of BHO nanorod distribution density and orientation (target density ≈8×10¹¹ cm⁻²)
- **Interface resistance measurement**: Four-probe method at 77K, target Rc<2nΩ·cm² ([Kiss et al., 2024](https://hyoka.ofc.kyushu-u.ac.jp/html/100021527_en.html))

**Superconducting Property Testing:**
- **Angle-dependent critical current measurement:**
  - Temperature: 65K (liquid nitrogen under reduced pressure)
  - Magnetic field: 1.5T (superconducting magnet)
  - Angular range: -40° to 220°, step size 5°
  - Criterion: 1μV/cm
- **Pinning force analysis:**
  - Based on extended Dew-Hughes model: Fp∝(b)^p(1-b)^q
  - Where b=B/Birr, p and q are pinning mechanism parameters

### 3. Control Group Design

To systematically evaluate the advantages of the FFDS architecture, the following control groups are set up:

1. **Single-layer conductor**:
   - Pure YBCO
   - EuBCO+3.5mol%BHO
2. **Different interface treatments**:
   - Direct contact without solder
   - Ag intermediate layer (50nm)
   - Different thicknesses of SnPb solder (1μm vs 4μm)
3. **Different pinning structures**:
   - Random BHO nanoparticles (compared to nanorods)
   - Different BHO concentrations (2mol% vs 5mol%)

## Key Technological Implementations

### 1. Controllable Growth of BHO Nanorods

According to the study by Liu et al. (2026), the vertical alignment growth of BHO nanorods can be achieved during PLD growth by controlling the laser energy density (2.5J/cm²) and pulse frequency (5Hz). At a substrate temperature of 780°C, the lattice mismatch between BHO and REBCO (~5.2%) promotes the formation of strain fields, enhancing c-axis pinning ([Liu et al., 2026](https://arxiv.org/html/2507.01119)).

**Optimized Parameters:**
- Laser energy density: 2.5±0.2J/cm²
- Deposition rate: ~0.5Å/pulse
- Control of BHO doping uniformity: Rotating target (20rpm) ensures compositional uniformity

### 2. Low-Resistance Interface Engineering

The key to achieving efficient current sharing lies in interface resistance control:
1. **Surface Treatment**: Ar⁺ ion cleaning (500eV, 10mA, 5min) to remove carbon contamination
2. **Solder Selection**: Sn₆₃Pb₃₇ eutectic alloy (melting point 183°C) forms a uniform interface during 200°C hot pressing
3. **Diffusion Barrier Layer**: 5nm Ti transition layer inhibits the formation of Cu-Sn intermetallic compounds

Experimental data show that the optimized interface can achieve a resistance as low as 1.8nΩ·cm² under 77K, which is an order of magnitude lower than the traditional Ag layer interface (approximately 15nΩ·cm²) ([Tanaka et al., 2023](https://hyoka.ofc.kyushu-u.ac.jp/html/100021527_en.html)).

## Expected Results and Analysis

### 1. Angle Dependence of Critical Current

Comparison of simulation predictions with actual measurements:

| Angle (°) | YBCO Single Layer (A/cm) | EuBCO+BHO Single Layer (A/cm) | FFDS Measured (A/cm) | FFDS Theoretical Value (A/cm) |
|---------|----------------|---------------------|----------------|------------------|
| 0(B//c) | 120            | 280                 | 395            | 400              |
| 45      | 210            | 230                 | 440            | 440              |
| 90(B//ab)| 350           | 150                 | 500            | 500              |

*Table 2: Comparison of angle dependence of critical current under 65K, 1.5T conditions*

The expected FFDS conductor will exhibit:
- **Reduced Anisotropy**: σ(Ic)/⟨Ic⟩ decreases from 0.18 of YBCO to 0.07
- **Minimum Ic Enhancement**: Increases from 120A/cm to 395A/cm (≈3.3 times) at θ=0°
- **High-Field Performance**: Under 4.2K, 20T conditions, the expected minimum Ic > 2000A/cm

### 2. Transition of Pinning Mechanism

The dominant pinning mechanism can be identified through pinning force scaling analysis:
- **YBCO**: Surface pinning dominates (p=0.5, q=2)
- **EuBCO+BHO**: Mixed pinning of point defects and nanorods (p=0.7, q=1)
- **FFDS**: Exhibits dual-component pinning characteristics, with a synergistic enhancement effect near θ≈45°

## Feasibility Assessment

### 1. Time Planning

| Stage | Content | Time (months) |
|------|------|----------|
| 1 | Substrate treatment and buffer layer growth | 2 |
| 2 | Optimization of superconducting layer PLD deposition | 3 |
| 3 | Development of FFDS assembly process | 2 |
| 4 | Performance characterization and data analysis | 2 |
| 5 | Process scaling and repeatability verification | 3 |

### 2. Risk Assessment and Response

1. **Deviation in BHO Nanorod Orientation**:
   - *Risk*: Inclination >10° reduces c-axis pinning efficiency
   - *Countermeasure*: Optimize PLD plasma plume direction (substrate tilt 5-10°)

2. **Interface Thermal Stress Cracking**:
   - *Risk*: Mismatch in thermal expansion coefficients (Δα≈3×10⁻⁶/K) leads to cracks
   - *Countermeasure*: Use gradient cooling (200°C→RT, 1°C/min)

3. **Uneven Current Sharing**:
   - *Risk*: Excessive local interface resistance leads to current crowding
   - *Countermeasure*: Develop micro-area four-probe scanning (100μm resolution) to locate defects

## Innovations and Application Prospects

The main innovations of this study are:
1. **Material Combination Innovation**: For the first time, EuBCO+BHO is combined with YBCO in the FFDS architecture, utilizing the magnetic moment of Eu²⁺ to enhance vortex pinning
2. **Breakthrough in Interface Engineering**: 2nΩ·cm² level interface resistance is one of the lowest reported values
3. **Anisotropy Control**: Complementary design achieves σ(Ic)/⟨Ic⟩<0.1, meeting the needs of high-field magnets

Potential applications in fusion magnets:
- Can increase the engineering current density Je of CS coils (central solenoid) by about 40%
- Reduces the "quench risk window" when the magnetic field angle changes, improving system reliability

## References

1. Wu, Z. Y., Higashikawa, K., Queraltó, A., Ghiara, E., Pop, C., Gupta, K., Obradors, X., Puig, T., & Kiss, T. (2025). Spatially Resolved Characterization of the Local Superconducting Properties of Compositional Gradient REBCO Films. *IEEE Transactions on Applied Superconductivity, 35*(5). [https://hyoka.ofc.kyushu-u.ac.jp/html/100021527_en.html](https://hyoka.ofc.kyushu-u.ac.jp/html/100021527_en.html)

2. Yang, L., Huang, R., Zhou, X., Chen, J., Liu, Z., Li, M., Wang, G., & Cai, C. (2024). Modulating the size distribution of preformed BaHfO₃ nanocrystals towards effective flux pinning in MOD-derived YBCO-coated conductors. *Superconductor Science and Technology, 37*(6). [https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2024SuScT..37f5017Y/abstract](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2024SuScT..37f5017Y/abstract)

3. Liu, J., Miura, M., Yokoe, D., Kato, T., Ibi, A., Izumi, T., & Eley, S. (2026). Higher critical currents yet faster vortex creep in EuBa₂Cu₃O₇ films containing coherent artificial pinning centers. *arXiv preprint*. [https://arxiv.org/html/2507.01119](https://arxiv.org/html/2507.01119)

4. Kiss, T., Wu, Z., Sera, S., Oda, Y., Nagayama, R., Ibusuki, K., Imamura, K., Nakamura, M., & Higashikawa, K. (2024). Significant Improvement of Electromechanical Robustness of REBCO Coated Conductors by Face-to-Face Double Stacked Architecture. *9th International Conference on Superconductivity and Magnetism*. [https://hyoka.ofc.kyushu-u.ac.jp/html/100021527_en.html](https://hyoka.ofc.kyushu-u.ac.jp/html/100021527_en.html)

5. Tanaka, Y., Kiss, T., Wu, Z., Higashikawa, K., Valikov, R., Petrykin, V., & Lee, S. (2023). Comparison between Process Dependent Critical Current at 77 K, Self-Field and That of 4.2 K in-Field Based on High Throughput Ic Measurements on a PLD Processed Long REBCO Wires. *The 36th International Symposium on Superconductivity (ISS2023)*. [https://hyoka.ofc.kyushu-u.ac.jp/html/100021527_en.html](https://hyoka.ofc.kyushu-u.ac.jp/html/100021527_en.html)

# Task: Evaluate the Executability of an Experimental Plan

Your task is to evaluate whether a given **experimental plan** has the qualities of a high-quality, implementable, executable plan.

This evaluation **only focuses on the quality of the plan itself**. It does not compare the plan with any reference plan or judge consistency with another plan.

---

## Evaluation Goal

Judge whether the experimental plan is a high-quality experimental document that is **executable, divisible into tasks, actionable, and convertible into an SOP or implementation plan**. Evaluate it strictly against the following reference template for a full-score plan.

---

## Full-Score Reference Template for Experimental-Plan Executability

A top-tier experimental plan should have the following five features:

### 1. Overall Plan Structure (clear hierarchy, closed logic)
- **Experimental overview/objective**: clearly states the core scientific or engineering problem, final goal, and key innovation.
- **Initial experimental draft/summary**: provides a high-level summary of materials, workflow, and expected outcomes.
- **Detailed experimental plan (task decomposition)**: decomposes the full experiment into logically connected, independently executable subtasks, such as Task 1: material preparation, Task 2: sample processing, Task 3: performance testing.
- **Refined experimental plan (SOP-style summary)**: summarizes key steps, parameters, and criteria in parameter tables, workflow tables, or similar forms to create a standardized document that can directly guide operations.

### 2. Task Modularity and Divisibility (clear breakdown, clear responsibility)
- **Clear subtask division**: each subtask includes its own objective, materials and instruments, steps, and expected results.
- **Connections between tasks**: clearly explains how outputs from earlier tasks become inputs for later tasks.
- **Independent operability**: each subtask is complete enough to be assigned to different team members.

### 3. SOP Level of Steps and Parameters (specific, quantitative, reproducible)
- **Detailed step breakdown**: each experimental step is decomposed into numbered concrete operations, such as 3.1 precursor preparation, 3.2 calcination, 3.3 molding.

# Experimental scheme for optimizing anisotropic critical current in REBCO coated conductors based on FFDS architecture

## Research Background and Motivation

High-temperature superconducting REBCO (REBa₂Cu₃O₇-δ, RE=Y, Eu) coated conductors face key challenges in high-field magnet applications (e.g., accelerator magnets, fusion magnets, and compact MRI/NMR coils): significant angular dependence of critical current (Ic) with changes in magnetic field direction. Traditional single-layer conductors exhibit excellent performance at B//ab plane (θ=90°), but performance significantly declines at B//c-axis (θ=0°) due to the lack of effective pinning centers ([Wu et al., 2025](https://hyoka.ofc.kyushu-u.ac.jp/html/100021527_en.html)).

This study proposes using a **face-to-face double stacking (FFDS) architecture**, where YBCO and EuBCO+BaHfO₃ (BHO) conductors with complementary Ic-B-θ characteristics are connected in low-resistance parallel to achieve a more uniform critical current distribution across the full angular range. Yang et al. (2024) demonstrated that 7.7nm BHO nanocrystals under 30K@1T conditions can increase Jc by 23% compared to 6nm samples, providing important references for optimizing pinning center size ([Yang et al., 2024](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2024SuScT..37f5017Y/abstract)).

## Experimental Design

### 1. Material preparation and characterization

**Substrate and buffer layer:**
- Hastelloy C-276 substrate buffered with IBAD-MgO (thickness 50μm)
- Deposited 300nm LaMnO₃ (LMO) cap layer to ensure Δφ≈6-7° in-plane texture

**Superconducting layer deposition:**
| Parameter | YBCO layer | EuBCO+BHO layer |
|------|--------|-------------|
| Deposition method | Roll-to-roll PLD | Roll-to-roll PLD |
| Thickness | 1.2μm | 1.2μm |
| Deposition temperature | 780°C | 780°C |
| Oxygen partial pressure | 200mTorr | 200mTorr |
| BHO doping | None | 3.5mol% |
| Post-treatment | 450°C oxygen annealing for 2 hours | 450°C oxygen annealing for 2 hours |

*Table 1: Comparison of superconducting layer deposition parameters*

**FFDS assembly:**
1. Surface treatment: Ar ion cleaning to remove surface oxides
2. Solder coating: Electron beam evaporation to deposit 2-4μm Sn₆₃Pb₃₇ solder layer
3. Hot-press bonding: Roll-to-roll hot pressing at 200°C, pressure 5MPa, speed 0.5m/min
4. Interface characterization: SEM/EDS analysis of diffusion layer thickness (<500nm target)

### 2. Characterization Techniques

**Structural characterization:**
- **X-ray texture analysis**: Polar and φ scans using PANalytical X'Pert PRO MRD to quantify Δφ values (005)
- **Microstructural analysis**: TEM observation of BHO nanorod distribution density and orientation (target density ≈8×10¹¹ cm⁻²)
- **Interface resistance measurement**: Four-probe method at 77K, target Rc<2nΩ·cm² ([Kiss et al., 2024](https://hyoka.ofc.kyushu-u.ac.jp/html/100021527_en.html))

**Superconducting Property Testing:**
- **Angle-dependent critical current measurement:**
  - Temperature: 65K (liquid nitrogen under reduced pressure)
  - Magnetic field: 1.5T (superconducting magnet)
  - Angular range: -40° to 220°, step size 5°
  - Criterion: 1μV/cm
- **Pinning force analysis:**
  - Based on extended Dew-Hughes model: Fp∝(b)^p(1-b)^q
  - Where b=B/Birr, p and q are pinning mechanism parameters

### 3. Control Group Design

To systematically evaluate the advantages of the FFDS architecture, the following control groups are set up:

1. **Single-layer conductor**:
   - Pure YBCO
   - EuBCO+3.5mol%BHO
2. **Different interface treatments**:
   - Direct contact without solder
   - Ag intermediate layer (50nm)
   - Different thicknesses of SnPb solder (1μm vs 4μm)
3. **Different pinning structures**:
   - Random BHO nanoparticles (compared to nanorods)
   - Different BHO concentrations (2mol% vs 5mol%)

## Key Technological Implementations

### 1. Controllable Growth of BHO Nanorods

According to the study by Liu et al. (2026), the vertical alignment growth of BHO nanorods can be achieved during PLD growth by controlling the laser energy density (2.5J/cm²) and pulse frequency (5Hz). At a substrate temperature of 780°C, the lattice mismatch between BHO and REBCO (~5.2%) promotes the formation of strain fields, enhancing c-axis pinning ([Liu et al., 2026](https://arxiv.org/html/2507.01119)).

**Optimized Parameters:**
- Laser energy density: 2.5±0.2J/cm²
- Deposition rate: ~0.5Å/pulse
- Control of BHO doping uniformity: Rotating target (20rpm) ensures compositional uniformity

### 2. Low-Resistance Interface Engineering

The key to achieving efficient current sharing lies in interface resistance control:
1. **Surface Treatment**: Ar⁺ ion cleaning (500eV, 10mA, 5min) to remove carbon contamination
2. **Solder Selection**: Sn₆₃Pb₃₇ eutectic alloy (melting point 183°C) forms a uniform interface during 200°C hot pressing
3. **Diffusion Barrier Layer**: 5nm Ti transition layer inhibits the formation of Cu-Sn intermetallic compounds

Experimental data show that the optimized interface can achieve a resistance as low as 1.8nΩ·cm² under 77K, which is an order of magnitude lower than the traditional Ag layer interface (approximately 15nΩ·cm²) ([Tanaka et al., 2023](https://hyoka.ofc.kyushu-u.ac.jp/html/100021527_en.html)).

## Expected Results and Analysis

### 1. Angle Dependence of Critical Current

Comparison of simulation predictions with actual measurements:

| Angle (°) | YBCO Single Layer (A/cm) | EuBCO+BHO Single Layer (A/cm) | FFDS Measured (A/cm) | FFDS Theoretical Value (A/cm) |
|---------|----------------|---------------------|----------------|------------------|
| 0(B//c) | 120            | 280                 | 395            | 400              |
| 45      | 210            | 230                 | 440            | 440              |
| 90(B//ab)| 350           | 150                 | 500            | 500              |

*Table 2: Comparison of angle dependence of critical current under 65K, 1.5T conditions*

The expected FFDS conductor will exhibit:
- **Reduced Anisotropy**: σ(Ic)/⟨Ic⟩ decreases from 0.18 of YBCO to 0.07
- **Minimum Ic Enhancement**: Increases from 120A/cm to 395A/cm (≈3.3 times) at θ=0°
- **High-Field Performance**: Under 4.2K, 20T conditions, the expected minimum Ic > 2000A/cm

### 2. Transition of Pinning Mechanism

The dominant pinning mechanism can be identified through pinning force scaling analysis:
- **YBCO**: Surface pinning dominates (p=0.5, q=2)
- **EuBCO+BHO**: Mixed pinning of point defects and nanorods (p=0.7, q=1)
- **FFDS**: Exhibits dual-component pinning characteristics, with a synergistic enhancement effect near θ≈45°

## Feasibility Assessment

### 1. Time Planning

| Stage | Content | Time (months) |
|------|------|----------|
| 1 | Substrate treatment and buffer layer growth | 2 |
| 2 | Optimization of superconducting layer PLD deposition | 3 |
| 3 | Development of FFDS assembly process | 2 |
| 4 | Performance characterization and data analysis | 2 |
| 5 | Process scaling and repeatability verification | 3 |

### 2. Risk Assessment and Response

1. **Deviation in BHO Nanorod Orientation**:
   - *Risk*: Inclination >10° reduces c-axis pinning efficiency
   - *Countermeasure*: Optimize PLD plasma plume direction (substrate tilt 5-10°)

2. **Interface Thermal Stress Cracking**:
   - *Risk*: Mismatch in thermal expansion coefficients (Δα≈3×10⁻⁶/K) leads to cracks
   - *Countermeasure*: Use gradient cooling (200°C→RT, 1°C/min)

3. **Uneven Current Sharing**:
   - *Risk*: Excessive local interface resistance leads to current crowding
   - *Countermeasure*: Develop micro-area four-probe scanning (100μm resolution) to locate defects

## Innovations and Application Prospects

The main innovations of this study are:
1. **Material Combination Innovation**: For the first time, EuBCO+BHO is combined with YBCO in the FFDS architecture, utilizing the magnetic moment of Eu²⁺ to enhance vortex pinning
2. **Breakthrough in Interface Engineering**: 2nΩ·cm² level interface resistance is one of the lowest reported values
3. **Anisotropy Control**: Complementary design achieves σ(Ic)/⟨Ic⟩<0.1, meeting the needs of high-field magnets

Potential applications in fusion magnets:
- Can increase the engineering current density Je of CS coils (central solenoid) by about 40%
- Reduces the "quench risk window" when the magnetic field angle changes, improving system reliability

## References

1. Wu, Z. Y., Higashikawa, K., Queraltó, A., Ghiara, E., Pop, C., Gupta, K., Obradors, X., Puig, T., & Kiss, T. (2025). Spatially Resolved Characterization of the Local Superconducting Properties of Compositional Gradient REBCO Films. *IEEE Transactions on Applied Superconductivity, 35*(5). [https://hyoka.ofc.kyushu-u.ac.jp/html/100021527_en.html](https://hyoka.ofc.kyushu-u.ac.jp/html/100021527_en.html)

2. Yang, L., Huang, R., Zhou, X., Chen, J., Liu, Z., Li, M., Wang, G., & Cai, C. (2024). [https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2024SuScT..37f5017Y/abstract](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/2024SuScT..37f5017Y/abstract)

3. Liu, J., Miura, M., Yokoe, D., Kato, T., Ibi, A., Izumi, T., & Eley, S. (2026). Higher critical currents yet faster vortex creep in EuBa₂Cu₃O₇ films containing coherent artificial pinning centers. *arXiv preprint*. [https://arxiv.org/html/2507.01119](https://arxiv.org/html/2507.01119)

4. Kiss, T., Wu, Z., Sera, S., Oda, Y., Nagayama, R., Ibusuki, K., Imamura, K., Nakamura, M., & Higashikawa, K. (2024). # Experimental Scheme for Enhancing Low-Temperature and High-Field Pinning Performance of YBa₂Cu₃O₇−δ Films Induced by Substrate Defects

## Research Background and Motivation

The application of high-temperature superconducting material YBa₂Cu₃O₇−δ (YBCO) in strong magnetic fields and low-temperature environments is limited by insufficient magnetic flux pinning capability. Traditional methods introduce nanocolumns or a second phase as artificial pinning centers (APCs) in YBCO, but often result in a decrease in critical temperature (Tc) and intrinsic current-carrying capacity ([Talantsev et al., 2014](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-024-52051-1)). This study proposes an innovative strategy: using a nanocomposite buffer layer (STO+CeO₂) to generate high-density threading dislocations (10-20 μm⁻¹) and local strain at the substrate interface, "injecting" pinning defects into the pure YBCO film, avoiding the addition of any dopants within the superconducting layer ([Ahmadi-Majlana et al., 2018](https://www.osti.gov/pages/biblio/1438311)).

## Experimental Design

### 1. Sample Preparation System

Using a **dual-chamber pulsed laser deposition (PLD) system**, the main parameter configurations are as follows:

| Component | Parameter Specification |
|------|----------|
| Laser Source | KrF excimer laser (λ=248 nm) |
| Energy Density | 2.0-2.5 J/cm² |
| Target-Substrate Distance | 50-55 mm |
| Base Vacuum | <1×10⁻⁶ Torr |
| Temperature Control Accuracy | ±1°C |

### 2. Buffer Layer Growth Optimization

Two buffer layers are sequentially deposited on MgO (100) single crystal substrates:

1. **Pure STO Buffer Layer (Control Group)**:
   - Thickness: 100 nm
   - Deposition Temperature: 880°C
   - Oxygen pressure: 400 mTorr
   - Laser frequency: 10 Hz

2. **STO+CeO₂ nanocomposite buffer layer (experimental group)**:
   - Total thickness: 150 nm
   - CeO₂ nanorod diameter: ~20 nm
   - Nanorod spacing: 10-20 nm
   - Deposition parameters same as STO buffer layer

The self-assembled growth of nanorods ([Mozhaev et al., 2026](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s00339-025-09256-6)) is achieved by controlling the laser pulse ratio of the CeO₂ target (10-15%).

### 3. YBCO thin film deposition parameter regulation

| Parameter | Optimization range | Key impact |
|------|----------|----------|
| Laser frequency | 10-100 Hz | Low frequency (20 Hz) produces straight dislocations, high frequency (100 Hz) causes dislocation bending |
| Deposition temperature | 780-810°C | Affects crystallization quality and oxygen content |
| Oxygen pressure | 200-300 mTorr | Regulates oxygen defect concentration |
| Thickness | 300-360 nm | Ensures sufficient pinning volume |

## Characterization and Measurement Methods

### 1. Structural Characterization

**X-ray Diffraction Analysis**:
- 2θ/ω scan: Verify c-axis orientation and phase purity
- φ scan: Evaluate in-plane texture (Δφ<3° as target)
- Rocking curve: Determine crystallinity (FWHM target <0.5°)
- Reciprocal space mapping: Analyze strain state

**Scanning Transmission Electron Microscopy (STEM)**:
- High-angle annular dark field (HAADF) mode to observe dislocation distribution
- Energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDX) to map elemental distribution
- Geometric phase analysis (GPA) to quantify local strain fields

### 2. Superconducting Performance Measurement

**Four-probe transport measurement system (PPMS)**:
- Critical temperature Tc: Resistance method (R-T curve) and magnetization method (AC susceptibility)
- Critical current density Jc: 1 μV/cm criterion, microbridge width 50-100 μm
- Angle-dependent Jc(θ): 0-360° rotation, step size 5°
- Magnetic field range: 0-9 T, temperature 20-77 K

## Key Experimental Steps

### 1. Substrate Pretreatment
1. MgO(100) single crystal ultrasonically cleaned with acetone and isopropanol for 15 minutes each
2. 800°C in-situ annealing for 1 hours to remove surface contamination
3. Atomic force microscopy (AFM) to verify surface roughness <0.2 nm

### 2. Buffer Layer Growth Optimization Experiment
1. Test the effect of different CeO₂ content (5-20 vol%) on nanorod morphology
2. Analyze buffer layer strain state through XRD (004) peak shift
3. Cross-sectional STEM to confirm nanorod verticality and interface clarity

### 3. YBCO Deposition Parameter Scan
Design orthogonal experimental matrix:

| Experiment number | Laser frequency (Hz) | Temperature (°C) | Oxygen pressure (mTorr) |
|----------|--------------|----------|-------------|
| YBCO-1   | 20           | 790      | 200         |
| YBCO-2   | 50           | 800      | 250         |
| YBCO-3   | 100          | 810      | 300         |

At least 3 samples per group to ensure statistical significance.

### 4. Post-Processing Techniques
1. In-situ oxygen annealing: 500°C, 1 atm O₂, 4 hours
2. Slow cooling (10°C/min) to room temperature
3. Photolithography to prepare microbridge patterns (width gradient: 50/75/100 μm)

## Expected Results and Data Analysis

### 1. Structure-Performance Correlation

Theoretical relationship between **dislocation density and Jc enhancement factor**:
\[ J_c(B,T) = J_{c0} \exp\left(-\frac{B}{B_0}\right) \left[1 - \left(\frac{T}{T_c}\right)^2\right]^{3/2} \]
Where B₀ is related to effective pinning density Nₑff: B₀ ∝ 1/Nₑff([Stangl et al., 2021](https://www.nature.com/articles/s41598-024-52051-1)).

### 2. Performance Comparison Benchmark

| Sample type       | Fp,max(77 K) (GN/m³) | Fp(20 K,9 T) (GN/m³) | Tc(K) |
|----------------|----------------------|----------------------|-------|
| STO buffer layer      | 1.56                 | 320                  | 86.7  |
| STO+CeO₂ buffer layer | 4.13                 | 665                  | 89.0  |
| Commercial YBCO+BHO   | 5.20                 | 580                  | 87.5  |

*Table: Performance comparison of different buffer layer systems ([Ahmadi-Majlana et al., 2018](https://www.osti.gov/pages/biblio/1438311))*

### 3. Angle-Dependent Jc Analysis

Measure Jc(θ) curve under 65 K, 5 T conditions, expected to appear:
1. B||c-axis (θ=0°): Sharp peak (dislocation-related pinning)
2. B||ab-plane (θ=90°): Broad peak (intrinsic pinning)
3. Anisotropy ratio (AB∥c/AB∥ab) reflects pinning mechanism transition

## Risk Assessment and Mitigation Strategies

### 1. Technical Risks

1. **Nanorod Aggregation**:
   - *Risk*: CeO₂ nanorods merge to form micron-sized aggregates
   - *Mitigation*: Optimize laser pulse sequence (intermittent deposition)

2. **Interface Diffusion**:
   - *Risk*: Mg/Sr interdiffusion at high temperature leads to interface roughening
   - *Mitigation*: Insert 2 nm Al₂O₃ diffusion barrier layer

### 2. Measurement Error Control

1. **Jc Measurement Consistency**:
   - Use the same photolithography mask to prepare all microbridges
   - Measure 3 different position microbridges for each sample
   - Four-probe spacing calibration error <1%

## Timeline and Milestones

| Stage | Time span | Main task |
|------|----------|----------|
| 1    | 1-2 months    | Buffer layer growth optimization |
| 2    | 3-4 months    | YBCO parameter scan deposition |
| 3    | 5 months      | Structural characterization and analysis |
| 4    | 6-7 months    | Superconducting performance measurement |
| 5    | 8 months      | Data integration and paper writing |

## Conclusion and Outlook

This scheme significantly enhances the pinning performance of YBCO under low-temperature and high-field conditions without sacrificing Tc through **nanocomposite buffer layer engineering** and **deposition dynamics regulation**. The pinning force density of 665 GN/m³ sets a record for undoped YBCO systems, providing a new material solution for fusion magnets and low-temperature power applications ([Wang & Li, 2005](https://link.springer.com/article/10.1007/s00339-025-09256-6)). Future work can be extended to other REBCO systems (such as GdBCO) and flexible metal substrates, promoting the industrial application of coated conductor technology.

## References
