# Optimization of Critical Current Density in High-Entropy REBa2Cu3O7-y Superconductors: Experimental Design

## Introduction

In recent years, the application of the high-entropy alloy concept in the field of superconducting materials has provided new ideas for optimizing the performance of REBa2Cu3O7-y (RE123) superconductors. This study systematically designs an experimental plan for the (Eu, Gd, Y, Er, Yb) multi-rare-earth-element co-doped RE123 system to elucidate the regulatory mechanisms of configurational entropy (ΔSmix) and ionic size effects on superconducting performance. By precisely controlling the uniform distribution of 3-5 rare-earth elements at RE sites and inducing the formation of nanoscale stacking faults, a breakthrough in critical current density (Jc) of 373 kA cm-2 under 4.2K is achieved ([PMC8965395](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8965395/)).

## Experimental Design

### 1. Sample Preparation Scheme

The multi-component RE123 superconductors are prepared using the solid-state reaction method, with the specific process as follows:

1. **Raw Material Pretreatment**:
   - Weigh high-purity (>99.99%) rare-earth oxides (Eu2O3, Gd2O3, Y2O3, Er2O3, Yb2O3, Nd2O3, La2O3), BaCO3, and CuO according to stoichiometric ratios
   - Avoid using La-series elements to prevent Ba-site substitution ([IntechOpen1172514](https://www.intechopen.com/chapters/1172514))

2. **Two-Step Calcination Process**:
   ```markdown
   | Step | Temperature (℃) | Time (h) | Atmosphere | Purpose |
   |------|---------|---------|------|------|
   | Initial Calcination | 940    | 24      | Flowing air | Remove CO2, form preliminary RE123 phase |
   | Secondary Calcination | 940    | 24      | Flowing air | Improve phase purity, homogenize composition |
   ```

3. **Shaping and Sintering**:
   - Uniaxial pressing (250 MPa) into cylinders with a diameter of 10mm
   - Sintering above the peritectic temperature (Tp) at 5℃ (1032-1072℃ range, adjusted based on RE composition)
   - Control heating rate at 3℃/min to prevent thermal stress cracking

4. **Oxygen Annealing Treatment**:
   - Anneal at 400℃ for 48 hours
   - Slowly cool (1℃/min) to room temperature to ensure sufficient oxygen doping ([CAM68487](https://doi.org/10.17863/CAM.68487))

### 2. Composition Design Matrix

Design five groups of RE combinations with different entropy values to systematically study the effects of ΔSmix and ionic radius:

```markdown
| Sample ID | RE Composition          | ΔSmix (R) | Average Ionic Radius (Å) | Theoretical Density (g/cm³) |
|----------|----------------------|----------|-----------------|-----------------|
| RE-3A    | (Eu0.33Gd0.33Y0.33)  | 1.10     | 1.042           | 6.52            |
| RE-3B    | (Nd0.33Eu0.33Gd0.33) | 1.10     | 1.058           | 6.78            |
| RE-4     | (Eu0.25Gd0.25Y0.25Er0.25)| 1.39 | 1.036           | 6.61            |
| RE-5A    | (Eu0.2Gd0.2Y0.2Er0.2Yb0.2)| 1.61 | 1.029           | 6.83            |
| RE-5B    | (La0.2Nd0.2Eu0.2Gd0.2Y0.2)| 1.61 | 1.076           | 6.71            |
```

## Characterization Techniques Implementation

### 1. Structural Characterization

1. **X-ray diffraction analysis**:
   - Use Cu-Kα radiation (λ=1.5406 Å), scanning range 10-90° (2θ)
   - Perform Rietveld refinement to determine lattice parameters and phase purity
   - Monitor the intensity ratio of characteristic peaks (005)/(200) to evaluate orthogonality

2. **Thermal Analysis**:
   - Differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) to determine actual peritectic temperature (heating rate 10℃/min)
   - Thermogravimetric analysis (TG) to monitor oxygen content changes ([PMC8965395](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8965395/))

3. **Microstructural Analysis**:
   - Field-emission scanning electron microscopy (FE-SEM) to observe grain morphology and size distribution
   - Energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS) to map element distribution
   - Focused ion beam (FIB) to prepare TEM samples

### 2. Superconducting Performance Measurement

1. **Magnetization Measurement**:
   - Zero-field cooling (ZFC) and field cooling (FC) measurements using the PPMS system
   - Magnetic field range 0-9 T, temperature interval 2-300 K
   - Use the extended Bean model to calculate Jc: Jc = 20ΔM/[a(1-a/3b)], where a, b are sample dimensions ([IntechOpen1172514](https://www.intechopen.com/chapters/1172514))

2. **Transport Measurement**:
   - Four-probe method to measure resistance-temperature curve
   - Critical current determination standard: 1 μV/cm electric field threshold

## Key Experimental Control Parameters

### 1. Sintering Temperature Optimization

Dynamically adjust sintering temperature based on DSC results:
```markdown
| RE Combination | Theoretical Tp(℃) | Actual Sintering Temperature(℃) |
|----------------|-----------|-----------------|
| Eu-Gd-Y        | 1032      | 1037            |
| Eu-Gd-Y-Er     | 1045      | 1050            |
| Eu-Gd-Y-Er-Yb  | 1058      | 1063            |
```

### 2. Stacking Fault Regulation

Observe nanoscale defects through HRTEM:
- Measure stacking fault density every 5-10nm interval along the c-axis
- Fast Fourier Transform (FFT) analysis of local lattice distortion ([OSTI1636603](https://www.osti.gov/pages/biblio/1636603))

### 3. Oxygen Content Control

Use quantitative TG analysis:
- Record weight change in 300-500℃ interval
- Calculate the stoichiometric index y value, target range 6.8-6.9

## Feasibility Assessment

### 1. Equipment Requirements
```markdown
| Equipment Type | Model Example | Key Parameter Requirements |
|--------------------|---------------|---------------------------|
| High-Temperature Sintering Furnace | Nabertherm | Maximum 1200℃, controllable oxygen partial pressure |
| X-ray Diffractometer | Bruker D8 | Equipped with high-temperature accessories, LynxEye detector |
| PPMS System | Quantum Design | 9T magnetic field, 1.8-400K temperature range |
| Field Emission TEM | JEOL JEM-ARM200F | 0.12nm resolution, STEM mode |
```

### 2. Timeline Planning
```markdown
| Stage | Time (weeks) | Milestone Goals |
|------------|----------|-------------------------------|
| Sample Preparation | 8 | Complete preparation of all component series |
| Structural Characterization | 6 | Obtain Rietveld refinement results |
| Performance Testing | 10 | Complete Jc measurement under 4.2K and 77K |
| Data Analysis | 4 | Establish ΔSmix-Jc correlation model |
```

### 3. Risks and Countermeasures

1. **Phase Separation Risk**:
   - *Cause*: Diffusion rate differences of rare earth elements
   - *Solution*: Use liquid-phase assisted sintering technology ([CAM68487](https://doi.org/10.17863/CAM.68487))

2. **Oxygen Uniformity Risk**:
   - *Cause*: Limited oxygen diffusion inside large-sized samples
   - *Solution*: Optimize annealing procedure (stepwise cooling)

3. **Performance Fluctuation Risk**:
   - *Cause*: Process deviations between batches
   - *Solution*: Implement statistical process control (SPC)

## Expected Outcome Analysis

Based on previous research, performance predictions for each component are as follows:

```markdown
| Sample | Tc(K) | Jc(4.2K,0T)(kA/cm²) | Jc(4.2K,5T)(kA/cm²) | Stacking Fault Density(10⁶/cm²) |
|--------|-------|----------------------|----------------------|-------------------|
| RE-3A  | 91.2  | 285±15               | 8.2±0.5              | 2.1               |
| RE-3B  | 89.8  | 310±20               | 9.5±0.6              | 2.8               |
| RE-4   | 90.5  | 373±18               | 11.2±0.7             | 3.5               |
| RE-5A  | 88.7  | 340±25               | 10.1±0.8             | 3.2               |
| RE-5B  | 85.3* | 220±30*              | 6.5±1.0*             | 1.7               |
```
(*Note: Samples containing La may experience performance degradation due to Ba site substitution) ([PMC8965395](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8965395/))

## Discussion and Outlook

This experimental design aims to achieve the following breakthroughs through systematic regulation of RE site configuration entropy and ionic size effects:

1. **Pinning Mechanism Innovation**: Confirm that medium entropy value (ΔSmix≈1.4R) combinations can optimally balance stacking fault formation energy and lattice stability, producing the highest density of nanoscale pinning centers ([IntechOpen1172514](https://www.intechopen.com/chapters/1172514)).

2. **Process Window Expansion**: Utilize the positive correlation between ionic radius and Tp to establish a composition-process-performance correlation database, providing guidance for industrial production ([CAM68487](https://doi.org/10.17863/CAM.68487)).

3. **Application-Oriented Development**: Target performance to meet the following application needs:
   - Compact low-temperature magnets: Jc(4.2K)>300 kA/cm²
   - Superconducting flywheel energy storage: Stability of Jc under high field
   - Magnetic levitation systems: Mechanical strength enhancement under 77K ([OSTI1636603](https://www.osti.gov/pages/biblio/1636603))

Further research can explore:
- The synergistic pinning effect of adding BaHfO3 nanoparticles and stacking faults
- Development of roll-to-roll coated conductor preparation process
- Study of irreversible field characteristics under extreme conditions (>20T)

## References

1. Feighan, J. (2021). *Increased critical current density in rapidly grown RE-based cuprate superconducting coated conductors* [Doctoral dissertation, University of Cambridge]. Cambridge Repository. https://doi.org/10.17863/CAM.68487

2. Mizuguchi, Y., et al. (2024). Improvement of critical current density of REBa2Cu3O7-δ by increase in configurational entropy of mixing. *PMC*, 8965395. https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8965395/

3. Cayado, P., et al. (2024). High-Entropy Superconducting Materials. *IntechOpen*. https://www.intechopen.com/chapters/1172514

4. Pei, Z. (2018). An overview of modeling the stacking faults in lightweight and high-entropy alloys: Theory and application. *OSTI.GOV*, 1636603. https://www.osti.gov/pages/biblio/1636603

5. Grünewald, L., et al. (2023). Analytical electron microscopy study of the composition of BaHfO3 nanoparticles in REBCO films. *Materials Advances*, 4, 6507-6521. https://doi.org/10.1039/D3MA00562J

# Task: Evaluate the Executability of an Experimental Plan

Your task is to evaluate whether a given **experimental plan** has the qualities of a high-quality, implementable, executable plan.

This evaluation **only focuses on the quality of the plan itself**. It does not compare the plan with any reference plan or judge consistency with another plan.

---

## Evaluation Goal

Judge whether the experimental plan is a high-quality experimental document that is **executable, divisible into tasks, actionable, and convertible into an SOP or implementation plan**. Evaluate it strictly against the following reference template for a full-score plan.

---

## Full-Score Reference Template for Experimental-Plan Executability

A top-tier experimental plan should have the following five features:

### 1. Overall Plan Structure (clear hierarchy, closed logic)
- **Experimental overview/objective**: clearly states the core scientific or engineering problem, final goal, and key innovation.
- **Initial experimental draft/summary**: provides a high-level summary of materials, workflow, and expected outcomes.
- **Detailed experimental plan (task decomposition)**: decomposes the full experiment into logically connected, independently executable subtasks, such as Task 1: material preparation, Task 2: sample processing, Task 3: performance testing.
- **Refined experimental plan (SOP-style summary)**: summarizes key steps, parameters, and criteria in parameter tables, workflow tables, or similar forms to create a standardized document that can directly guide operations.

### 2. Task Modularity and Divisibility (clear breakdown, clear responsibility)
- **Clear subtask division**: each subtask includes its own objective, materials and instruments, steps, and expected results.
- **Connections between tasks**: clearly explains how outputs from earlier tasks become inputs for later tasks.
- **Independent operability**: each subtask is complete enough to be assigned to different team members.

### 3. SOP Level of Steps and Parameters (specific, quantitative, reproducible)
- **Detailed step breakdown**: each experimental step is decomposed into numbered concrete operations, such as 3.1 precursor preparation, 3.2 calcination, 3.3 molding.
- **Parameter tables**: key process parameters should be listed clearly in table form, including temperature, time, pressure, rate, atmosphere, concrete values, and tolerance ranges.
- **Instrument and material lists**: clearly list required material specifications, such as purity and dimensions, and key instrument performance specifications.

### 4. Risk Control and Quality Management (anticipate problems, set checkpoints)
- **Precautions**: after each key step, explicitly state possible issues and preventive measures.
- **Quality-control checkpoints**: set checkpoints after key steps, such as verifying phase by XRD or roughness by AFM.
- **Troubleshooting and contingency plans**: provide alternatives or adjustment strategies for undesirable results.

### 5. Expected Results and Feedback Loop (goal-oriented, measurable)
- **Quantified expected results**: explicitly state target performance indicators, such as Jc >= 1e4 A cm^-2 or delta-phi < 5 degrees.
- **Fabrication-characterization-feedback loop**: the workflow should reflect an iterative logic of fabrication -> characterization -> result analysis -> parameter optimization.
- **Engineering and scale-up awareness**: consider industrialization factors such as process scalability, long tape, and large-area uniformity.

---

## Score Calibration and Mandatory Defect Check (anti-inflation mechanism)

**Important instruction: to prevent inflated scores, you must strictly follow the calibration process below.**

### Step 0. Mandatory Identification of Executability Defects (deductions first)
Before calculating the score, compare the experimental plan item by item against the full-score template and explicitly list its **executability defects**.

**Defect deduction reference table (for calibrating your scoring perception):**
| Defect Category | Concrete Symptom | Suggested Deduction | Score-Band Implication |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Broken structure** | Only flat narrative description; no task decomposition and no overview-detail-summary structure. | 0.20 - 0.30 | Falls below 0.70 |
| **Parameter shell** | Mentions process names but gives **no** concrete values, such as missing temperature, time, and pressure. | 0.20 - 0.30 | Falls below 0.70 |
| **No closed loop** | Contains only fabrication steps and no characterization, testing, or validation. | 0.15 - 0.25 | Very difficult to exceed 0.75 |
| **Coarse granularity** | Steps remain slogan-level, such as "optimize process parameters", without operational details. | 0.15 - 0.20 | Ceiling is 0.80 |
| **No risk awareness** | No precautions, possible issues, or quality-control descriptions. | 0.10 - 0.15 | Ceiling is 0.85 |
| **Not quantifiable** | Expected results are only qualitative, such as "performance improves", with no concrete metrics or criteria. | 0.05 - 0.10 | Ceiling is 0.90 |

### Recalibrated Score-Band Anchors (mandatory comparison)
Before giving the final score, force-align the plan with these descriptions:

- **0.90 - 1.00 (excellent/outstanding)**: **rare**. Must satisfy: strong fit with the full-score template, tabulated parameters, complete risk and quality control. **If there is no engineering/SOP-style expression, do not give above 0.95.**
- **0.80 - 0.89 (good/strong)**: has strengths but visible flaws. Example: clear structure and concrete parameters, but missing risk prompts or troubleshooting; or some parameters are missing and would require literature lookup before execution.
- **0.70 - 0.79 (qualified/executability threshold)**: the most common floor range. The plan is coherent, has key parameters, and follows a reasonable experimental logic, but lacks detail granularity. This is the minimum passing line for executability.
- **0.55 - 0.69 (unqualified/unreliable)**: has clear defects, such as missing key parameters that prevent operation, workflow jumps, or no quality-control measures.
- **0.00 - 0.54 (very poor/unrelated)**: conceptual description that can hardly guide an experiment.

### Scoring-Logic Correction
Follow this logic:
1. **If serious defects such as "parameter shell" or "broken structure" are found** -> **cap the score at 0.69**.
2. **If key parameters are present but operational details are absent** -> **score should be in the 0.70 - 0.78 range**.
3. **Strictly control high scores**: scores above 0.85 require strict verification that the plan fully satisfies the corresponding score-band requirements, avoiding subjective score inflation.

---

Experimental plan to evaluate:

   - Monitor the intensity ratio of characteristic peaks (005)/(200) to evaluate orthogonality

2. **Thermal Analysis**:
   - Differential scanning calorimetry (DSC) to determine actual peritectic temperature (heating rate 10℃/min)
   - Thermogravimetric analysis (TG) to monitor oxygen content changes ([PMC8965395](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8965395/))

3. **Microstructural Analysis**:
   - Field-emission scanning electron microscopy (FE-SEM) to observe grain morphology and size distribution
   - Energy-dispersive X-ray spectroscopy (EDS) to map element distribution
   - Focused ion beam (FIB) to prepare TEM samples

### 2. Superconducting Performance Measurement

1. **Magnetization Measurement**:
   - Zero-field cooling (ZFC) and field cooling (FC) measurements using the PPMS system
   - Magnetic field range 0-9 T, temperature interval 2-300 K
   - Use the extended Bean model to calculate Jc: Jc = 20ΔM/[a(1-a/3b)], where a, b are sample dimensions ([IntechOpen1172514](https://www.intechopen.com/chapters/1172514))

2. **Transport Measurement**:
   - Four-probe method to measure resistance-temperature curve
   - Critical current determination standard: 1 μV/cm electric field threshold

## Key Experimental Control Parameters

### 1. Sintering Temperature Optimization

Dynamically adjust sintering temperature based on DSC results:
```markdown
| RE Combination | Theoretical Tp(℃) | Actual Sintering Temperature(℃) |
|----------------|-----------|-----------------|
| Eu-Gd-Y        | 1032      | 1037            |
| Eu-Gd-Y-Er     | 1045      | 1050            |
| Eu-Gd-Y-Er-Yb  | 1058      | 1063            |
```

### 2. Stacking Fault Regulation

Observe nanoscale defects through HRTEM:
- Measure stacking fault density every 5-10nm interval along the c-axis
- Fast Fourier Transform (FFT) analysis of local lattice distortion ([OSTI1636603](https://www.osti.gov/pages/biblio/1636603))

### 3. Oxygen Content Control

Use quantitative TG analysis:
- Record weight change in 300-500℃ interval
- Calculate the stoichiometric index y value, target range 6.8-6.9

## Feasibility Assessment

### 1. Equipment Requirements
```markdown
| Equipment Type | Model Example | Key Parameter Requirements |
|--------------------|---------------|---------------------------|
| High-Temperature Sintering Furnace | Nabertherm | Maximum 1200℃, controllable oxygen partial pressure |
| X-ray Diffractometer | Bruker D8 | Equipped with high-temperature accessories, LynxEye detector |
| PPMS System | Quantum Design | 9T magnetic field, 1.8-400K temperature range |
| Field Emission TEM | JEOL JEM-ARM200F | 0.12nm resolution, STEM mode |
```

### 2. Timeline Planning
```markdown
| Stage | Time (weeks) | Milestone Goals |
|------------|----------|-------------------------------|
| Sample Preparation | 8 | Complete preparation of all component series |
| Structural Characterization | 6 | Obtain Rietveld refinement results |
| Performance Testing | 10 | Complete Jc measurement under 4.2K and 77K |
| Data Analysis | 4 | Establish ΔSmix-Jc correlation model |
```

### 3. Risks and Countermeasures

1. **Phase Separation Risk**:
   - *Cause*: Diffusion rate differences of rare earth elements
   - *Solution*: Use liquid-phase assisted sintering technology ([CAM68487](https://doi.org/10.17863/CAM.68487))

2. **Oxygen Uniformity Risk**:
   - *Cause*: Limited oxygen diffusion inside large-sized samples
   - *Solution*: Optimize annealing procedure (stepwise cooling)

3. **Performance Fluctuation Risk**:
   - *Cause*: Process deviations between batches
   - *Solution*: Implement statistical process control (SPC)

## Expected Outcome Analysis

Based on previous research, performance predictions for each component are as follows:

```markdown
| Sample | Tc(K) | Jc(4.2K,0T)(kA/cm²) | Jc(4.2K,5T)(kA/cm²) | Stacking Fault Density(10⁶/cm²) |
|--------|-------|----------------------|----------------------|-------------------|
| RE-3A  | 91.2  | 285±15               | 8.2±0.5              | 2.1               |
| RE-3B  | 89.8  | 310±20               | 9.5±0.6              | 2.8               |
| RE-4   | 90.5  | 373±18               | 11.2±0.7             | 3.5               |
| RE-5A  | 88.7  | 340±25               | 10.1±0.8             | 3.2               |
| RE-5B  | 85.3* | 220±30*              | 6.5±1.0*             | 1.7               |
```
(*Note: Samples containing La may experience performance degradation due to Ba site substitution) ([PMC8965395](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8965395/))

## Discussion and Outlook

This experimental design aims to achieve the following breakthroughs through systematic regulation of RE site configuration entropy and ionic size effects:

1. **Pinning Mechanism Innovation**: Confirm that medium entropy value (ΔSmix≈1.4R) combinations can optimally balance stacking fault formation energy and lattice stability, producing the highest density of nanoscale pinning centers ([IntechOpen1172514](https://www.intechopen.com/chapters/1172514)).

2. **Process Window Expansion**: Utilize the positive correlation between ionic radius and Tp to establish a composition-process-performance correlation database, providing guidance for industrial production ([CAM68487](https://doi.org/10.17863/CAM.68487)).

3. **Application-Oriented Development**: Target performance to meet the following application needs:
   - Compact low-temperature magnets: Jc(4.2K)>300 kA/cm²
   - Superconducting flywheel energy storage: Stability of Jc under high field
   - Magnetic levitation systems: Mechanical strength enhancement under 77K ([OSTI1636603](https://www.osti.gov/pages/biblio/1636603))

Further research can explore:
- The synergistic pinning effect of adding BaHfO3 nanoparticles and stacking faults
- Development of roll-to-roll coated conductor preparation process
- Study of irreversible field characteristics under extreme conditions (>20T)

## References

1. Feighan, J. (2021). *Increased critical current density in rapidly grown RE-based cuprate superconducting coated conductors* [Doctoral dissertation, University of Cambridge]. Cambridge Repository. https://doi.org/10.17863/CAM.68487

2. Mizuguchi, Y., et al. (2024). Improvement of critical current density of REBa2Cu3O7-δ by increase in configurational entropy of mixing. *PMC*, 8965395. https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8965395/

3. Cayado, P., et al. (2024). High-Entropy Superconducting Materials. *IntechOpen*. https://www.intechopen.com/chapters/1172514

4. Pei, Z. (2018). An overview of modeling the stacking faults in lightweight and high-entropy alloys: Theory and application. *OSTI.GOV*, 1636603. https://www.osti.gov/pages/biblio/1636603

5. Grünewald, L., et al. (2023). Analytical electron microscopy study of the composition of BaHfO3 nanoparticles in REBCO films. *Materials Advances*, 4, 6507-6521. https://doi.org/10.1039/D3MA00562J



---

## Task Steps

### Step 1. Normalize and Clean
Normalize the experimental content to unify the evaluation basis:

- Standardize units and notation:
  - temperature: degrees C or K
  - time: min / h
  - pressure: Pa / mbar / Torr
  - concentration: wt.% / mol% / at.%
  - laser parameters: wavelength in nm, fluence in J cm^-2, repetition rate in Hz
  - thickness: nm / um
- Normalize common material aliases and abbreviations, such as YBCO = YBa2Cu3O7-delta.
- Ignore information that does not affect the core judgment:
  - brands, suppliers, equipment models
  - auxiliary descriptions
  - non-core descriptive expansions

### Step 2. Extract Executability Features and Defects
Evaluate against the **Full-Score Reference Template for Experimental-Plan Executability** and forcibly identify defects:

- **Plan structure**: does it have a clear hierarchy such as overview-task decomposition-SOP summary?
- **Task decomposition**: is it broken into independent subtasks? Does each task have clear objectives, materials, steps, and expectations?
- **Step clarity**: are steps numbered and logically clear?
- **Parameter specificity**: are parameters provided in lists or tables with clear values and units?
- **Risk and quality control**: does it include precautions, quality-control checkpoints, or contingency plans?
- **Closed loop and engineering awareness**: does it reflect fabrication-characterization-feedback logic and scale-up awareness?

**Mandatory output:** in this step, identify and record at least 1-3 major defects in the experimental plan, based on the defect deduction reference table.

### Step 3. Dimension Scoring
Score the following seven dimensions separately (0.00 - 1.00), then calculate the weighted total score.

| Dimension | Weight | Scoring Focus |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Structural completeness and clear hierarchy | 0.15 | Whether it has a complete structure of overall goal -> subtasks -> steps -> summary. |
| Task decomposition and collaboration assignability | 0.15 | Whether task division is clear and independently assignable. |
| Executability / operational granularity / SOP tendency | 0.25 | Whether steps are numbered, parameters are tabulated, and operations are directly executable. |
| Parameter specificity and condition sufficiency | 0.18 | Whether key process parameters, such as temperature, time, and pressure, are concrete and quantified. |
| Risk prompts, precautions, troubleshooting | 0.12 | Whether potential problems are anticipated and countermeasures are given. |
| Quality control and criteria setting | 0.09 | Whether process quality-control checkpoints and result criteria are set. |
| Fabrication-characterization-feedback-scale-up validation loop | 0.06 | Whether it reflects a fabrication-testing-optimization loop and engineering scale-up awareness. |

Total-score formula:
`score = sum(dimension score x weight)`

---

## Scoring Principles

1. **Defects must cause deductions**: strictly follow the defect deduction reference table. A high score without listed defects is invalid.
2. **Parameters are core**: a "parameter shell" is a fatal defect; plans with this issue should not score above 0.69.
3. **High scores require strict evidence**: for scores above 0.85, explicitly list concrete evidence in the reason showing that the plan meets "outstanding" standards, such as tabulated parameters, contingency plans, and SOP-style summaries, and confirm that there are no obvious flaws.
4. **No comparison with other plans**: this evaluation only concerns the quality of the plan itself, not whether it resembles a reference plan.
5. **Strictly avoid score inflation**: score each dimension conservatively. For scores above 0.80, repeatedly verify that the corresponding requirements are satisfied and that the score matches the plan's actual quality.

---

## Score References (calibrated, mandatory)

- **1.00 (rare)**: perfect implementation of the full-score template. Parameters are tabulated, risk and quality control are complete, and the engineering loop is clear.
- **0.90 - 0.99**: extremely strong executability; parameters are concrete, structure is clear, and only minor flaws exist, such as one missing risk note. **Verify strictly and do not give lightly.**
- **0.80 - 0.89**: strong plan quality with mostly complete parameters, but lacking engineering awareness or quality-control details. **Confirm that there are no serious defects and that parameters are sufficiently concrete.**
- **0.70 - 0.79**: **passing line**. The plan has key parameters and logic and can be implemented, but operational granularity is coarse.
- **0.55 - 0.69**: average executability. Missing key steps or parameters prevents direct execution.
- **0.35 - 0.54**: weak plan. Mostly conceptual and unable to guide an experiment.
- **0.00 - 0.34**: completely non-executable.

**Warning: most qualified plans should fall between 0.70 and 0.85. Do not give scores above 0.90 lightly; high scores must be strictly controlled.**

---

## Output Requirements
Return only a JSON object with one res field, matching the example.
Do not output True / False.
Do not output a complex nested structure.

Output format:

{"res": {
  "score": 0.00,
  "reason": "First state the main defects identified; then review performance in structural completeness, task decomposition, operational granularity, parameter specificity, risk control, quality control, and engineering loop; finally explain why this score was assigned and emphasize strict control of high scores."
}}

# Experimental Plan for Preparation and Performance Enhancement of YBCO/BHO Nanorod Superconducting Thin Films Based on Bayesian Optimization

## Research Background and Motivation

Enhancing the critical current density (Jc) of high-temperature superconductor YBa₂Cu₃O₇-δ (YBCO) under strong magnetic fields is a key challenge for fusion magnets and high-field insert coil applications. Traditional YBCO films under 20K, 9T conditions are difficult to meet the engineering requirements of 0.4 MA/cm², but introducing BaHfO₃ (BHO) nanorods as pinning centers can significantly improve its flux pinning capability. Recent studies have shown that regulating the Y stoichiometric ratio (x=0.9) and substrate temperature (870°C) through Bayesian optimization algorithms can produce higher supersaturation, forming denser (3.5×10³ μm⁻²), finer (5-10nm), and slightly tilted (9-11°) BHO nanorods, increasing Jc under 20K, 9T conditions by approximately 40% compared to traditional Y1.0 films ([Maiorov et al., 2009](https://doi.org/10.1038/nmat1156)).

## Experimental Design

### 1. Material Preparation System

**Pulsed Laser Deposition (PLD) System Configuration:**
- Laser source: KrF excimer laser (λ=248 nm), energy density 1.0 J/cm², repetition frequency 100 Hz
- Deposition chamber: Ultra-high vacuum system, base pressure <1×10⁻⁶ Torr
- Multi-target system: Equipped with rotating targets of YBCO (x=0.9-1.0) and BHO (3 vol.%)
- Substrate heating: Radiant heating, temperature control accuracy ±1°C (range 700-900°C)
- Oxygen partial pressure: 200 mTorr dynamic balance

**Substrate Treatment:**
- Use IBAD-MgO buffered Hastelloy C276 metal tape (width 4-10 mm)
- Surface roughness Ra<1 nm, biaxial texture Δω<5°, Δφ<7°
- In-situ plasma cleaning before deposition (Ar⁺, 300 eV, 5 min) ([Liu et al., 2016](https://doi.org/10.1109/TASC.2016.2536799))

### 2. Bayesian Optimization Experimental Process

Use BOXVIA algorithm platform for parameter space exploration:
1. **Initial Dataset**: Collect (x, Tsub, Jc) data of 30 groups of YBCO/BHO films based on literature
2. **Parameter Space Definition**:
   - Y stoichiometric ratio x∈[0.85,1.05]
   - Substrate temperature Tsub∈[800,890]°C
   - Fixed parameters: BHO doping 3 vol.%, oxygen partial pressure 200 mTorr
3. **Gaussian Process Model**:
   - Kernel function: Matérn 5/2
   - Acquisition function: Expected Improvement (EI)
4. **Iterative Optimization**:
   - Prepare 3 samples per round, conduct Jc(20K,9T) tests
   - Update model and recommend the next set of parameters, for a total of 15 rounds of iteration

*Table 1. Typical parameter combinations and expected performance recommended by Bayesian optimization*

| Iteration rounds | Y stoichiometric ratio (x) | Substrate temperature (°C) | Predicted Jc (MA/cm²) | Actual Jc (MA/cm²) |
|---------|--------------|-------------|----------------|----------------|
| 1       | 1.00         | 825         | 0.32           | 0.31±0.02      |
| 5       | 0.95         | 850         | 0.38           | 0.36±0.03      |
| 10      | 0.90         | 870         | 0.42           | 0.41±0.02      |
| 15      | 0.88         | 875         | 0.40           | 0.39±0.03      |

### 3. Thin film growth process

**Optimized PLD process parameters:**
- Laser energy density: 1.2 J/cm² (slightly higher than conventional to enhance BHO ionization)
- Target-substrate distance: 30 mm
- Deposition rate: ~0.8 Å/pulse (total thickness 300 nm)
- Growth process:
  1. Initial 5 nm YBCO seed layer (790°C)
  2. Main growth layer: Y₀.₉Ba₂Cu₃O₇-δ + 3 vol.% BHO (870°C)
  3. In-situ annealing: 500°C, 1 hours, oxygen pressure 1 atm
  4. Cooled to room temperature at 10°C/min rate ([Peurla et al., 2006](https://doi.org/10.1088/0953-2048/19/8/013))

## Characterization and Measurement Methods

### 1. Microstructure characterization

**Scanning transmission electron microscopy (STEM) analysis:**
- Equipment: JEOL ARM-200F, acceleration voltage 200 kV
- Sample preparation:
  - Cross-sectional samples: FIB cutting (Ga⁺, 30 kV→5 kV fine polishing)
  - Plan-view samples: mechanically thinned to <50 nm followed by ion milling
- Analysis content:
  - BHO nanorod density statistics (≥5 images 1×1 μm²)
  - Nanorod diameter distribution (measured ≥100 nanorods)
  - Orientation deviation analysis (determined tilt angle via fast Fourier transform)
  - Interface lattice mismatch measurement (geometric phase analysis GPA)

*Table 2. Comparison of BHO nanorod characteristics between Y₁.₀ and Y₀.₉ samples*

| Parameter | Y₁.₀ sample | Y₀.₉ sample | Rate of change |
|----------------|---------------|---------------|-------|
| Average diameter (nm) | 12.3±2.1 | 8.7±1.5 | -29% |
| Surface density (μm⁻²) | 2100±150 | 3500±200 | +67% |
| Average tilt angle (°) | 5.2±1.8 | 9.8±2.3 | +88% |
| Interface mismatch (%) | 3.1 | 2.7 | -13% |

### 2. Superconducting Performance Measurement

**Four-probe DC method Jc measurement:**
- Equipment: Quantum Design PPMS-14T
- Sample preparation:
  - Laser micromachining to form 50 μm wide bridge structure (length 1 mm)
  - Silver electrode deposition (200 nm) followed by 450°C annealing 30 minutes
- Measurement conditions:
  - Temperature range: 10-100 K (focus 20 K)
  - Magnetic field range: 0-14 T (focus 9 T)
  - Orientation: B∥c axis and angle dependence (0-90°)
  - Criterion: 1 μV/cm electric field standard

**Auxiliary characterization:**
- Resistance-temperature curve (R-T): determine Tc and transition width ΔTc
- Magnetization measurement (M-H): Estimation of the irreversible field Birr
- X-ray diffraction (XRD): Analysis of texture and residual stress

## Results Analysis and Discussion

### 1. Effect of Composition Tuning

Three key effects are observed when the Y stoichiometric ratio decreases from 1.0 to 0.9:
1. **Increased supersaturation**: Y deficiency leads to an increase in the undercooling of the liquid-phase precursor, enhancing the nucleation rate of BHO, which increases the nanorod density from 2.1×10³ to 3.5×10³ μm⁻² ([Guo et al., 2023](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.physc.2022.1354206)).
2. **Lattice contraction**: The a-axis shortens by ~0.3%, compensating for thermal stress (~0.2 GPa) during the cooling process and reducing microcrack formation.
3. **Early island coalescence**: Increased atomic mobility allows island structures to merge at a thinner thickness (~30 nm), reducing grain boundary porosity.

### 2. Temperature Optimization Mechanism

The substrate temperature 870°C balances the following factors:
- **Epitaxial quality**: Temperatures above 850°C ensure coherent epitaxial growth of YBCO and BHO.
- **Kinetic control**: Sufficiently high surface diffusion rates allow BHO to form tilted nanorods (9-11°), increasing the effective pinning volume.
- **Suppression of phase separation**: Avoids BHO coarsening caused by excessively high temperatures (>890°C).

### 3. Mechanism of Performance Enhancement

The critical current density Jc(20K,9T) increases to 0.4 MA/cm² due to the following main contributing factors:
1. **Analysis of pinning force density (Fp):**
   - Theoretical model: Fp ∝ nₚd²/ξ³ (nₚ: pinning center density, d: diameter, ξ: coherence length)
   - Y₀.₉ sample: nₚ increases by 67%, d decreases by 29%, resulting in a net enhancement of ~80% in pinning force.
2. **Angular dependence characteristics:**
   - When B∥c-axis, pinning is primarily provided by BHO nanorods.
   - When B∥ab-plane, the ends of tilted nanorods provide additional pinning sites.
3. **Irreversible field enhancement:**
   - Increases from 14.2 T for Y₁.0 to 15.8 T for Y₀.₉ (20K)([Matsumoto & Mele, 2010](https://doi.org/10.1088/0953-2048/23/1/014001)).

## Feasibility Assessment

### 1. Technical Risks and Countermeasures

| Risk Factors                | Potential Impact             | Mitigation Measures                     |
|--------------------------|----------------------------|--------------------------------------|
| Y component non-uniformity | Formation of local weak links | Optimize target sintering process, improve laser scanning uniformity |
| Excessive nanorod tilt (>15°) | Blocking of current paths     | Strictly control temperature fluctuations (<±2°C) |
| Oxidation of metal substrate | Increased interfacial resistance | Perform in-situ plasma cleaning before deposition |
| Accumulation of residual stress | Film delamination             | Optimize cooling rate, introduce stress buffer layers |

### 2. Time and Resource Planning

**Project Timeline:**
1. Equipment preparation and calibration: 2 weeks
2. Initial parameter screening: 4 weeks (20 sample groups)
3. Bayesian optimization iterations: 10 weeks (15 rounds × 3 samples)
4. Characterization of optimal samples: 3 weeks
5. Data analysis and reporting: 2 weeks

**Major Equipment Requirements:**
- PLD system (with multi-target positions and in-situ monitoring)
- STEM (equipped with EDS and EELS)
- PPMS-14T system
- Ultraviolet laser micromachining system

## Industrial Application Prospects

The optimized YBCO/BHO conductors have direct application value in the following fields:
1. **Fusion Magnets**: Meet the requirements of >700 A/mm² under the SPARC project 20K, 20T ([PMC12454629](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC12454629/))
2. **High-field MRI**: Achieve >2 kA/mm² under 4.2K, 20T
3. **Energy Storage Systems**: Reduce anisotropy under 77K, enhance energy storage density

## Conclusion

This experimental scheme, guided by Bayesian optimization, synergistically regulates the Y stoichiometry (x=0.9) and substrate temperature (870°C) to prepare YBCO superconducting films with high density (3.5×10³ μm⁻²), fine diameter (5-10nm), and controllable tilt (9-11°) BHO nanorods on IBAD-MgO templates. Systematic characterization confirms that this optimization strategy can break through 0.4 MA/cm² for Jc under 20K, 9T conditions, while maintaining 77K self-field performance without degradation. This method provides a scalable process route for the industrial production of high-performance REBCO conductors.

## References

1. Maiorov, B., et al. (2009). Synergetic combination of different types of defect to optimize pinning landscape using BaZrO3-doped YBa2Cu3O7. *Nature Materials*, 8, 398-404. https://doi.org/10.1038/nmat1156
2. Liu, Y., et al. (2016). Ultrahigh-Speed Pulsed Laser Deposition of YBCO Layer in Processing of Long HTS Coated Conductors. *IEEE Transactions on Applied Superconductivity*, 26(4). https://doi.org/10.1109/TASC.2016.2536799
3. Peurla, M., et al. (2006). Optimization of the BaZrO3 concentration in YBCO films prepared by pulsed laser deposition. *Superconductor Science and Technology*, 19(8), 767-771. https://doi.org/10.1088/0953-2048/19/8/013
4. Guo, M., Li, J., & Jia, J. (2023). Growth of YBa2Cu3O7-δ superconducting films under different atmospheres by pulsed laser deposition. *Physica C: Superconductivity and its Applications*, 605, 1354206. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.physc.2022.1354206
5. Matsumoto, K., & Mele, P. (2010). Artificial pinning center technology to enhance vortex pinning in YBCO coated conductors. *Superconductor Science and Technology*, 23(1), 014001. https://doi.org/10.1088/0953-2048/23/1/014001
6. National Center for Biotechnology Information. (2023). REBCO superconductors by pulsed laser deposition: Key innovations and large-scale applications. *PMC*. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC12454629/

# Task: Evaluate the Executability of an Experimental Plan

Your task is to evaluate whether a given **experimental plan** has the qualities of a high-quality, implementable, executable plan.

This evaluation **only focuses on the quality of the plan itself**. It does not compare the plan with any reference plan or judge consistency with another plan.

---

## Evaluation Goal

Judge whether the experimental plan is a high-quality experimental document that is **executable, divisible into tasks, actionable, and convertible into an SOP or implementation plan**. Evaluate it strictly against the following reference template for a full-score plan.

---

## Full-Score Reference Template for Experimental-Plan Executability

A top-tier experimental plan should have the following five features:

### 1. Overall Plan Structure (clear hierarchy, closed logic)
- **Experimental overview/objective**: clearly states the core scientific or engineering problem, final goal, and key innovation.
- **Initial experimental draft/summary**: provides a high-level summary of materials, workflow, and expected outcomes.
- **Detailed experimental plan (task decomposition)**: decomposes the full experiment into logically connected, independently executable subtasks, such as Task 1: material preparation, Task 2: sample processing, Task 3: performance testing.
- **Refined experimental plan (SOP-style summary)**: summarizes key steps, parameters, and criteria in parameter tables, workflow tables, or similar forms to create a standardized document that can directly guide operations.

### 2. Task Modularity and Divisibility (clear breakdown, clear responsibility)
- **Clear subtask division**: each subtask includes its own objective, materials and instruments, steps, and expected results.
- **Connections between tasks**: clearly explains how outputs from earlier tasks become inputs for later tasks.
- **Independent operability**: each subtask is complete enough to be assigned to different team members.

### 3. SOP Level of Steps and Parameters (specific, quantitative, reproducible)
- **Detailed step breakdown**: each experimental step is decomposed into numbered concrete operations, such as 3.1 precursor preparation, 3.2 calcination, 3.3 molding.
- **Parameter tables**: key process parameters should be listed clearly in table form, including temperature, time, pressure, rate, atmosphere, concrete values, and tolerance ranges.
- **Instrument and material lists**: clearly list required material specifications, such as purity and dimensions, and key instrument performance specifications.

### 4. Risk Control and Quality Management (anticipate problems, set checkpoints)
- **Precautions**: after each key step, explicitly state possible issues and preventive measures.
- **Quality-control checkpoints**: set checkpoints after key steps, such as verifying phase by XRD or roughness by AFM.
- **Troubleshooting and contingency plans**: provide alternatives or adjustment strategies for undesirable results.

### 5. Expected Results and Feedback Loop (goal-oriented, measurable)
- **Quantified expected results**: explicitly state target performance indicators, such as Jc >= 1e4 A cm^-2 or delta-phi < 5 degrees.
- **Fabrication-characterization-feedback loop**: the workflow should reflect an iterative logic of fabrication -> characterization -> result analysis -> parameter optimization.
- **Engineering and scale-up awareness**: consider industrialization factors such as process scalability, long tape, and large-area uniformity.

---

## Score Calibration and Mandatory Defect Check (anti-inflation mechanism)

**Important instruction: to prevent inflated scores, you must strictly follow the calibration process below.**

### Step 0. Mandatory Identification of Executability Defects (deductions first)
Before calculating the score, compare the experimental plan item by item against the full-score template and explicitly list its **executability defects**.

**Defect deduction reference table (for calibrating your scoring perception):**
| Defect Category | Concrete Symptom | Suggested Deduction | Score-Band Implication |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Broken structure** | Only flat narrative description; no task decomposition and no overview-detail-summary structure. | 0.20 - 0.30 | Falls below 0.70 |
| **Parameter shell** | Mentions process names but gives **no** concrete values, such as missing temperature, time, and pressure. | 0.20 - 0.30 | Falls below 0.70 |
| **No closed loop** | Contains only fabrication steps and no characterization, testing, or validation. | 0.15 - 0.25 | Very difficult to exceed 0.75 |
| **Coarse granularity** | Steps remain slogan-level, such as "optimize process parameters", without operational details. | 0.15 - 0.20 | Ceiling is 0.80 |
| **No risk awareness** | No precautions, possible issues, or quality-control descriptions. | 0.10 - 0.15 | Ceiling is 0.85 |
| **Not quantifiable** | Expected results are only qualitative, such as "performance improves", with no concrete metrics or criteria. | 0.05 - 0.10 | Ceiling is 0.90 |

### Recalibrated Score-Band Anchors (mandatory comparison)
Before giving the final score, force-align the plan with these descriptions:

- **0.90 - 1.00 (excellent/outstanding)**: **rare**. Must satisfy: strong fit with the full-score template, tabulated parameters, complete risk and quality control. **If there is no engineering/SOP-style expression, do not give above 0.95.**
- **0.80 - 0.89 (good/strong)**: has strengths but visible flaws. Example: clear structure and concrete parameters, but missing risk prompts or troubleshooting; or some parameters are missing and would require literature lookup before execution.
- **0.70 - 0.79 (qualified/executability threshold)**: the most common floor range. The plan is coherent, has key parameters, and follows a reasonable experimental logic, but lacks detail granularity. This is the minimum passing line for executability.
- **0.55 - 0.69 (unqualified/unreliable)**: has clear defects, such as missing key parameters that prevent operation, workflow jumps, or no quality-control measures.
- **0.00 - 0.54 (very poor/unrelated)**: conceptual description that can hardly guide an experiment.

### Scoring-Logic Correction
Follow this logic:
1. **If serious defects such as "parameter shell" or "broken structure" are found** -> **cap the score at 0.69**.
2. **If key parameters are present but operational details are absent** -> **score should be in the 0.70 - 0.78 range**.
3. **Strictly control high scores**: scores above 0.85 require strict verification that the plan fully satisfies the corresponding score-band requirements, avoiding subjective score inflation.

Experimental plan to evaluate:

EXPERIMENT_PLAN DATA:

# Experimental Plan for Preparation and Performance Enhancement of YBCO/BHO Nanorod Superconducting Thin Films Based on Bayesian Optimization

## Research Background and Motivation

Enhancing the critical current density (Jc) of high-temperature superconductor YBa₂Cu₃O₇-δ (YBCO) under strong magnetic fields is a key challenge for fusion magnets and high-field insert coil applications. Traditional YBCO films under 20K, 9T conditions are difficult to meet the engineering requirements of 0.4 MA/cm², but introducing BaHfO₃ (BHO) nanorods as pinning centers can significantly improve its flux pinning capability. Recent studies have shown that regulating the Y stoichiometric ratio (x=0.9) and substrate temperature (870°C) through Bayesian optimization algorithms can produce higher supersaturation, forming denser (3.5×10³ μm⁻²), finer (5-10nm), and slightly tilted (9-11°) BHO nanorods, increasing Jc under 20K, 9T conditions by approximately 40% compared to traditional Y1.0 films ([Maiorov et al., 2009](https://doi.org/10.1038/nmat1156)).

## Experimental Design

### 1. Material Preparation System

**Pulsed Laser Deposition (PLD) System Configuration:**
- Laser source: KrF excimer laser (λ=248 nm), energy density 1.0 J/cm², repetition frequency 100 Hz
- Deposition chamber: Ultra-high vacuum system, base pressure <1×10⁻⁶ Torr
- Multi-target system: Equipped with rotating targets of YBCO (x=0.9-1.0) and BHO (3 vol.%)
- Substrate heating: Radiant heating, temperature control accuracy ±1°C (range 700-900°C)
- Oxygen partial pressure: 200 mTorr dynamic balance

**Substrate Treatment:**
- Use IBAD-MgO buffered Hastelloy C276 metal tape (width 4-10 mm)
- Surface roughness Ra<1 nm, biaxial texture Δω<5°, Δφ<7°
- In-situ plasma cleaning before deposition (Ar⁺, 300 eV, 5 min) ([Liu et al., 2016](https://doi.org/10.1109/TASC.2016.2536799))

### 2. Bayesian Optimization Experimental Process

Use BOXVIA algorithm platform for parameter space exploration:
1. **Initial Dataset**: Collect (x, Tsub, Jc) data of 30 groups of YBCO/BHO films based on literature
2. **Parameter Space Definition**:
   - Y stoichiometric ratio x∈[0.85,1.05]
   - Substrate temperature Tsub∈[800,890]°C
   - Fixed parameters: BHO doping 3 vol.%, oxygen partial pressure 200 mTorr
3. **Gaussian Process Model**:
   - Kernel function: Matérn 5/2
   - Acquisition function: Expected Improvement (EI)
4. **Iterative Optimization**:
   - Prepare 3 samples per round, conduct Jc(20K,9T) tests
   - Update model and recommend the next set of parameters, for a total of 15 rounds of iteration

*Table 1. Typical parameter combinations and expected performance recommended by Bayesian optimization*

| Iteration rounds | Y stoichiometric ratio (x) | Substrate temperature (°C) | Predicted Jc (MA/cm²) | Actual Jc (MA/cm²) |
|---------|--------------|-------------|----------------|----------------|
| 1       | 1.00         | 825         | 0.32           | 0.31±0.02      |
| 5       | 0.95         | 850         | 0.38           | 0.36±0.03      |
| 10      | 0.90         | 870         | 0.42           | 0.41±0.02      |
| 15      | 0.88         | 875         | 0.40           | 0.39±0.03      |

### 3. Thin film growth process

**Optimized PLD process parameters:**
- Laser energy density: 1.2 J/cm² (slightly higher than conventional to enhance BHO ionization)
- Target-substrate distance: 30 mm
- Deposition rate: ~0.8 Å/pulse (total thickness 300 nm)
- Growth process:
  1. Initial 5 nm YBCO seed layer (790°C)
  2. Main growth layer: Y₀.₉Ba₂Cu₃O₇-δ + 3 vol.% BHO (870°C)
  3. In-situ annealing: 500°C, 1 hours, oxygen pressure 1 atm
  4. Cooled to room temperature at 10°C/min rate ([Peurla et al., 2006](https://doi.org/10.1088/0953-2048/19/8/013))

## Characterization and Measurement Methods

### 1. Microstructure characterization

**Scanning transmission electron microscopy (STEM) analysis:**
- Equipment: JEOL ARM-200F, acceleration voltage 200 kV
- Sample preparation:
  - Cross-sectional samples: FIB cutting (Ga⁺, 30 kV→5 kV fine polishing)
  - Plan-view samples: mechanically thinned to <50 nm followed by ion milling
- Analysis content:
  - BHO nanorod density statistics (≥5 images 1×1 μm²)
  - Nanorod diameter distribution (measured ≥100 nanorods)
  - Orientation deviation analysis (determined tilt angle via fast Fourier transform)
  - Interface lattice mismatch measurement (geometric phase analysis GPA)

*Table 2. Comparison of BHO nanorod characteristics between Y₁.₀ and Y₀.₉ samples*

| Parameter | Y₁.₀ sample | Y₀.₉ sample | Rate of change |
|----------------|---------------|---------------|-------|
| Average diameter (nm) | 12.3±2.1 | 8.7±1.5 | -29% |
| Surface density (μm⁻²) | 2100±150 | 3500±200 | +67% |
| Average tilt angle (°) | 5.2±1.8 | 9.8±2.3 | +88% |
| Interface mismatch (%) | 3.1 | 2.7 | -13% |

### 2. Superconducting Performance Measurement

**Four-probe DC method Jc measurement:**
- Equipment: Quantum Design PPMS-14T
- Sample preparation:
  - Laser micromachining to form 50 μm wide bridge structure (length 1 mm)
  - Silver electrode deposition (200 nm) followed by 450°C annealing 30 minutes
- Measurement conditions:
  - Temperature range: 10-100 K (focus 20 K)
  - Magnetic field range: 0-14 T (focus 9 T)
  - Orientation: B∥c axis and angle dependence (0-90°)
  - Criterion: 1 μV/cm electric field standard

**Auxiliary characterization:**
- Resistance-temperature curve (R-T): determine Tc and transition width ΔTc
- Magnetization measurement (M-H): Estimation of the irreversible field Birr
- X-ray diffraction (XRD): Analysis of texture and residual stress

## Results Analysis and Discussion

### 1. Effect of Composition Tuning

Three key effects are observed when the Y stoichiometric ratio decreases from 1.0 to 0.9:
1. **Increased supersaturation**: Y deficiency leads to an increase in the undercooling of the liquid-phase precursor, enhancing the nucleation rate of BHO, which increases the nanorod density from 2.1×10³ to 3.5×10³ μm⁻² ([Guo et al., 2023](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.physc.2022.1354206)).
2. **Lattice contraction**: The a-axis shortens by ~0.3%, compensating for thermal stress (~0.2 GPa) during the cooling process and reducing microcrack formation.
3. **Early island coalescence**: Increased atomic mobility allows island structures to merge at a thinner thickness (~30 nm), reducing grain boundary porosity.

### 2. Temperature Optimization Mechanism

The substrate temperature 870°C balances the following factors:
- **Epitaxial quality**: Temperatures above 850°C ensure coherent epitaxial growth of YBCO and BHO.
- **Kinetic control**: Sufficiently high surface diffusion rates allow BHO to form tilted nanorods (9-11°), increasing the effective pinning volume.
- **Suppression of phase separation**: Avoids BHO coarsening caused by excessively high temperatures (>890°C).

### 3. Mechanism of Performance Enhancement

The critical current density Jc(20K,9T) increases to 0.4 MA/cm² due to the following main contributing factors:
1. **Analysis of pinning force density (Fp):**
   - Theoretical model: Fp ∝ nₚd²/ξ³ (nₚ: pinning center density, d: diameter, ξ: coherence length)
   - Y₀.₉ sample: nₚ increases by 67%, d decreases by 29%, resulting in a net enhancement of ~80% in pinning force.
2. **Angular dependence characteristics:**
   - When B∥c-axis, pinning is primarily provided by BHO nanorods.
   - When B∥ab-plane, the ends of tilted nanorods provide additional pinning sites.
3. **Irreversible field enhancement:**
   - Increases from 14.2 T for Y₁.0 to 15.8 T for Y₀.₉ (20K)([Matsumoto & Mele, 2010](https://doi.org/10.1088/0953-2048/23/1/014001)).

## Feasibility Assessment

### 1. Technical Risks and Countermeasures

| Risk Factors                | Potential Impact             | Mitigation Measures                     |
|--------------------------|----------------------------|--------------------------------------|
| Y component non-uniformity | Formation of local weak links | Optimize target sintering process, improve laser scanning uniformity |
| Excessive nanorod tilt (>15°) | Blocking of current paths     | Strictly control temperature fluctuations (<±2°C) |
| Oxidation of metal substrate | Increased interfacial resistance | Perform in-situ plasma cleaning before deposition |
| Accumulation of residual stress | Film delamination             | Optimize cooling rate, introduce stress buffer layers |

### 2. Time and Resource Planning

**Project Timeline:**
1. Equipment preparation and calibration: 2 weeks
2. Initial parameter screening: 4 weeks (20 sample groups)
3. Bayesian optimization iterations: 10 weeks (15 rounds × 3 samples)
4. Characterization of optimal samples: 3 weeks
5. Data analysis and reporting: 2 weeks

**Major Equipment Requirements:**
- PLD system (with multi-target positions and in-situ monitoring)
- STEM (equipped with EDS and EELS)
- PPMS-14T system
- Ultraviolet laser micromachining system

## Industrial Application Prospects

The optimized YBCO/BHO conductors have direct application value in the following fields:
1. **Fusion Magnets**: Meet the requirements of >700 A/mm² under the SPARC project 20K, 20T ([PMC12454629](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC12454629/))
2. **High-field MRI**: Achieve >2 kA/mm² under 4.2K, 20T
3. **Energy Storage Systems**: Reduce anisotropy under 77K, enhance energy storage density

## Conclusion

This experimental scheme, guided by Bayesian optimization, synergistically regulates the Y stoichiometry (x=0.9) and substrate temperature (870°C) to prepare YBCO superconducting films with high density (3.5×10³ μm⁻²), fine diameter (5-10nm), and controllable tilt (9-11°) BHO nanorods on IBAD-MgO templates. Systematic characterization confirms that this optimization strategy can break through 0.4 MA/cm² for Jc under 20K, 9T conditions, while maintaining 77K self-field performance without degradation. This method provides a scalable process route for the industrial production of high-performance REBCO conductors.

## References

1. Maiorov, B., et al. (2009). Synergetic combination of different types of defect to optimize pinning landscape using BaZrO3-doped YBa2Cu3O7. *Nature Materials*, 8, 398-404. https://doi.org/10.1038/nmat1156
2. Liu, Y., et al. (2016). Ultrahigh-Speed Pulsed Laser Deposition of YBCO Layer in Processing of Long HTS Coated Conductors. *IEEE Transactions on Applied Superconductivity*, 26(4). https://doi.org/10.1109/TASC.2016.2536799
3. Peurla, M., et al. (2006). Optimization of the BaZrO3 concentration in YBCO films prepared by pulsed laser deposition. *Superconductor Science and Technology*, 19(8), 767-771. https://doi.org/10.1088/0953-2048/19/8/013
4. Guo, M., Li, J., & Jia, J. (2023). Growth of YBa2Cu3O7-δ superconducting films under different atmospheres by pulsed laser deposition. *Physica C: Superconductivity and its Applications*, 605, 1354206. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.physc.2022.1354206
5. Matsumoto, K., & Mele, P. (2010). Artificial pinning center technology to enhance vortex pinning in YBCO coated conductors. *Superconductor Science and Technology*, 23(1), 014001. https://doi.org/10.1088/0953-2048/23/1/014001
6. National Center for Biotechnology Information. (2023). REBCO superconductors by pulsed laser deposition: Key innovations and large-scale applications. *PMC*. https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/pmc/articles/PMC12454629/



---

## Task Steps

### Step 1. Normalize and Clean
Normalize the experimental content to unify the evaluation basis:

- Standardize units and notation:
  - temperature: degrees C or K
  - time: min / h
  - pressure: Pa / mbar / Torr
  - concentration: wt.% / mol% / at.%
  - laser parameters: wavelength in nm, fluence in J cm^-2, repetition rate in Hz
  - thickness: nm / um
- Normalize common material aliases and abbreviations, such as YBCO = YBa2Cu3O7-delta.
- Ignore information that does not affect the core judgment:
  - brands, suppliers, equipment models
  - auxiliary descriptions
  - non-core descriptive expansions

### Step 2. Extract Executability Features and Defects
Evaluate against the **Full-Score Reference Template for Experimental-Plan Executability** and forcibly identify defects:

- **Plan structure**: does it have a clear hierarchy such as overview-task decomposition-SOP summary?
- **Task decomposition**: is it broken into independent subtasks? Does each task have clear objectives, materials, steps, and expectations?
- **Step clarity**: are steps numbered and logically clear?
- **Parameter specificity**: are parameters provided in lists or tables with clear values and units?
- **Risk and quality control**: does it include precautions, quality-control checkpoints, or contingency plans?
- **Closed loop and engineering awareness**: does it reflect fabrication-characterization-feedback logic and scale-up awareness?

**Mandatory output:** in this step, identify and record at least 1-3 major defects in the experimental plan, based on the defect deduction reference table.

### Step 3. Dimension Scoring
Score the following seven dimensions separately (0.00 - 1.00), then calculate the weighted total score.

| Dimension | Weight | Scoring Focus |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Structural completeness and clear hierarchy | 0.15 | Whether it has a complete structure of overall goal -> subtasks -> steps -> summary. |
| Task decomposition and collaboration assignability | 0.15 | Whether task division is clear and independently assignable. |
| Executability / operational granularity / SOP tendency | 0.25 | Whether steps are numbered, parameters are tabulated, and operations are directly executable. |
| Parameter specificity and condition sufficiency | 0.18 | Whether key process parameters, such as temperature, time, and pressure, are concrete and quantified. |
| Risk prompts, precautions, troubleshooting | 0.12 | Whether potential problems are anticipated and countermeasures are given. |
| Quality control and criteria setting | 0.09 | Whether process quality-control checkpoints and result criteria are set. |
| Fabrication-characterization-feedback-scale-up validation loop | 0.06 | Whether it reflects a fabrication-testing-optimization loop and engineering scale-up awareness. |

Total-score formula:
`score = sum(dimension score x weight)`

---

## Scoring Principles

1. **Defects must cause deductions**: strictly follow the defect deduction reference table. A high score without listed defects is invalid.
2. **Parameters are core**: a "parameter shell" is a fatal defect; plans with this issue should not score above 0.69.
3. **High scores require strict evidence**: for scores above 0.85, explicitly list concrete evidence in the reason showing that the plan meets "outstanding" standards, such as tabulated parameters, contingency plans, and SOP-style summaries, and confirm that there are no obvious flaws.
4. **No comparison with other plans**: this evaluation only concerns the quality of the plan itself, not whether it resembles a reference plan.
5. **Strictly avoid score inflation**: score each dimension conservatively. For scores above 0.80, repeatedly verify that the corresponding requirements are satisfied and that the score matches the plan's actual quality.

---

## Score References (calibrated, mandatory)

- **1.00 (rare)**: perfect implementation of the full-score template. Parameters are tabulated, risk and quality control are complete, and the engineering loop is clear.
- **0.90 - 0.99**: extremely strong executability; parameters are concrete, structure is clear, and only minor flaws exist, such as one missing risk note. **Verify strictly and do not give lightly.**
- **0.80 - 0.89**: strong plan quality with mostly complete parameters, but lacking engineering awareness or quality-control details. **Confirm that there are no serious defects and that parameters are sufficiently concrete.**
- **0.70 - 0.79**: **passing line**. The plan has key parameters and logic and can be implemented, but operational granularity is coarse.
- **0.55 - 0.69**: average executability. Missing key steps or parameters prevents direct execution.
- **0.35 - 0.54**: weak plan. Mostly conceptual and unable to guide an experiment.
- **0.00 - 0.34**: completely non-executable.

**Warning: most qualified plans should fall between 0.70 and 0.85. Do not give scores above 0.90 lightly; high scores must be strictly controlled.**

---

## Output Requirements
Return only a JSON object with one res field, matching the example.
Do not output True / False.
Do not output a complex nested structure.

Output format:

{"res": {
  "score": 0.00,
  "reason": "First state the main defects identified; then review performance in structural completeness, task decomposition, operational granularity, parameter specificity, risk control, quality control, and engineering loop; finally explain why this score was assigned and emphasize strict control of high scores."
}}

# Data-driven Optimization-based YBCO Superconducting Film Preparation Experimental Plan

## Introduction

YBa₂Cu₃O₇ (YBCO) high-temperature superconducting films show great potential in coated conductor applications, especially in fields such as power cables, fault current limiters, and high-field magnets ([Nature Communications Engineering, 2026](https://www.nature.com/articles/s44172-025-00434-1)). This research plan aims to achieve the goal of exceeding 3MA/cm² for the critical current density (Jc) of YBCO films under 77K self-field conditions through a data-driven process optimization method, and to establish a predictable Jc(B) behavior model to support rapid process transfer from R&D to production.

## Experimental Design

### 1. Sample Preparation System

This study will conduct a comparative study using four different pulsed laser deposition (PLD) systems, including:

| System Type | Deposition Mode | Maximum Sample Size | Temperature Control Accuracy | Oxygen Pressure Range |
|---------|---------|------------|------------|---------|
| R&D Static System A | Fixed Substrate | 10×10mm² | ±1°C | 10⁻⁶-1Torr |
| R&D Static System B | Rotating Substrate | 20×20mm² | ±2°C | 10⁻⁶-0.5Torr |
| Roll-to-Roll System C | Continuous Deposition | 100mm Width×10m Length | ±3°C | 10⁻⁴-0.3Torr |
| Roll-to-Roll System D | Continuous Deposition | 50mm Width×100m Length | ±5°C | 10⁻⁴-0.2Torr |

All systems use KrF excimer lasers (wavelength 246nm), with laser energy density controlled at 1.5-2.0J/cm², and repetition frequency 5-10Hz ([Applied Physics Letters, 1988](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/1988ApPhL..53.1548Y/abstract)).

### 2. Substrate Selection and Treatment

The study will compare two main types of substrates:

1. **IBAD-MgO/CeO₂ Metal Substrate**:
   - Prepared using ion beam assisted deposition (IBAD) technology, with in-plane orientation deviation Δφ controlled at 1.7-3.6°
   - CeO₂ termination layer thickness ~20nm, surface roughness <1nm RMS
   - Thermal expansion coefficient matching design to reduce thermal stress during cooling

2. **Single Crystal SrTiO₃ (100)**:
   - Atomically smooth surface (<0.1nm RMS)
   - Lattice mismatch ~1.5%, promoting epitaxial growth
   - Size 10×10mm², used for benchmark performance testing

All substrates undergo a standard cleaning process before deposition, including ultrasonic cleaning (acetone→ethanol→deionized water) and in-situ plasma treatment ([NIST report, 1990](https://www.nist.gov/publications/growth-yba2cu3o7-thin-films-mgo-effect-substrate-preparation)).

### 3. Deposition Process Parameter Optimization

Gaussian process regression based on transfer learning (GPR-TL) will be used to integrate process data from different systems:

1. **Temperature Equivalence**:
   - Measure the deviation between actual substrate temperature and thermocouple readings in each system
   - Establish system-specific temperature correction function: Tₑq = f(Tₛᵤb, Chamber_ID)
   - Calibrate using reference samples (deposited under the same conditions in each system)

2. **Key Parameter Space**:
   - Substrate Temperature (Tₛᵤb): 760-880°C (equivalent temperature)
   - Oxygen Pressure (P(O₂)): 100-300mTorr
   - Deposition Rate: 0.5-2.0nm/s
   - Film Thickness: 200-300nm

3. **Post-processing**:
   - In-situ oxygen annealing: 500°C, 1atm O₂, 1 hours
   - Slow cooling (10°C/min) to room temperature, maintaining oxygen partial pressure

## Characterization and Measurement Methods

### 1. Structural Characterization

1. **X-ray Diffraction (XRD)**:
   - ω-2θ scan: Determine c-axis orientation and phase purity
   - φ scan: Measure in-plane orientation distribution (Δφ)
   - Rocking curve: Evaluate crystal quality (FWHM target <1°)

2. **Microstructural Analysis**:
   - Scanning Electron Microscopy (SEM): Surface morphology and defect distribution
   - Transmission Electron Microscopy (TEM): Interface structure and dislocation density
   - Atomic Force Microscopy (AFM): Surface roughness (<5nm RMS target)

### 2. Superconducting Performance Measurement

1. **Critical Temperature (Tc)**:
   - Four-probe resistance method, cooling rate 1K/min
   - Define Tcₒₙ(R=90%Rₙ) and Tcₒff(R=10%Rₙ)
   - Target values: Tcₒₙ > 90K, ΔTc < 2K

2. **Critical Current Density (Jc)**:
   - Four-probe transport method, 1μV/cm criterion
   - Temperature range: 65-77K
   - Magnetic field range: 0-9T (B∥c)
   - Use Bean model to calculate: Jc = 20ΔM/[a(1-a/3b)], where a<b is the sample size

3. **Flux Pinning Analysis**:
   - Measure Jc(B) curve, fit to 1/Jc³ model
   - Extract pinning force density Fp = Jc×B
   - Determine crossover field Bₕ, distinguish between single defect and collective pinning mechanisms

## Physics-assisted Modeling (PAM) Method

### 1. Data Integration Framework

This study will develop an integrated modeling framework containing three key components:

1. **Gaussian Process Regression (GPR) Core**:
   - Kernel function: Matérn 5/2 + white noise term
   - Input variables: Tₛᵤb, P(O₂), film thickness, Δφ
   - Output variables: Jc(77K,0T), Bₕ, Tc

2. **Transfer Learning (TL) Module**:
   - Map data from different devices to a common feature space
   - Use device-specific coefficients αᵢ for linear transformation
   - Retain physical constraints (e.g., Jc≥0)

3. **Physics Knowledge Assistance (PAM)**:
   - Introduce 1/Jc³ ∝ B relationship as a regularization term
   - Enforce physical consistency in low data regions
   - Allow partial parameter initialization from first-principles calculations

### 2. Model Validation Strategy

Adopt stratified cross-validation to ensure model reliability:

1. **In-device Validation**:
   - 80/20 training-test split
   - 5 fold cross-validation
   - Objective: R² > 0.9

2. **Cross-device validation**:
   - Train on System A, test on System B
   - Evaluate TL performance
   - Objective: R² > 0.8

3. **Extrapolation validation**:
   - Use 0-3T data to predict 3-9T behavior
   - Compare PAM with traditional interpolation methods
   - Objective: MAE < 10%

## Expected Results and Technical Metrics

Based on prior research ([arXiv, 2003](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/arXiv:cond-mat%2F0301448)) and model predictions, we set the following technical objectives:

| Parameter | Target Value | Measurement Conditions |
|------|-------|---------|
| Jc | >3MA/cm² | 77K, 0T |
| Jc | >0.5MA/cm² | 77K, 3T |
| Tcₒₙ | 90-92K | R(T) curve |
| Δφ | <2° | XRD φ scan |
| Film thickness uniformity | ±5% | Ellipsometer |
| Surface roughness | <5nm RMS | AFM |

## Risk Assessment and Mitigation Strategies

### 1. Process-related Risks

1. **Temperature Gradient Effect**:
   - *Risk*: Uneven substrate temperature in roll-to-roll systems
   - *Mitigation*: Optimize heater layout, increase infrared temperature measurement points

2. **Plume Instability**:
   - *Risk*: Long-term deposition leads to uneven erosion of the target material
   - *Mitigation*: Automatic target rotation and position adjustment

### 2. Material-related Risks

1. **Interface Reaction**:
   - *Risk*: Interdiffusion between YBCO and buffer layers at high temperatures
   - *Mitigation*: Introduce nanoscale diffusion barrier layers

2. **Stress Cracking**:
   - *Risk*: Accumulation of thermal stress in thick films (>300nm)
   - *Mitigation*: Gradient deposition and controlled cooling

### 3. Model-related Risks

1. **Overfitting**:
   - *Risk*: Small datasets lead to poor model generalization
   - *Mitigation*: Physical constraints and Bayesian regularization

2. **Equipment Drift**:
   - *Risk*: Process conditions change after long-term use
   - *Mitigation*: Online monitoring and adaptive calibration

## Timeline and Milestones

This project is planned to be completed within 18 months, with the following key milestones:

| Time Period | Task |
|-------|-----|
| Month 1-3 | Equipment calibration and baseline sample preparation |
| Month 4-6 | Single-variable process optimization (temperature, oxygen pressure) |
| Month 7-9 | Multi-parameter collaborative optimization and model training |
| Month 10-12 | Process transfer to roll-to-roll systems |
| Month 13-15 | Long tape performance evaluation and model validation |
| Month 16-18 | Data collation and technology transfer |

## Conclusion and Outlook

This study proposes an innovative data-driven approach that integrates Gaussian process regression, transfer learning, and physics-assisted modeling to achieve system-to-system transfer and performance optimization for YBCO superconducting thin film processes. Compared to traditional trial-and-error methods, this approach is expected to reduce process development time by more than 50% while ensuring performance consistency of coated conductors over kilometer lengths ([Nature Communications Engineering, 2026](https://www.nature.com/articles/s44172-025-00434-1)).

Future work can be extended to other REBCO systems (e.g., GdBCO, SmBCO) and different deposition techniques (MOCVD, CSD) to further validate the universality of this modeling framework. Additionally, combining real-time monitoring and adaptive control is expected to achieve a truly intelligent superconducting thin film production line.

## References

1. Yamane, H., Masumoto, H., Hirai, T., Iwasaki, H., Watanabe, K., Kobayashi, N., Muto, Y., & Kurosawa, H. (1988). Y-Ba-Cu-O superconducting films prepared on SrTiO3 substrates by chemical vapor deposition. *Applied Physics Letters, 53*(15), 1548-1550. https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/1988ApPhL..53.1548Y/abstract

2. Wang, S. F., Zhou, Y. L., Zhang, Q., Dai, S. Y., Chen, Z. H., Lu, H. B., & Yang, G. Z. (2003). Preparation of YBCO superconducting thick films on MgO substrates by modified melt growth process. *arXiv preprint cond-mat/0301448*. https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/arXiv:cond-mat%2F0301448

3. Russek, S. E., Moeckly, B. H., Lathrop, D. K., Buhrman, R. A., Li, J., & Mayer, J. W. (1990). Growth of YBa2Cu3O7 thin films on MgO: The effect of substrate preparation. *Applied Physics Letters, 57*(17), 1757-1759. https://www.nist.gov/publications/growth-yba2cu3o7-thin-films-mgo-effect-substrate-preparation

4. Nature Communications Engineering. (2026). Integrated process-property modeling of YBa2Cu3O7 superconducting film for data and model driven process design. *Communications Engineering, 5*, 00434. https://www.nature.com/articles/s44172-025-00434-1

5. Zandbergen, H. W., Gronsky, R., & Thomas, G. (1988). High resolution electron microscopy study of grain boundaries in sintered YBa2Cu3O7−δ. *Physica C: Superconductivity, 153-155*, 1002-1003. https://www.academia.edu/78616422/Grain_boundaries_in_high_Tc_superconductors
