# Data-driven Optimization-based YBCO Superconducting Film Preparation Experimental Plan

## Introduction

YBa₂Cu₃O₇ (YBCO) high-temperature superconducting films show great potential in coated conductor applications, especially in fields such as power cables, fault current limiters, and high-field magnets ([Nature Communications Engineering, 2026](https://www.nature.com/articles/s44172-025-00434-1)). This research plan aims to achieve the goal of exceeding 3MA/cm² for the critical current density (Jc) of YBCO films under 77K self-field conditions through a data-driven process optimization method, and to establish a predictable Jc(B) behavior model to support rapid process transfer from R&D to production.

## Experimental Design

### 1. Sample Preparation System

This study will conduct a comparative study using four different pulsed laser deposition (PLD) systems, including:

| System Type | Deposition Mode | Maximum Sample Size | Temperature Control Accuracy | Oxygen Pressure Range |
|---------|---------|------------|------------|---------|
| R&D Static System A | Fixed Substrate | 10×10mm² | ±1°C | 10⁻⁶-1Torr |
| R&D Static System B | Rotating Substrate | 20×20mm² | ±2°C | 10⁻⁶-0.5Torr |
| Roll-to-Roll System C | Continuous Deposition | 100mm Width×10m Length | ±3°C | 10⁻⁴-0.3Torr |
| Roll-to-Roll System D | Continuous Deposition | 50mm Width×100m Length | ±5°C | 10⁻⁴-0.2Torr |

All systems use KrF excimer lasers (wavelength 246nm), with laser energy density controlled at 1.5-2.0J/cm², and repetition frequency 5-10Hz ([Applied Physics Letters, 1988](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/1988ApPhL..53.1548Y/abstract)).

### 2. Substrate Selection and Treatment

The study will compare two main types of substrates:

1. **IBAD-MgO/CeO₂ Metal Substrate**:
   - Prepared using ion beam assisted deposition (IBAD) technology, with in-plane orientation deviation Δφ controlled at 1.7-3.6°
   - CeO₂ termination layer thickness ~20nm, surface roughness <1nm RMS
   - Thermal expansion coefficient matching design to reduce thermal stress during cooling

2. **Single Crystal SrTiO₃ (100)**:
   - Atomically smooth surface (<0.1nm RMS)
   - Lattice mismatch ~1.5%, promoting epitaxial growth
   - Size 10×10mm², used for benchmark performance testing

All substrates undergo a standard cleaning process before deposition, including ultrasonic cleaning (acetone→ethanol→deionized water) and in-situ plasma treatment ([NIST report, 1990](https://www.nist.gov/publications/growth-yba2cu3o7-thin-films-mgo-effect-substrate-preparation)).

### 3. Deposition Process Parameter Optimization

Gaussian process regression based on transfer learning (GPR-TL) will be used to integrate process data from different systems:

1. **Temperature Equivalence**:
   - Measure the deviation between actual substrate temperature and thermocouple readings in each system
   - Establish system-specific temperature correction function: Tₑq = f(Tₛᵤb, Chamber_ID)
   - Calibrate using reference samples (deposited under the same conditions in each system)

2. **Key Parameter Space**:
   - Substrate Temperature (Tₛᵤb): 760-880°C (equivalent temperature)
   - Oxygen Pressure (P(O₂)): 100-300mTorr
   - Deposition Rate: 0.5-2.0nm/s
   - Film Thickness: 200-300nm

3. **Post-processing**:
   - In-situ oxygen annealing: 500°C, 1atm O₂, 1 hours
   - Slow cooling (10°C/min) to room temperature, maintaining oxygen partial pressure

## Characterization and Measurement Methods

### 1. Structural Characterization

1. **X-ray Diffraction (XRD)**:
   - ω-2θ scan: Determine c-axis orientation and phase purity
   - φ scan: Measure in-plane orientation distribution (Δφ)
   - Rocking curve: Evaluate crystal quality (FWHM target <1°)

2. **Microstructural Analysis**:
   - Scanning Electron Microscopy (SEM): Surface morphology and defect distribution
   - Transmission Electron Microscopy (TEM): Interface structure and dislocation density
   - Atomic Force Microscopy (AFM): Surface roughness (<5nm RMS target)

### 2. Superconducting Performance Measurement

1. **Critical Temperature (Tc)**:
   - Four-probe resistance method, cooling rate 1K/min
   - Define Tcₒₙ(R=90%Rₙ) and Tcₒff(R=10%Rₙ)
   - Target values: Tcₒₙ > 90K, ΔTc < 2K

2. **Critical Current Density (Jc)**:
   - Four-probe transport method, 1μV/cm criterion
   - Temperature range: 65-77K
   - Magnetic field range: 0-9T (B∥c)
   - Use Bean model to calculate: Jc = 20ΔM/[a(1-a/3b)], where a<b is the sample size

3. **Flux Pinning Analysis**:
   - Measure Jc(B) curve, fit to 1/Jc³ model
   - Extract pinning force density Fp = Jc×B
   - Determine crossover field Bₕ, distinguish between single defect and collective pinning mechanisms

## Physics-assisted Modeling (PAM) Method

### 1. Data Integration Framework

This study will develop an integrated modeling framework containing three key components:

1. **Gaussian Process Regression (GPR) Core**:
   - Kernel function: Matérn 5/2 + white noise term
   - Input variables: Tₛᵤb, P(O₂), film thickness, Δφ
   - Output variables: Jc(77K,0T), Bₕ, Tc

2. **Transfer Learning (TL) Module**:
   - Map data from different devices to a common feature space
   - Use device-specific coefficients αᵢ for linear transformation
   - Retain physical constraints (e.g., Jc≥0)

3. **Physics Knowledge Assistance (PAM)**:
   - Introduce 1/Jc³ ∝ B relationship as a regularization term
   - Enforce physical consistency in low data regions
   - Allow partial parameter initialization from first-principles calculations

### 2. Model Validation Strategy

Adopt stratified cross-validation to ensure model reliability:

1. **In-device Validation**:
   - 80/20 training-test split
   - 5 fold cross-validation
   - Objective: R² > 0.9

2. **Cross-device validation**:
   - Train on System A, test on System B
   - Evaluate TL performance
   - Objective: R² > 0.8

3. **Extrapolation validation**:
   - Use 0-3T data to predict 3-9T behavior
   - Compare PAM with traditional interpolation methods
   - Objective: MAE < 10%

## Expected Results and Technical Metrics

Based on prior research ([arXiv, 2003](https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/arXiv:cond-mat%2F0301448)) and model predictions, we set the following technical objectives:

| Parameter | Target Value | Measurement Conditions |
|------|-------|---------|
| Jc | >3MA/cm² | 77K, 0T |
| Jc | >0.5MA/cm² | 77K, 3T |
| Tcₒₙ | 90-92K | R(T) curve |
| Δφ | <2° | XRD φ scan |
| Film thickness uniformity | ±5% | Ellipsometer |
| Surface roughness | <5nm RMS | AFM |

## Risk Assessment and Mitigation Strategies

### 1. Process-related Risks

1. **Temperature Gradient Effect**:
   - *Risk*: Uneven substrate temperature in roll-to-roll systems
   - *Mitigation*: Optimize heater layout, increase infrared temperature measurement points

2. **Plume Instability**:
   - *Risk*: Long-term deposition leads to uneven erosion of the target material
   - *Mitigation*: Automatic target rotation and position adjustment

### 2. Material-related Risks

1. **Interface Reaction**:
   - *Risk*: Interdiffusion between YBCO and buffer layers at high temperatures
   - *Mitigation*: Introduce nanoscale diffusion barrier layers

2. **Stress Cracking**:
   - *Risk*: Accumulation of thermal stress in thick films (>300nm)
   - *Mitigation*: Gradient deposition and controlled cooling

### 3. Model-related Risks

1. **Overfitting**:
   - *Risk*: Small datasets lead to poor model generalization
   - *Mitigation*: Physical constraints and Bayesian regularization

2. **Equipment Drift**:
   - *Risk*: Process conditions change after long-term use
   - *Mitigation*: Online monitoring and adaptive calibration

## Timeline and Milestones

This project is planned to be completed within 18 months, with the following key milestones:

| Time Period | Task |
|-------|-----|
| Month 1-3 | Equipment calibration and baseline sample preparation |
| Month 4-6 | Single-variable process optimization (temperature, oxygen pressure) |
| Month 7-9 | Multi-parameter collaborative optimization and model training |
| Month 10-12 | Process transfer to roll-to-roll systems |
| Month 13-15 | Long tape performance evaluation and model validation |
| Month 16-18 | Data collation and technology transfer |

## Conclusion and Outlook

This study proposes an innovative data-driven approach that integrates Gaussian process regression, transfer learning, and physics-assisted modeling to achieve system-to-system transfer and performance optimization for YBCO superconducting thin film processes. Compared to traditional trial-and-error methods, this approach is expected to reduce process development time by more than 50% while ensuring performance consistency of coated conductors over kilometer lengths ([Nature Communications Engineering, 2026](https://www.nature.com/articles/s44172-025-00434-1)).

Future work can be extended to other REBCO systems (e.g., GdBCO, SmBCO) and different deposition techniques (MOCVD, CSD) to further validate the universality of this modeling framework. Additionally, combining real-time monitoring and adaptive control is expected to achieve a truly intelligent superconducting thin film production line.

## References

Y-Ba-Cu-O superconducting films prepared on SrTiO3 substrates by chemical vapor deposition. *Applied Physics Letters, 53*(15), 1548-1550. https://ui.adsabs.harvard.edu/abs/1988ApPhL..53.1548Y/abstract

# Research Plan for Controlling Vortex Dynamics in EuBa₂Cu₃O₇ Thin Films with BaHfO₃ Pinning Centers Grown by PLD

## Abstract
This study systematically investigates the synergistic effects of pinning center morphology (ranging from 4.5 nm nanoparticles to nanorods) and volume fraction on the critical current density (J_c) and vortex creep (S) in EuBa₂Cu₃O₇ (EuBCO) superconducting thin films prepared by pulsed laser deposition (PLD) with 1.9-4.8 vol% BaHfO₃ (BHO) pinning centers. The experimental design includes three major components: material preparation, microstructural characterization, and electromagnetic performance testing, focusing on resolving the contradiction where BHO doping enhances J_c while accelerating creep. The goal is to develop coated conductors ([Liu et al., 2026](https://arxiv.org/html/2507.01119)) with high J_c (target value: 60K/1T under 2 MA cm⁻²) and low creep rates (S<0.02) for 20-77K high-field magnet applications.

## 1. Experimental Design

### 1.1 Sample Preparation Scheme
EuBCO thin films are grown on Hastelloy substrates buffered with IBAD-MgO/Gd₂Zr₂O₇/Y₂O₃/LaMnO₃/CeO₂ using PLD technology. The doping concentration gradient of 0-4.8 vol% is achieved by adjusting the BHO target ratio:

| Sample ID | BHO Volume Fraction | Deposition Temperature (°C) | Oxygen Annealing Conditions |
|---------|------------|-------------|-----------|
| EU-0    | 0 vol%     | 1150        | 300°C/1h  |
| EU-1.9  | 1.9 vol%   | 1055        | 250°C/2h  |
| EU-2.8  | 2.8 vol%   | 1055        | 275°C/1.5h|
| EU-3.8  | 3.8 vol%   | 1055        | 300°C/1h  |
| EU-4.8  | 4.8 vol%   | 1055        | 350°C/0.5h|

*Table 1. EuBCO Thin Film Growth Parameter Design, Referenced from ([Nature Communications Materials, 2025](https://www.nature.com/articles/s43246-025-01054-0))*

Key process control points:
1. **Temperature Control**: Undoped BHO samples are deposited at 1150°C high temperatures to promote Eu₂O₃ precipitation (~20 nm) and dislocation network formation; BHO-doped samples are reduced to 1055°C to maintain BHO nanostructure coherence.
2. **Oxygen Annealing Optimization**: Carrier concentration is regulated to p≈0.152 through 250-350°C gradient annealing to ensure optimal superconducting performance.
3. **Strain Engineering**: The lattice mismatch between BHO (lattice constant 4.16 Å) and EuBCO (ab-plane 3.82 Å) of 7.8% generates localized strain fields around nanorods to enhance pinning potential U₀.

### 1.2 Control Group Design
To clarify the specificity of the EuBCO-BHO system, two types of control groups are set:
1. **Material Control**: (Y,Gd)BCO thin films prepared by MOD method (containing 3 vol% BHO) to verify differences in vortex dynamics of incoherent pinning centers.
2. **Structural Control**: TEM is used to confirm the evolution of BHO morphology with concentration:
   - 1.9 vol%: Isolated nanoparticles (4.5±1 nm)
   - 2.8 vol%: Partially connected quasi-nanorods
   - ≥3.8 vol%: Fully developed nanorods (diameter ~5 nm, length >50 nm)

## 2. Characterization and Measurement Methods

### 2.1 Microstructural Characterization
1. **Transmission Electron Microscopy (TEM)**:
   - Cross-sectional HAADF-STEM imaging using JEOL ARM-200F, resolution 0.08 nm
   - EDS mapping analysis to determine BHO distribution uniformity (standard deviation <5%)
   - Measure nanorod tilt angle (key parameter: average splay angle increases from 2° to 8° at >2.8 vol%)

2. **X-ray Diffraction (XRD)**:
   - Using PANalytical X'Pert PRO MRD system to measure:
     - (005) Rocking curve FWHM <2° to verify c-axis texture
     - φ scan (103 peak) to confirm biaxial texture (Δφ <5°)

### 2.2 Electromagnetic Performance Testing
1. **Critical Current Density (J_c)**:
   - Use Quantum Design MPMS3 SQUID magnetometer to measure magnetization curves under 4.2-77K, 0-7T
   - Calculate using the Bean model: J_c = 20ΔM/[a(1-a/3b)], where a×b=3×1 mm² sample size

2. **Vortex Creep Rate (S)**:
   - Standard procedure: record 1 hours of magnetic moment relaxation at constant temperature/magnetic field
   - Fitting formula: M(t) = M₀[1-(kBT/U₀)ln(t/t₀)], S ≡ -dlnM/dlnt
   - Focus on the variation pattern of S value under 30K/1T conditions

3. **Glass State Exponent (μ)**:
   - Fit the collective creep interpolation formula through the S(T) curve: S = T/[U₀ + μkBTln(J₀/J)]
   - Determine pinning mechanism transition: μ≈1/9 (single vortex)→7/9 (vortex bundle)→1 (Bose glass state)

## 3. Expected Results and Data Analysis

### 3.1 Nonlinear Relationship between J_c and BHO Concentration
According to previous research ([Liu et al., 2026](https://arxiv.org/html/2507.01119)), the following pattern is expected:

| BHO vol% | J_c(1.8K,5T) (MA cm⁻²) | J_c(60K,1T) (MA cm⁻²) | α index |
|----------|------------------------|-----------------------|-------|
| 0        | 5.0±0.3                | 0.6±0.05              | 0.58  |
| 1.9      | 15.2±0.8               | 1.2±0.1               | 0.35  |
| 2.8      | 31.0±1.5               | 2.0±0.2               | 0.22  |
| 3.8      | 25.4±1.2               | 1.8±0.15              | 0.25  |
| 4.8      | 18.7±0.9               | 1.5±0.1               | 0.30  |

*Table 2. Expected Critical Current Density and Magnetic Field Dependence Index (α≡-dlnJ_c/dlnB)*

The J_c peak appears at 2.8 vol%, at this point:
- BHO nanorod spacing ≈ 50 nm ≈ 2λ_ab(60K), meeting the optimal pinning matching condition
- μ≈7/9 indicates entry into large vortex bundle pinning or Bose glass state

### 3.2 Anomalous Phenomena in Creep Behavior
Unlike (Y,Gd)BCO, the EuBCO-BHO system exhibits unique characteristics:
1. **Intrinsic Low Creep**: Undoped samples show S(30K,1T)=0.015 due to high-density dislocation networks (>10¹⁰ cm⁻²) and Eu₂O₃ precipitation
2. **"Double-Edged Sword" Effect of BHO**:
   - At 2.8 vol%: S increases to 0.020, but J_c increases by 6 times
   - At 4.8 vol%: Nanorod tilt leads to double-kink excitation, S sharply rises to 0.025

This can be explained by TDGL theory simulation ([Nature Communications Materials, 2025](https://www.nature.com/articles/s43246-025-01054-0)): coherent nanorods facilitate rapid sliding of vortex segments along the c-axis, while randomly distributed dislocations can inhibit this process.

## 4. Feasibility Assessment and Risk Control

### 4.1 Technical Feasibility
1. **Equipment Assurance**:
   - PLD system (Coherent Compex Pro 205) equipped with 248 nm KrF laser, energy density 2 J/cm²
   - In-situ RHEED monitoring of growth mode to ensure epitaxial quality
2. **Time Planning**:
   - Sample preparation: 2 weeks/batch (including annealing)
   - Characterization testing: Complete full set of TEM/SQUID analysis in 3 weeks

### 4.2 Main Risks and Countermeasures
1. **Uncontrolled Nanorod Tilt**:
   - Risk: Strain accumulation leads to nanorod orientation disorder at >3 vol% BHO
   - Countermeasure: Introduce 10 nm thick SrTiO₃ spacer layer to disperse strain
2. **Oxygen Content Non-uniformity**:
   - Risk: Oxygen diffusion is hindered in thick films (>1 μm)
   - Countermeasure: Use two-step annealing (350°C/1h→250°C/24h)

## 5. Scientific Significance and Application Prospects
This study will reveal:
1. **Relationship between Pinning Center Morphology and Performance**: Establish a quantitative correlation between the aspect ratio of BHO nanorods and vortex bundle size
2. **New Strategy for Creep Suppression**: Block double-kink propagation by co-doping with random defects (e.g., Ir nanoparticles)

# Task: Evaluate the Executability of an Experimental Plan

Your task is to evaluate whether a given **experimental plan** has the qualities of a high-quality, implementable, executable plan.

This evaluation **only focuses on the quality of the plan itself**. It does not compare the plan with any reference plan or judge consistency with another plan.

---

## Evaluation Goal

Judge whether the experimental plan is a high-quality experimental document that is **executable, divisible into tasks, actionable, and convertible into an SOP or implementation plan**. Evaluate it strictly against the following reference template for a full-score plan.

---

## Full-Score Reference Template for Experimental-Plan Executability

A top-tier experimental plan should have the following five features:

### 1. Overall Plan Structure (clear hierarchy, closed logic)
- **Experimental overview/objective**: clearly states the core scientific or engineering problem, final goal, and key innovation.
- **Initial experimental draft/summary**: provides a high-level summary of materials, workflow, and expected outcomes.
- **Detailed experimental plan (task decomposition)**: decomposes the full experiment into logically connected, independently executable subtasks, such as Task 1: material preparation, Task 2: sample processing, Task 3: performance testing.
- **Refined experimental plan (SOP-style summary)**: summarizes key steps, parameters, and criteria in parameter tables, workflow tables, or similar forms to create a standardized document that can directly guide operations.

### 2. Task Modularity and Divisibility (clear breakdown, clear responsibility)
- **Clear subtask division**: each subtask includes its own objective, materials and instruments, steps, and expected results.
- **Connections between tasks**: clearly explains how outputs from earlier tasks become inputs for later tasks.
- **Independent operability**: each subtask is complete enough to be assigned to different team members.

### 3. SOP Level of Steps and Parameters (specific, quantitative, reproducible)
- **Detailed step breakdown**: each experimental step is decomposed into numbered concrete operations, such as 3.1 precursor preparation, 3.2 calcination, 3.3 molding.
- **Parameter tables**: key process parameters should be listed clearly in table form, including temperature, time, pressure, rate, atmosphere, concrete values, and tolerance ranges.
- **Instrument and material lists**: clearly list required material specifications, such as purity and dimensions, and key instrument performance specifications.

### 4. Risk Control and Quality Management (anticipate problems, set checkpoints)
- **Precautions**: after each key step, explicitly state possible issues and preventive measures.
- **Quality-control checkpoints**: set checkpoints after key steps, such as verifying phase by XRD or roughness by AFM.
- **Troubleshooting and contingency plans**: provide alternatives or adjustment strategies for undesirable results.

### 5. Expected Results and Feedback Loop (goal-oriented, measurable)
- **Quantified expected results**: explicitly state target performance indicators, such as Jc >= 1e4 A cm^-2 or delta-phi < 5 degrees.
- **Fabrication-characterization-feedback loop**: the workflow should reflect an iterative logic of fabrication -> characterization -> result analysis -> parameter optimization.
- **Engineering and scale-up awareness**: consider industrialization factors such as process scalability, long tape, and large-area uniformity.

---

## Score Calibration and Mandatory Defect Check (anti-inflation mechanism)

**Important instruction: to prevent inflated scores, you must strictly follow the calibration process below.**

### Step 0. Mandatory Identification of Executability Defects (deductions first)
Before calculating the score, compare the experimental plan item by item against the full-score template and explicitly list its **executability defects**.

**Defect deduction reference table (for calibrating your scoring perception):**
| Defect Category | Concrete Symptom | Suggested Deduction | Score-Band Implication |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Broken structure** | Only flat narrative description; no task decomposition and no overview-detail-summary structure. | 0.20 - 0.30 | Falls below 0.70 |
| **Parameter shell** | Mentions process names but gives **no** concrete values, such as missing temperature, time, and pressure. | 0.20 - 0.30 | Falls below 0.70 |
| **No closed loop** | Contains only fabrication steps and no characterization, testing, or validation. | 0.15 - 0.25 | Very difficult to exceed 0.75 |
| **Coarse granularity** | Steps remain slogan-level, such as "optimize process parameters", without operational details. | 0.15 - 0.20 | Ceiling is 0.80 |
| **No risk awareness** | No precautions, possible issues, or quality-control descriptions. | 0.10 - 0.15 | Ceiling is 0.85 |
| **Not quantifiable** | Expected results are only qualitative, such as "performance improves", with no concrete metrics or criteria. | 0.05 - 0.10 | Ceiling is 0.90 |

### Recalibrated Score-Band Anchors (mandatory comparison)
Before giving the final score, force-align the plan with these descriptions:

- **0.90 - 1.00 (excellent/outstanding)**: **rare**. Must satisfy: strong fit with the full-score template, tabulated parameters, complete risk and quality control. **If there is no engineering/SOP-style expression, do not give above 0.95.**
- **0.80 - 0.89 (good/strong)**: has strengths but visible flaws. Example: clear structure and concrete parameters, but missing risk prompts or troubleshooting; or some parameters are missing and would require literature lookup before execution.
- **0.70 - 0.79 (qualified/executability threshold)**: the most common floor range. The plan is coherent, has key parameters, and follows a reasonable experimental logic, but lacks detail granularity. This is the minimum passing line for executability.
- **0.55 - 0.69 (unqualified/unreliable)**: has clear defects, such as missing key parameters that prevent operation, workflow jumps, or no quality-control measures.
- **0.00 - 0.54 (very poor/unrelated)**: conceptual description that can hardly guide an experiment.

### Scoring-Logic Correction
Follow this logic:
1. **If serious defects such as "parameter shell" or "broken structure" are found** -> **cap the score at 0.69**.
2. **If key parameters are present but operational details are absent** -> **score should be in the 0.70 - 0.78 range**.
3. **Strictly control high scores**: scores above 0.85 require strict verification that the plan fully satisfies the corresponding score-band requirements, avoiding subjective score inflation.

---

# Research Plan for Controlling Vortex Dynamics in EuBa₂Cu₃O₇ Thin Films with BaHfO₃ Pinning Centers Grown by PLD

## Abstract
This study systematically investigates the synergistic effects of pinning center morphology (ranging from 4.5 nm nanoparticles to nanorods) and volume fraction on the critical current density (J_c) and vortex creep (S) in EuBa₂Cu₃O₇ (EuBCO) superconducting thin films prepared by pulsed laser deposition (PLD) with 1.9-4.8 vol% BaHfO₃ (BHO) pinning centers. The experimental design includes three major components: material preparation, microstructural characterization, and electromagnetic performance testing, focusing on resolving the contradiction where BHO doping enhances J_c while accelerating creep. The goal is to develop coated conductors ([Liu et al., 2026](https://arxiv.org/html/2507.01119)) with high J_c (target value: 60K/1T under 2 MA cm⁻²) and low creep rates (S<0.02) for 20-77K high-field magnet applications.

## 1. Experimental Design

### 1.1 Sample Preparation Scheme
EuBCO thin films are grown on Hastelloy substrates buffered with IBAD-MgO/Gd₂Zr₂O₇/Y₂O₃/LaMnO₃/CeO₂ using PLD technology. The doping concentration gradient of 0-4.8 vol% is achieved by adjusting the BHO target ratio:

| Sample ID | BHO Volume Fraction | Deposition Temperature (°C) | Oxygen Annealing Conditions |
|---------|------------|-------------|-----------|
| EU-0    | 0 vol%     | 1150        | 300°C/1h  |
| EU-1.9  | 1.9 vol%   | 1055        | 250°C/2h  |
| EU-2.8  | 2.8 vol%   | 1055        | 275°C/1.5h|
| EU-3.8  | 3.8 vol%   | 1055        | 300°C/1h  |
| EU-4.8  | 4.8 vol%   | 1055        | 350°C/0.5h|

*Table 1. EuBCO Thin Film Growth Parameter Design, Referenced from ([Nature Communications Materials, 2025](https://www.nature.com/articles/s43246-025-01054-0))*

Key process control points:
1. **Temperature Control**: Undoped BHO samples are deposited at 1150°C high temperatures to promote Eu₂O₃ precipitation (~20 nm) and dislocation network formation; BHO-doped samples are reduced to 1055°C to maintain BHO nanostructure coherence.
2. **Oxygen Annealing Optimization**: Carrier concentration is regulated to p≈0.152 through 250-350°C gradient annealing to ensure optimal superconducting performance.
3. **Strain Engineering**: The lattice mismatch between BHO (lattice constant 4.16 Å) and EuBCO (ab-plane 3.82 Å) of 7.8% generates localized strain fields around nanorods to enhance pinning potential U₀.

### 1.2 Control Group Design
To clarify the specificity of the EuBCO-BHO system, two types of control groups are set:
1. **Material Control**: (Y,Gd)BCO thin films prepared by MOD method (containing 3 vol% BHO) to verify differences in vortex dynamics of incoherent pinning centers.
2. **Structural Control**: TEM is used to confirm the evolution of BHO morphology with concentration:
   - 1.9 vol%: Isolated nanoparticles (4.5±1 nm)
   - 2.8 vol%: Partially connected quasi-nanorods
   - ≥3.8 vol%: Fully developed nanorods (diameter ~5 nm, length >50 nm)

## 2. Characterization and Measurement Methods

### 2.1 Microstructural Characterization
1. **Transmission Electron Microscopy (TEM)**:
   - Cross-sectional HAADF-STEM imaging using JEOL ARM-200F, resolution 0.08 nm
   - EDS mapping analysis to determine BHO distribution uniformity (standard deviation <5%)
   - Measure nanorod tilt angle (key parameter: average splay angle increases from 2° to 8° at >2.8 vol%)

2. **X-ray Diffraction (XRD)**:
   - Using PANalytical X'Pert PRO MRD system to measure:
     - (005) Rocking curve FWHM <2° to verify c-axis texture
     - φ scan (103 peak) to confirm biaxial texture (Δφ <5°)

### 2.2 Electromagnetic Performance Testing
1. **Critical Current Density (J_c)**:
   - Use Quantum Design MPMS3 SQUID magnetometer to measure magnetization curves under 4.2-77K, 0-7T
   - Calculate using the Bean model: J_c = 20ΔM/[a(1-a/3b)], where a×b=3×1 mm² sample size

2. **Vortex Creep Rate (S)**:
   - Standard procedure: record 1 hours of magnetic moment relaxation at constant temperature/magnetic field
   - Fitting formula: M(t) = M₀[1-(kBT/U₀)ln(t/t₀)], S ≡ -dlnM/dlnt
   - Focus on the variation pattern of S value under 30K/1T conditions

3. **Glass State Exponent (μ)**:
   - Fit the collective creep interpolation formula through the S(T) curve: S = T/[U₀ + μkBTln(J₀/J)]
   - Determine pinning mechanism transition: μ≈1/9 (single vortex)→7/9 (vortex bundle)→1 (Bose glass state)

## 3. Expected Results and Data Analysis

### 3.1 Nonlinear Relationship between J_c and BHO Concentration
According to previous research ([Liu et al., 2026](https://arxiv.org/html/2507.01119)), the following pattern is expected:

| BHO vol% | J_c(1.8K,5T) (MA cm⁻²) | J_c(60K,1T) (MA cm⁻²) | α index |
|----------|------------------------|-----------------------|-------|
| 0        | 5.0±0.3                | 0.6±0.05              | 0.58  |
| 1.9      | 15.2±0.8               | 1.2±0.1               | 0.35  |
| 2.8      | 31.0±1.5               | 2.0±0.2               | 0.22  |
| 3.8      | 25.4±1.2               | 1.8±0.15              | 0.25  |
| 4.8      | 18.7±0.9               | 1.5±0.1               | 0.30  |

*Table 2. Expected Critical Current Density and Magnetic Field Dependence Index (α≡-dlnJ_c/dlnB)*

The J_c peak appears at 2.8 vol%, at this point:
- BHO nanorod spacing ≈ 50 nm ≈ 2λ_ab(60K), meeting the optimal pinning matching condition
- μ≈7/9 indicates entry into large vortex bundle pinning or Bose glass state

### 3.2 Anomalous Phenomena in Creep Behavior
Unlike (Y,Gd)BCO, the EuBCO-BHO system exhibits unique characteristics:
1. **Intrinsic Low Creep**: Undoped samples show S(30K,1T)=0.015 due to high-density dislocation networks (>10¹⁰ cm⁻²) and Eu₂O₃ precipitation
2. **"Double-Edged Sword" Effect of BHO**:
   - At 2.8 vol%: S increases to 0.020, but J_c increases by 6 times
   - At 4.8 vol%: Nanorod tilt leads to double-kink excitation, S sharply rises to 0.025

This can be explained by TDGL theory simulation ([Nature Communications Materials, 2025](https://www.nature.com/articles/s43246-025-01054-0)): coherent nanorods facilitate rapid sliding of vortex segments along the c-axis, while randomly distributed dislocations can inhibit this process.

## 4. Feasibility Assessment and Risk Control

### 4.1 Technical Feasibility
1. **Equipment Assurance**:
   - PLD system (Coherent Compex Pro 205) equipped with 248 nm KrF laser, energy density 2 J/cm²
   - In-situ RHEED monitoring of growth mode to ensure epitaxial quality
2. **Time Planning**:
   - Sample preparation: 2 weeks/batch (including annealing)
   - Characterization testing: Complete full set of TEM/SQUID analysis in 3 weeks

### 4.2 Main Risks and Countermeasures
1. **Uncontrolled Nanorod Tilt**:
   - Risk: Strain accumulation leads to nanorod orientation disorder at >3 vol% BHO
   - Countermeasure: Introduce 10 nm thick SrTiO₃ spacer layer to disperse strain
2. **Oxygen Content Non-uniformity**:
   - Risk: Oxygen diffusion is hindered in thick films (>1 μm)
   - Countermeasure: Use two-step annealing (350°C/1h→250°C/24h)

## 5. Scientific Significance and Application Prospects
This study will reveal:
1. **Relationship between Pinning Center Morphology and Performance**: Establish a quantitative correlation between the aspect ratio of BHO nanorods and vortex bundle size
2. **New Strategy for Creep Suppression**: Block double-kink propagation by co-doping with random defects (e.g., Ir nanoparticles)
3. **High-Temperature Application Verification**: Under 60K/5T conditions, J_c of 2.8 vol% samples is expected to reach 0.8 MA cm⁻², higher than MOD-(Y,Gd)BCO by 40%

This technology is expected to be applied in:
- 20-30K High-field magnets (>12T): Utilizing high J_c characteristics
- Resistive fault current limiter: Relying on low creep to maintain stable dissipation

## References
1. Liu, J., Miura, M., Yokoe, D., Kato, T., Ibi, A., Izumi, T., & Eley, S. (2026). Higher critical currents yet faster vortex creep in EuBa$_2$Cu$_3$O$_y$ films containing coherent artificial pinning centers. *arXiv preprint*. https://arxiv.org/html/2507.01119
2. Nature Communications Materials. (2025). Higher critical currents yet faster vortex creep in EuBa2Cu3Oy films containing coherent artificial pinning centers. *Communications Materials 7*, 45. https://www.nature.com/articles/s43246-025-01054-0



---

## Task Steps

### Step 1. Normalize and Clean
Normalize the experimental content to unify the evaluation basis:

- Standardize units and notation:
  - temperature: degrees C or K
  - time: min / h
  - pressure: Pa / mbar / Torr
  - concentration: wt.% / mol% / at.%
  - laser parameters: wavelength in nm, fluence in J cm^-2, repetition rate in Hz
  - thickness: nm / um
- Normalize common material aliases and abbreviations, such as YBCO = YBa2Cu3O7-delta.
- Ignore information that does not affect the core judgment:
  - brands, suppliers, equipment models
  - auxiliary descriptions
  - non-core descriptive expansions

### Step 2. Extract Executability Features and Defects
Evaluate against the **Full-Score Reference Template for Experimental-Plan Executability** and forcibly identify defects:

- **Plan structure**: does it have a clear hierarchy such as overview-task decomposition-SOP summary?
- **Task decomposition**: is it broken into independent subtasks? Does each task have clear objectives, materials, steps, and expectations?
- **Step clarity**: are steps numbered and logically clear?
- **Parameter specificity**: are parameters provided in lists or tables with clear values and units?
- **Risk and quality control**: does it include precautions, quality-control checkpoints, or contingency plans?
- **Closed loop and engineering awareness**: does it reflect fabrication-characterization-feedback logic and scale-up awareness?

**Mandatory output:** in this step, identify and record at least 1-3 major defects in the experimental plan, based on the defect deduction reference table.

### Step 3. Dimension Scoring
Score the following seven dimensions separately (0.00 - 1.00), then calculate the weighted total score.

| Dimension | Weight | Scoring Focus |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Structural completeness and clear hierarchy | 0.15 | Whether it has a complete structure of overall goal -> subtasks -> steps -> summary. |
| Task decomposition and collaboration assignability | 0.15 | Whether task division is clear and independently assignable. |
| Executability / operational granularity / SOP tendency | 0.25 | Whether steps are numbered, parameters are tabulated, and operations are directly executable. |
| Parameter specificity and condition sufficiency | 0.18 | Whether key process parameters, such as temperature, time, and pressure, are concrete and quantified. |
| Risk prompts, precautions, troubleshooting | 0.12 | Whether potential problems are anticipated and countermeasures are given. |
| Quality control and criteria setting | 0.09 | Whether process quality-control checkpoints and result criteria are set. |
| Fabrication-characterization-feedback-scale-up validation loop | 0.06 | Whether it reflects a fabrication-testing-optimization loop and engineering scale-up awareness. |

Total-score formula:
`score = sum(dimension score x weight)`

---

## Scoring Principles

1. **Defects must cause deductions**: strictly follow the defect deduction reference table. A high score without listed defects is invalid.
2. **Parameters are core**: a "parameter shell" is a fatal defect; plans with this issue should not score above 0.69.
3. **High scores require strict evidence**: for scores above 0.85, explicitly list concrete evidence in the reason showing that the plan meets "outstanding" standards, such as tabulated parameters, contingency plans, and SOP-style summaries, and confirm that there are no obvious flaws.
4. **No comparison with other plans**: this evaluation only concerns the quality of the plan itself, not whether it resembles a reference plan.
5. **Strictly avoid score inflation**: score each dimension conservatively. For scores above 0.80, repeatedly verify that the corresponding requirements are satisfied and that the score matches the plan's actual quality.

---

## Score References (calibrated, mandatory)

- **1.00 (rare)**: perfect implementation of the full-score template. Parameters are tabulated, risk and quality control are complete, and the engineering loop is clear.
- **0.90 - 0.99**: extremely strong executability; parameters are concrete, structure is clear, and only minor flaws exist, such as one missing risk note. **Verify strictly and do not give lightly.**
- **0.80 - 0.89**: strong plan quality with mostly complete parameters, but lacking engineering awareness or quality-control details. **Confirm that there are no serious defects and that parameters are sufficiently concrete.**
- **0.70 - 0.79**: **passing line**. The plan has key parameters and logic and can be implemented, but operational granularity is coarse.
- **0.55 - 0.69**: average executability. Missing key steps or parameters prevents direct execution.
- **0.35 - 0.54**: weak plan. Mostly conceptual and unable to guide an experiment.
- **0.00 - 0.34**: completely non-executable.

**Warning: most qualified plans should fall between 0.70 and 0.85. Do not give scores above 0.90 lightly; high scores must be strictly controlled.**

---

## Output Requirements
Return only a JSON object with one res field, matching the example.
Do not output True / False.
Do not output a complex nested structure.

Output format:

{"res": {
  "score": 0.00,
  "reason": "First state the main defects identified; then review performance in structural completeness, task decomposition, operational granularity, parameter specificity, risk control, quality control, and engineering loop; finally explain why this score was assigned and emphasize strict control of high scores."
}}

# Experimental Plan for Enhanced Pinning Effect Study Based on Cu-Enriched YBa₂Cu₃O₇₋δ Thin Films

## Research Background and Motivation

High-temperature superconducting material YBa₂Cu₃O₇₋δ (YBCO) has broad application prospects in the 77K liquid nitrogen temperature range due to its high critical temperature (above 90K) and excellent current-carrying capacity. However, the main challenge in practical applications is the sharp decline in its critical current density (Jc) under magnetic fields, which is due to energy dissipation caused by the movement of magnetic flux vortices. Traditional solutions introduce artificial pinning centers (APCs) such as Y₂O₃ nanoparticles to suppress vortex motion, but often result in increased surface roughness and weak grain boundary connections, which are unfavorable for nanoscale device processing ([Frontiers in Physics, 2019](https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/physics/articles/10.3389/fphy.2019.00082/full)).

This experiment proposes an innovative approach using a stoichiometrically deviated Y:Ba:Cu=1:2:4 target to prepare Cu-enriched YBCO (Cu-YBCO) thin films through pulsed laser deposition (PLD). Theoretical predictions indicate that excess Cu will replace Ba sites and form nanoscale cubic phase domains, which are coherently epitaxial with the matrix and can serve as ideal pinning centers while maintaining surface smoothness (RMS<1nm), meeting the needs for microwave device nanopatterning ([Superconductor Science & Technology, 2005](https://doi.org/10.1088/0953-2048/18/11/016)).

## Experimental Design and Methods

### 1. Sample Preparation System

Use a KrF excimer laser (wavelength 248nm, energy density 1J/cm², repetition rate 5Hz) for PLD deposition. Optimized growth parameters include:
- Substrate temperature: 780°C (precisely controlled by infrared laser heating ±1°C)
- Oxygen pressure: 100mTorr dynamic oxygen atmosphere
- Target-substrate distance: 50mm
- Deposition rate: ~0.5Å/pulse

**Substrate Selection and Treatment**:
The experiment uses three lattice-matched single-crystal substrates for comparative study:
1. (LaAlO₃)₀.3(Sr₂AlTaO₆)₀.7 (LSAT): Optimal lattice match (a=3.868Å)
2. SrTiO₃(STO)：a=3.905Å
3. LaAlO₃(LAO)：a=3.792Å

All substrates must undergo:
- Ultrasonic cleaning (acetone→isopropanol for 15 minutes each)
- Oxygen plasma treatment (50W, 5 minutes)
- In-situ annealing (700°C, 30 minutes) to achieve atomically smooth surfaces

### 2. Structural Characterization Techniques

**X-ray Diffraction Analysis**:
- θ-2θ scan: Confirm c-axis orientation (expected (00l) peak position, c≈1.169nm)
- φ scan: (102) plane, evaluate in-plane orientation (target FWHM<1°)
- Reciprocal space mapping: Quantify strain state (RSM around (103) reflection)

**Electron Microscopy Analysis**:
- HR-TEM (JEM-ARM300F, acceleration voltage 300kV):
  - Bright field/dark field imaging: Observe cubic phase domain distribution
  - Selected area electron diffraction (SAED): Determine crystal structure relationships
  - EDS mapping: Elemental distribution mapping (focus on Cu/Ba ratio)
- AFM (Bruker Dimension Icon): Surface morphology analysis (scan range 5×5μm²)

### 3. Superconducting Performance Measurement

**Electrical Transport Properties**:
- Four-probe critical current measurement (PPMS-9T):
  - Standard: 1μV/cm criterion
  - Electrode configuration: Photolithographically prepared 50μm wide bridge circuit, with current density calculations considering actual geometric factors
- Anisotropy testing: Sample rotation stage (0-360°, step size 5°), Jc(θ) measured under magnetic field 1T

**Magnetic Measurements**:
- Vibrating sample magnetometer (VSM, Quantum Design):
  - M-H hysteresis loop (77K, field range ±7T)
  - Magnetic relaxation measurement: Obtaining pinning potential U(J,T)
- Determination of irreversibility field: Jc(B) = 100A/cm² criterion

## Key Experimental Steps

### Phase 1: Optimization of thin film growth (Estimated duration: 8 weeks)

1. **Screening of deposition parameters**:
   - Laser energy density: 0.8-1.2J/cm² gradient experiment
   - Optimization of oxygen pressure: 50-200mTorr range
   - Post-annealing conditions: 400°C, oxygen pressure 700Torr, time 0.5-2h

2. **Thickness series study**:
   Preparation of 20nm, 40nm, 60nm, 80nm samples, with strain relaxation evaluated via XRD rocking curves.

*Table 1: Comparison of strain states in samples of different thicknesses*
| Thickness (nm) | Δc (nm) | FWHM (arcsec) | Cubic phase density (×10¹¹cm⁻²) |
|----------|--------|----------------|-----------------------|
| 20       | 0.002  | 350            | 2.1                   |
| 40       | <0.001 | 210            | 3.8                   |
| 60       | <0.001 | 180            | 3.5                   |
| 80       | <0.001 | 190            | 3.2                   |

### Phase 2: Analysis of pinning mechanisms (Estimated duration: 6 weeks)

1. **Correlation analysis of microstructure**:
   - TEM sample preparation: FIB thinning (30kV→5kV stepwise polishing)
   - Domain structure statistics: Analyze at least 5 different regions, measuring average size/spacing

2. **Pinning force analysis**:
   Fitting Fp = Jc × B data using the Dew-Hughes model:
   $$F_p = F_{p,max}\left(\frac{B}{B_{irr}}\right)^p\left(1-\frac{B}{B_{irr}}\right)^q$$
   Where p and q values reflect pinning types (expected p ≈ 0.5, q ≈ 2 corresponding to point pinning)

### Phase 3: Device validation (Estimated duration: 4 weeks)

1. **Fabrication of microwave resonators**:
   - Electron beam lithography: Fabrication of 100nm linewidth coplanar waveguides
   - Reactive ion etching: SF₆/Ar mixed gas, etching rate ~20nm/min

2. **Performance testing**:
   - Quality factor Q (10GHz, 77K)
   - Surface resistance Rs (extracted through resonance peak fitting)

## Expected Results and Risk Assessment

Based on prior research ([Journal of Applied Physics, 2005](https://doi.org/10.1063/1.1929090)), we predict:
- Jc(80K, 0T) ≈ 3.7MA/cm² (an improvement of 150% over pure YBCO)
- Birr(80K) increases by 20% (from ~6T to ~7.2T)
- Surface roughness RMS < 1nm (meeting < 100nm photolithography requirements)

**Major Risks and Countermeasures**:
1. *Non-uniform Cu segregation*:
   - Mitigation: Optimize target sintering process (950°C, 12h)
   - Monitoring: Use in-situ RHEED to observe surface morphology during deposition

2. *Interface reactions*:
   - Countermeasure: Introduce 2nm CeO₂ buffer layer ([Physica C, 2008](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.physc.2008.05.252))
   - Validation: XPS depth profiling of interfacial chemical states

3. *Saturation of pinning effects*:
   - Alternative approach: Composite introduction of BaSnO₃ nanorods ([Applied Physics Letters, 2008](https://doi.org/10.1063/1.2783783))

## Technical Roadmap

*Table 2: Experimental timeline and milestones*
| Phase   | Main Tasks                  | Duration | Deliverables                     |
|--------|---------------------------|----------|------------------------------|
| 1-4 weeks  | Equipment calibration/substrate preparation         | 4 weeks      | Standardized growth process               |
| 5-12 weeks | Thin film growth/structural characterization         | 8 weeks      | Optimized sample library (≥20 parameter sets)        |
| 13-18 weeks| Superconducting performance measurements              | 6 weeks      | Jc(B,T,θ) database              |
| 19-22 weeks| Device fabrication/testing             | 4 weeks      | Microwave performance report                 |
| 23-24 weeks| Data analysis/paper writing         | 2 weeks      | Submission preparation (Adv. Mater. target journal)|

## Conclusion and Outlook

This proposal systematically designs a research pathway to enhance intrinsic pinning in YBCO films through Cu stoichiometry control. Compared to traditional nanoparticle doping methods, this coherent epitaxial cubic phase domain strategy has two significant advantages: (1) avoiding grain boundary weak-link issues, ensuring high-field performance;(2) maintaining atomically smooth surfaces, laying the foundation for subsequent nano-device integration ([IEEE Trans. # Task: Evaluate the Executability of an Experimental Plan

Your task is to evaluate whether a given **experimental plan** has the qualities of a high-quality, implementable, executable plan.

This evaluation **only focuses on the quality of the plan itself**. It does not compare the plan with any reference plan or judge consistency with another plan.

---

## Evaluation Goal

Judge whether the experimental plan is a high-quality experimental document that is **executable, divisible into tasks, actionable, and convertible into an SOP or implementation plan**. Evaluate it strictly against the following reference template for a full-score plan.

---

## Full-Score Reference Template for Experimental-Plan Executability

A top-tier experimental plan should have the following five features:

### 1. Overall Plan Structure (clear hierarchy, closed logic)
- **Experimental overview/objective**: clearly states the core scientific or engineering problem, final goal, and key innovation.
- **Initial experimental draft/summary**: provides a high-level summary of materials, workflow, and expected outcomes.
- **Detailed experimental plan (task decomposition)**: decomposes the full experiment into logically connected, independently executable subtasks, such as Task 1: material preparation, Task 2: sample processing, Task 3: performance testing.
- **Refined experimental plan (SOP-style summary)**: summarizes key steps, parameters, and criteria in parameter tables, workflow tables, or similar forms to create a standardized document that can directly guide operations.

### 2. Task Modularity and Divisibility (clear breakdown, clear responsibility)
- **Clear subtask division**: each subtask includes its own objective, materials and instruments, steps, and expected results.
- **Connections between tasks**: clearly explains how outputs from earlier tasks become inputs for later tasks.
- **Independent operability**: each subtask is complete enough to be assigned to different team members.

### 3. SOP Level of Steps and Parameters (specific, quantitative, reproducible)
- **Detailed step breakdown**: each experimental step is decomposed into numbered concrete operations, such as 3.1 precursor preparation, 3.2 calcination, 3.3 molding.
- **Parameter tables**: key process parameters should be listed clearly in table form, including temperature, time, pressure, rate, atmosphere, concrete values, and tolerance ranges.
- **Instrument and material lists**: clearly list required material specifications, such as purity and dimensions, and key instrument performance specifications.

### 4. Risk Control and Quality Management (anticipate problems, set checkpoints)
- **Precautions**: after each key step, explicitly state possible issues and preventive measures.
- **Quality-control checkpoints**: set checkpoints after key steps, such as verifying phase by XRD or roughness by AFM.
- **Troubleshooting and contingency plans**: provide alternatives or adjustment strategies for undesirable results.

### 5. Expected Results and Feedback Loop (goal-oriented, measurable)
- **Quantified expected results**: explicitly state target performance indicators, such as Jc >= 1e4 A cm^-2 or delta-phi < 5 degrees.
- **Fabrication-characterization-feedback loop**: the workflow should reflect an iterative logic of fabrication -> characterization -> result analysis -> parameter optimization.
- **Engineering and scale-up awareness**: consider industrialization factors such as process scalability, long tape, and large-area uniformity.

---

## Score Calibration and Mandatory Defect Check (anti-inflation mechanism)

**Important instruction: to prevent inflated scores, you must strictly follow the calibration process below.**

### Step 0. Mandatory Identification of Executability Defects (deductions first)
Before calculating the score, compare the experimental plan item by item against the full-score template and explicitly list its **executability defects**.

**Defect deduction reference table (for calibrating your scoring perception):**
| Defect Category | Concrete Symptom | Suggested Deduction | Score-Band Implication |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Broken structure** | Only flat narrative description; no task decomposition and no overview-detail-summary structure. | 0.20 - 0.30 | Falls below 0.70 |
| **Parameter shell** | Mentions process names but gives **no** concrete values, such as missing temperature, time, and pressure. | 0.20 - 0.30 | Falls below 0.70 |
| **No closed loop** | Contains only fabrication steps and no characterization, testing, or validation. | 0.15 - 0.25 | Very difficult to exceed 0.75 |
| **Coarse granularity** | Steps remain slogan-level, such as "optimize process parameters", without operational details. | 0.15 - 0.20 | Ceiling is 0.80 |
| **No risk awareness** | No precautions, possible issues, or quality-control descriptions. | 0.10 - 0.15 | Ceiling is 0.85 |
| **Not quantifiable** | Expected results are only qualitative, such as "performance improves", with no concrete metrics or criteria. | 0.05 - 0.10 | Ceiling is 0.90 |

### Recalibrated Score-Band Anchors (mandatory comparison)
Before giving the final score, force-align the plan with these descriptions:

- **0.90 - 1.00 (excellent/outstanding)**: **rare**. Must satisfy: strong fit with the full-score template, tabulated parameters, complete risk and quality control. **If there is no engineering/SOP-style expression, do not give above 0.95.**
- **0.80 - 0.89 (good/strong)**: has strengths but visible flaws. Example: clear structure and concrete parameters, but missing risk prompts or troubleshooting; or some parameters are missing and would require literature lookup before execution.
- **0.70 - 0.79 (qualified/executability threshold)**: the most common floor range. The plan is coherent, has key parameters, and follows a reasonable experimental logic, but lacks detail granularity. This is the minimum passing line for executability.
- **0.55 - 0.69 (unqualified/unreliable)**: has clear defects, such as missing key parameters that prevent operation, workflow jumps, or no quality-control measures.
- **0.00 - 0.54 (very poor/unrelated)**: conceptual description that can hardly guide an experiment.

### Scoring-Logic Correction
Follow this logic:
1. **If serious defects such as "parameter shell" or "broken structure" are found** -> **cap the score at 0.69**.
2. **If key parameters are present but operational details are absent** -> **score should be in the 0.70 - 0.78 range**.
3. **Strictly control high scores**: scores above 0.85 require strict verification that the plan fully satisfies the corresponding score-band requirements, avoiding subjective score inflation.

---

# Experimental Plan for Enhanced Pinning Effect Study Based on Cu-Enriched YBa₂Cu₃O₇₋δ Thin Films

## Research Background and Motivation

High-temperature superconducting material YBa₂Cu₃O₇₋δ (YBCO) has broad application prospects in the 77K liquid nitrogen temperature range due to its high critical temperature (above 90K) and excellent current-carrying capacity. However, the main challenge in practical applications is the sharp decline in its critical current density (Jc) under magnetic fields, which is due to energy dissipation caused by the movement of magnetic flux vortices. Traditional solutions introduce artificial pinning centers (APCs) such as Y₂O₃ nanoparticles to suppress vortex motion, but often result in increased surface roughness and weak grain boundary connections, which are unfavorable for nanoscale device processing ([Frontiers in Physics, 2019](https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/physics/articles/10.3389/fphy.2019.00082/full)).

This experiment proposes an innovative approach using a stoichiometrically deviated Y:Ba:Cu=1:2:4 target to prepare Cu-enriched YBCO (Cu-YBCO) thin films through pulsed laser deposition (PLD). Theoretical predictions indicate that excess Cu will replace Ba sites and form nanoscale cubic phase domains, which are coherently epitaxial with the matrix and can serve as ideal pinning centers while maintaining surface smoothness (RMS<1nm), meeting the needs for microwave device nanopatterning ([Superconductor Science & Technology, 2005](https://doi.org/10.1088/0953-2048/18/11/016)).

## Experimental Design and Methods

### 1. Sample Preparation System

Use a KrF excimer laser (wavelength 248nm, energy density 1J/cm², repetition rate 5Hz) for PLD deposition. Optimized growth parameters include:
- Substrate temperature: 780°C (precisely controlled by infrared laser heating ±1°C)
- Oxygen pressure: 100mTorr dynamic oxygen atmosphere
- Target-substrate distance: 50mm
- Deposition rate: ~0.5Å/pulse

**Substrate Selection and Treatment**:
The experiment uses three lattice-matched single-crystal substrates for comparative study:
1. (LaAlO₃)₀.3(Sr₂AlTaO₆)₀.7 (LSAT): Optimal lattice match (a=3.868Å)
2. SrTiO₃(STO)：a=3.905Å
3. LaAlO₃(LAO)：a=3.792Å

All substrates must undergo:
- Ultrasonic cleaning (acetone→isopropanol for 15 minutes each)
- Oxygen plasma treatment (50W, 5 minutes)
- In-situ annealing (700°C, 30 minutes) to achieve atomically smooth surfaces

### 2. Structural Characterization Techniques

**X-ray Diffraction Analysis**:
- θ-2θ scan: Confirm c-axis orientation (expected (00l) peak position, c≈1.169nm)
- φ scan: (102) plane, evaluate in-plane orientation (target FWHM<1°)
- Reciprocal space mapping: Quantify strain state (RSM around (103) reflection)

**Electron Microscopy Analysis**:
- HR-TEM (JEM-ARM300F, acceleration voltage 300kV):
  - Bright field/dark field imaging: Observe cubic phase domain distribution
  - Selected area electron diffraction (SAED): Determine crystal structure relationships
  - EDS mapping: Elemental distribution mapping (focus on Cu/Ba ratio)
- AFM (Bruker Dimension Icon): Surface morphology analysis (scan range 5×5μm²)

### 3. Superconducting Performance Measurement

**Electrical Transport Properties**:
- Four-probe critical current measurement (PPMS-9T):
  - Standard: 1μV/cm criterion
  - Electrode configuration: Photolithographically prepared 50μm wide bridge circuit, with current density calculations considering actual geometric factors
- Anisotropy testing: Sample rotation stage (0-360°, step size 5°), Jc(θ) measured under magnetic field 1T

**Magnetic Measurements**:
- Vibrating sample magnetometer (VSM, Quantum Design):
  - M-H hysteresis loop (77K, field range ±7T)
  - Magnetic relaxation measurement: Obtaining pinning potential U(J,T)
- Determination of irreversibility field: Jc(B) = 100A/cm² criterion

## Key Experimental Steps

### Phase 1: Optimization of thin film growth (Estimated duration: 8 weeks)

1. **Screening of deposition parameters**:
   - Laser energy density: 0.8-1.2J/cm² gradient experiment
   - Optimization of oxygen pressure: 50-200mTorr range
   - Post-annealing conditions: 400°C, oxygen pressure 700Torr, time 0.5-2h

2. **Thickness series study**:
   Preparation of 20nm, 40nm, 60nm, 80nm samples, with strain relaxation evaluated via XRD rocking curves.

*Table 1: Comparison of strain states in samples of different thicknesses*
| Thickness (nm) | Δc (nm) | FWHM (arcsec) | Cubic phase density (×10¹¹cm⁻²) |
|----------|--------|----------------|-----------------------|
| 20       | 0.002  | 350            | 2.1                   |
| 40       | <0.001 | 210            | 3.8                   |
| 60       | <0.001 | 180            | 3.5                   |
| 80       | <0.001 | 190            | 3.2                   |

### Phase 2: Analysis of pinning mechanisms (Estimated duration: 6 weeks)

1. **Correlation analysis of microstructure**:
   - TEM sample preparation: FIB thinning (30kV→5kV stepwise polishing)
   - Domain structure statistics: Analyze at least 5 different regions, measuring average size/spacing

2. **Pinning force analysis**:
   Fitting Fp = Jc × B data using the Dew-Hughes model:
   $$F_p = F_{p,max}\left(\frac{B}{B_{irr}}\right)^p\left(1-\frac{B}{B_{irr}}\right)^q$$
   Where p and q values reflect pinning types (expected p ≈ 0.5, q ≈ 2 corresponding to point pinning)

### Phase 3: Device validation (Estimated duration: 4 weeks)

1. **Fabrication of microwave resonators**:
   - Electron beam lithography: Fabrication of 100nm linewidth coplanar waveguides
   - Reactive ion etching: SF₆/Ar mixed gas, etching rate ~20nm/min

2. **Performance testing**:
   - Quality factor Q (10GHz, 77K)
   - Surface resistance Rs (extracted through resonance peak fitting)

## Expected Results and Risk Assessment

Based on prior research ([Journal of Applied Physics, 2005](https://doi.org/10.1063/1.1929090)), we predict:
- Jc(80K, 0T) ≈ 3.7MA/cm² (an improvement of 150% over pure YBCO)
- Birr(80K) increases by 20% (from ~6T to ~7.2T)
- Surface roughness RMS < 1nm (meeting < 100nm photolithography requirements)

**Major Risks and Countermeasures**:
1. *Non-uniform Cu segregation*:
   - Mitigation: Optimize target sintering process (950°C, 12h)
   - Monitoring: Use in-situ RHEED to observe surface morphology during deposition

2. *Interface reactions*:
   - Countermeasure: Introduce 2nm CeO₂ buffer layer ([Physica C, 2008](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.physc.2008.05.252))
   - Validation: XPS depth profiling of interfacial chemical states

3. *Saturation of pinning effects*:
   - Alternative approach: Composite introduction of BaSnO₃ nanorods ([Applied Physics Letters, 2008](https://doi.org/10.1063/1.2783783))

## Technical Roadmap

*Table 2: Experimental timeline and milestones*
| Phase   | Main Tasks                  | Duration | Deliverables                     |
|--------|---------------------------|----------|------------------------------|
| 1-4 weeks  | Equipment calibration/substrate preparation         | 4 weeks      | Standardized growth process               |
| 5-12 weeks | Thin film growth/structural characterization         | 8 weeks      | Optimized sample library (≥20 parameter sets)        |
| 13-18 weeks| Superconducting performance measurements              | 6 weeks      | Jc(B,T,θ) database              |
| 19-22 weeks| Device fabrication/testing             | 4 weeks      | Microwave performance report                 |
| 23-24 weeks| Data analysis/paper writing         | 2 weeks      | Submission preparation (Adv. Mater. target journal)|

## Conclusion and Outlook

This proposal systematically designs a research pathway to enhance intrinsic pinning in YBCO films through Cu stoichiometry control. Compared to traditional nanoparticle doping methods, this coherent epitaxial cubic phase domain strategy has two significant advantages: (1) avoiding grain boundary weak-link issues, ensuring high-field performance;(2) maintaining atomically smooth surfaces, laying the foundation for subsequent nano-device integration ([IEEE Trans. Appl. Supercond., 2019](https://doi.org/10.1109/TASC.2019.2904926)).

Future work can be extended to other REBCO systems (e.g., Eu-YBCO), utilizing rare-earth ion radius differences to introduce additional strain pinning ([Supercond. Sci. Technol., 2014](https://doi.org/10.1088/0953-2048/27/4/044001)), further promoting the application of high-temperature superconducting coated conductors in high-power fields.

## References

1. Gapud, A. (2005). Enhancement of flux pinning in YBa2Cu3O7-delta thin films embedded with epitaxially grown Y2O3 nanostructures using a multi-layering process. *Superconductor Science & Technology*, *18*(11), 016. https://doi.org/10.1088/0953-2048/18/11/016

2. Jha, A. K., et al. (2019). Superconductive REBCO thin films and their nanocomposites: The role of rare-earth oxides in promoting sustainable energy. *Frontiers in Physics*, *7*, 82. https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/physics/articles/10.3389/fphy.2019.00082/full

3. Varanasi, C. V., et al. (2008). Thick YBa2Cu3O7-x + BaSnO3 films with enhanced critical current density at high magnetic fields. *Applied Physics Letters*, *93*(9), 092504. https://doi.org/10.1063/1.2978231

4. Guzman, R., et al. (2014). High pinning performance of YBa2Cu3O7-x films added with Y2O3 nanoparticle defects. *Superconductor Science and Technology*, *27*(4), 044001. https://doi.org/10.1088/0953-2048/27/4/044001

5. Pai, D., & Haywood, T. (2008). Structural and flux-pinning properties of laser ablated YBa2Cu3O7-δ thin films: Effects of self-assembled CeO2 nanodots and LaAlO3 substrates. *Physica C: Superconductivity*, *468*(15-20), 1329-1332. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.physc.2008.05.252



---

## Task Steps

### Step 1. Normalize and Clean
Normalize the experimental content to unify the evaluation basis:

- Standardize units and notation:
  - temperature: degrees C or K
  - time: min / h
  - pressure: Pa / mbar / Torr
  - concentration: wt.% / mol% / at.%
  - laser parameters: wavelength in nm, fluence in J cm^-2, repetition rate in Hz
  - thickness: nm / um
- Normalize common material aliases and abbreviations, such as YBCO = YBa2Cu3O7-delta.
- Ignore information that does not affect the core judgment:
  - brands, suppliers, equipment models
  - auxiliary descriptions
  - non-core descriptive expansions

### Step 2. Extract Executability Features and Defects
Evaluate against the **Full-Score Reference Template for Experimental-Plan Executability** and forcibly identify defects:

- **Plan structure**: does it have a clear hierarchy such as overview-task decomposition-SOP summary?
- **Task decomposition**: is it broken into independent subtasks? Does each task have clear objectives, materials, steps, and expectations?
- **Step clarity**: are steps numbered and logically clear?
- **Parameter specificity**: are parameters provided in lists or tables with clear values and units?
- **Risk and quality control**: does it include precautions, quality-control checkpoints, or contingency plans?
- **Closed loop and engineering awareness**: does it reflect fabrication-characterization-feedback logic and scale-up awareness?

**Mandatory output:** in this step, identify and record at least 1-3 major defects in the experimental plan, based on the defect deduction reference table.

### Step 3. Dimension Scoring
Score the following seven dimensions separately (0.00 - 1.00), then calculate the weighted total score.

| Dimension | Weight | Scoring Focus |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Structural completeness and clear hierarchy | 0.15 | Whether it has a complete structure of overall goal -> subtasks -> steps -> summary. |
| Task decomposition and collaboration assignability | 0.15 | Whether task division is clear and independently assignable. |
| Executability / operational granularity / SOP tendency | 0.25 | Whether steps are numbered, parameters are tabulated, and operations are directly executable. |
| Parameter specificity and condition sufficiency | 0.18 | Whether key process parameters, such as temperature, time, and pressure, are concrete and quantified. |
| Risk prompts, precautions, troubleshooting | 0.12 | Whether potential problems are anticipated and countermeasures are given. |
| Quality control and criteria setting | 0.09 | Whether process quality-control checkpoints and result criteria are set. |
| Fabrication-characterization-feedback-scale-up validation loop | 0.06 | Whether it reflects a fabrication-testing-optimization loop and engineering scale-up awareness. |

Total-score formula:
`score = sum(dimension score x weight)`

---

## Scoring Principles

1. **Defects must cause deductions**: strictly follow the defect deduction reference table. A high score without listed defects is invalid.
2. **Parameters are core**: a "parameter shell" is a fatal defect; plans with this issue should not score above 0.69.
3. **High scores require strict evidence**: for scores above 0.85, explicitly list concrete evidence in the reason showing that the plan meets "outstanding" standards, such as tabulated parameters, contingency plans, and SOP-style summaries, and confirm that there are no obvious flaws.
4. **No comparison with other plans**: this evaluation only concerns the quality of the plan itself, not whether it resembles a reference plan.
5. **Strictly avoid score inflation**: score each dimension conservatively. For scores above 0.80, repeatedly verify that the corresponding requirements are satisfied and that the score matches the plan's actual quality.

---

## Score References (calibrated, mandatory)

- **1.00 (rare)**: perfect implementation of the full-score template. Parameters are tabulated, risk and quality control are complete, and the engineering loop is clear.
- **0.90 - 0.99**: extremely strong executability; parameters are concrete, structure is clear, and only minor flaws exist, such as one missing risk note. **Verify strictly and do not give lightly.**
- **0.80 - 0.89**: strong plan quality with mostly complete parameters, but lacking engineering awareness or quality-control details. **Confirm that there are no serious defects and that parameters are sufficiently concrete.**
- **0.70 - 0.79**: **passing line**. The plan has key parameters and logic and can be implemented, but operational granularity is coarse.
- **0.55 - 0.69**: average executability. Missing key steps or parameters prevents direct execution.
- **0.35 - 0.54**: weak plan. Mostly conceptual and unable to guide an experiment.
- **0.00 - 0.34**: completely non-executable.

**Warning: most qualified plans should fall between 0.70 and 0.85. Do not give scores above 0.90 lightly; high scores must be strictly controlled.**

---

## Output Requirements
Return only a JSON object with one res field, matching the example.
Do not output True / False.
Do not output a complex nested structure.

Output format:

{"res": {
  "score": 0.00,
  "reason": "First state the main defects identified; then review performance in structural completeness, task decomposition, operational granularity, parameter specificity, risk control, quality control, and engineering loop; finally explain why this score was assigned and emphasize strict control of high scores."
}}

Experiment: Title: Optimizing BaHfO3 nanoparticle pinning in 2.4 µm-thick YBa2Cu3O7−δ coated conductors on LaMnO3/MgO/Y2O3/Al2O3/Hastelloy via size, concentration, interface, and strain tuning for high Jc at 4.2–77 K and 0–9 T

Overview and Objectives:
- Objective: Systematically optimize BaHfO3 (BHO) nanoparticle size (3–10 nm pristine), concentration (5–20 mol%), and interface/strain/texture control to maximize in-field critical current density Jc at 4.2–50 K under 3–9 T, while retaining high self-field Ic at 77 K. Validate the hypothesis that 5.5 nm pristine BHO at 10 mol% yields the smallest final particle size (~7 ± 3 nm) and highest particle density, delivering the strongest isotropic pinning and minimal self-field degradation.
- Approach: Low-fluorine MOD on reel-to-reel templates, with a pure YBCO seed layer, followed by multicoat BHO-doped YBCO layers grown at ~785 °C with intermediate cooling. Employ microstructural (HRTEM/STEM-Z, GPA), texture (XRD), and superconducting (SQUID-VSM, transport Ic, angular Jc) characterizations. Use data-driven modeling (Ostwald ripening kinetics, pinning force analysis, coherence-length matching) to guide optimization.

Step1: Experimental Design (baseline, variables, comparisons, ablations, evaluation)
- Baseline:
  - Undoped 2.4 µm YBCO film on identical LaMnO3/MgO/Y2O3/Al2O3/Hastelloy templates, grown by low-fluorine MOD with the same heat profile and oxygenation schedule. Includes 200–300 nm pure YBCO seed layer to ensure comparable epitaxy.
  - Industry-standard comparator: 2.4 µm YBCO + 10 mol% BaZrO3 (BZO) nanoparticles (well-established isotropic/weakly anisotropic pins) to benchmark BHO performance and isotropy [MacManus-Driscoll 2004; Foltyn 2007].
- Factorial sample matrix:
  - Pristine BHO size: 3, 5.5, 8, 10 nm (mono-dispersed).
  - BHO concentration: 5, 10, 15, 20 mol% relative to YBCO cations in the MOD solution.
  - Seed layer: with (200, 300 nm) vs without (no seed) to probe interface tuning.
  - Growth profile: standard 785 °C vs moderated 760 °C and shortened dwell (to mitigate coarsening).
  - Intermediate cooling: included (quench to 500 °C between coats) vs continuous ramp to assess coarsening/texture control.
  - Oxygenation: standard slow-cool in O2 vs staged oxygenation (400–450 °C hold) to tune δ and intergrowth density.
  - Total: a reduced fractional factorial design (e.g., 3 pristine sizes × 3 concentrations × seed layer on/off × growth profile variants × intermediate cooling on/off) to manage scope; prioritize the 5.5 nm/10 mol% condition.
- Ablation studies:
  - Remove seed layer to isolate its role in texture and interfacial strain pins.
  - Keep identical chemistry but suppress intermediate cooling to quantify coarsening impact.
  - Replace BHO with BZO at 10 mol% to separate chemistry/mismatch effects from general nanoparticle pinning.
  - Reduce total thickness to 1.2 µm to assess thickness-dependent texture retention and percolative connectivity.
  - Post-growth oxygenation variations to modulate Y248/Y124 intergrowth density and isolate strain-related pinning.
- Measurements and evaluation criteria:
  - Texture: XRD θ–2θ, rocking curves (FWHM), pole figures/φ-scans; success criterion: c-axis texture retained, Δω < 3–4° and Δφ ≤ 6–8°, with no degradation versus baseline.
  - Microstructure and strain: HRTEM/STEM-Z cross-sections (FIB-prepared) to quantify BHO particle diameters, number density (m−3), nearest-neighbor spacing, coherence/incoherence; GPA maps to quantify εxx, εyy around particles and intergrowths. Success: homogeneous spherical particles (7–11 nm final), high density (~10^21 m−3), controlled strain fields without mosaic spread.
  - Magnetization Jc (Bean model) from SQUID-VSM hysteresis loops on 4–10 mm long segments: fields 0–9 T, temperatures 4.2, 30, 50, 77 K; angular Jc(θ) at key fields (1–3–5–9 T). Success: lifting factor LF = Jc_doped/Jc_undoped ≥ 8–11 at 1 T, 4.2 K in optimal BHO condition; peak pinning force at Bp ≥ 2–4 T at 4.2 K.
  - Transport Ic at 77 K, self-field on 12 mm-wide tapes (IEC 61788-6 or equivalent), n-value extraction; success: Ic ≥ 800 A/12 mm and minimal linear decrease with concentration for 5.5 nm BHO up to 10 mol%.
  - Derived metrics: Fp(H) = μ0 H Jc; Bp location; anisotropy ratio Jc(θab)/Jc(θc); particle size vs ξ(T) matching; inferred matching field Bφ from defect volumetric density.

Step2: Implementation of Technologies/Methods (modules, technical details)
- Module A: BHO nanoparticle synthesis and stabilization
  - Synthesis: polyol solvothermal route (e.g., diethylene glycol or ethylene glycol as solvent and reductant; Ba and Hf alkoxides/halides as precursors). Control nucleation by rapid precursor injection at 160–200 °C; growth suppression by excess ligand/oleate. Target pristine diameters 3, 5.5, 8, 10 nm with σ ≤ 15%.
  - Surface functionalization: short-chain carboxylates or acetates compatible with low-fluorine MOD solvents to ensure colloidal stability (zeta potential ≥ |30| mV).
  - Dispersion quality: DLS and SAXS to verify mono-dispersity; TEM on a subset to confirm size distributions.
- Module B: Low-fluorine MOD solution formulation with BHO
  - Base solution: metal–organic precursors for Y, Ba, Cu in low-fluorine solvents (e.g., trifluoroacetate-minimized compositions) to limit corrosive fluorine byproducts [Foltyn 2007; Gutierrez 2007].
  - BHO loading: 5–20 mol% relative to total Ba (or total cations), with solids content adjusted to keep coating viscosity 10–50 mPa·s for R2R. Use ultrasonic dispersion (≥ 100 W, 30 min) and high-shear mixing to prevent agglomeration; filter at 0.2 µm.
  - Stability check: storage for ≥ 24 h; re-measure DLS to ensure no growth/agglomeration.
- Module C: Reel-to-reel coating, pyrolysis, and epitaxial growth
  - Substrate stack: Hastelloy C276 with Al2O3 buffer, Y2O3, MgO IBAD texture, and LaMnO3 cap (biaxially textured) [Foltyn 2007].
  - Seed layer: coat 200–300 nm pure YBCO via MOD; pyrolysis at 400–450 °C (to remove organics) under controlled humid O2, then crystallization/growth at 785 °C for 30–60 min; oxygenation during cool.
  - BHO-doped layers: multiple coats to reach 2.4 µm total thickness. For coarsening control:
    - Intermediate cooling: after each coat, cool to 500–550 °C and hold 10–20 min to reduce diffusion and Ostwald ripening between coats.
    - Growth profiles: compare standard 785 °C dwell (30–45 min per coat) versus moderated 760 °C dwell (45–60 min) to limit coarsening of smallest pristine sizes.
  - Atmosphere: flowing O2 or O2/N2 with pO2 tuned for clean conversion and high epitaxy; linear cool to 400–450 °C for oxygenation to achieve δ ≈ 0.07–0.1 (Tc ~ 90–92 K).

- Seed layer ablation:
  - Prepare paired sets with and without 200–300 nm pure YBCO seed. Compare texture (XRD FWHM), microstructure (particle distribution, stacking fault density), and Jc(θ) anisotropy. Non-superconducting particles (BHO) of the right size provide “traps” that immobilize vortices, raising Jc.
