Experiment:
Step1: Objectives and Hypotheses
- Objective: Establish an optimized process window (nanocrystal size, loading, and heat treatment) for MOD-derived YBa2Cu3O7−δ (YBCO) coated conductors with embedded BaHfO3 (BHO) nanocrystals that maximizes low-temperature, in-field critical current density Jc while preserving sharp biaxial texture and high self-field Jc at 77 K.
- Hypotheses:
  1) Increasing BHO content from 5 to 15 mol% (relative to Y) increases the density of three-dimensional (3D), isotropic artificial pinning centers and nano-strain fields, shifting Fp,max to higher fields and enhancing Jc at 20–30 K and 3–7 T without degrading YBCO texture if coarsening is suppressed.
  2) A two-step crystallization (pre-growth at 785 °C followed by short final growth at 785–795 °C) suppresses coarsening and preserves monodisperse BHO nanocrystals, enabling higher optimal BHO content than single-step growth.
  3) Selecting 6.5 nm BHO nanocrystals instead of 5.5 nm at otherwise identical loading reduces instability-driven coarsening and yields higher Jc at 0–1 T (4.2–30 K) without compromising high-field performance.
  4) Coherent BHO inclusions generate nano-strain that further enhances 3D pinning without introducing macroscopic residual stress that degrades the 1.5 µm-thick YBCO film.

Step2: Experimental Design – Sample Matrix, Baselines, Controls, and Ablations
- Substrate architecture: Commercial Hastelloy C-276 tape with oxide buffer stack LMO (~30 nm)/IBAD-MgO (~10 nm)/Y2O3 (~100 nm)/Al2O3 (~5 nm) ensuring biaxial texture (in-plane Δφ ≤ 3°, out-of-plane Δω ≤ 2°). Use the same spool for all samples to minimize variability.
- Film thickness target: 1.5 ± 0.1 µm for all samples. Thickness measured by cross-sectional SEM and profilometry.
- BHO nanocrystal size sets: 5.5 ± 0.5 nm and 6.5 ± 0.5 nm (TEM-verified).
- BHO loading series: 0, 5, 10, 12.5, 15 mol% (relative to Y content in YBCO precursor).
- Heat treatment routes:
  A) Two-step crystallization: pre-growth at 785 °C (30 min), final growth at 790–795 °C (10–15 min).
  B) Single-step crystallization: 790–795 °C (40–45 min) with otherwise identical conditions.
- Baselines and comparisons:
  1) Pristine YBCO (0% BHO) grown by two-step route (gold standard baseline).
  2) 5 mol% BHO (both 5.5 and 6.5 nm) by single-step route (conventional control).
  3) 10 and 15 mol% BHO (6.5 nm) by two-step vs single-step (to isolate effect of two-step).
  4) Size ablation at fixed content: 5.5 nm vs 6.5 nm at 10 and 15 mol% under identical two-step conditions.
  5) Loading ablation at fixed size: 6.5 nm at 5, 10, 12.5, 15 mol% (two-step).
- Replication: n = 3 independent tapes per condition; from each tape cut three 4 × 4 mm pieces for magnetometry and one cross-sectional TEM lamella to assess microstructure variability.
- Criteria for success:
  • Self-field Jc(77 K) ≥ 2 MA cm⁻² and Tc ≥ 90 K for all optimized samples.
  • At 30 K & 3 T, Jc ≥ 2.5 × pristine; maximize Fp,max and shift to higher B.
  • Biaxial texture maintained (Δφ ≤ 3°, Δω ≤ 2°).
  • No through-thickness cracks; surface roughness RMS ≤ 20 nm over 10 µm scans.

Step3: Implementation – Precursor Chemistry and Nanoparticle Dispersion
- YBCO LF-MOD solution:
  • Metal–organic salts in 2-methoxyethanol/propionic acid: Y and Cu as 2-ethylhexanoates, Ba partly as trifluoroacetate (low-F formulation, F/Ba molar ratio 0.3–0.5) to minimize HF generation while forming transient BaF2 for phase-pure YBCO conversion.
  • Metal stoichiometry Y:Ba:Cu = 1:2:3 within ±1%.
  • Solids content adjusted for 120–150 nm dry-thickness per coat; viscosity 10–20 mPa·s at 25 °C.
- BHO nanoparticle incorporation:
  • Preformed cubic perovskite BaHfO3 nanocrystals of target size (5.5 or 6.5 nm), ligand-capped (e.g., short-chain carboxylates).
  • Ligand exchange to propionate or acetate to ensure compatibility and dispersion in MOD solvent. Final ligand content verified by FTIR and TGA to ensure clean burn-out.
  • Ultrasonication (100 W, 30 min) and high-shear mixing (10,000 rpm, 10 min) to break agglomerates; filtration through 0.2 µm PTFE filter.
  • Nanoparticle loading set to 5–15 mol% vs Y: compute required BHO mass using densities (ρYBCO ≈ 6.3 g cm⁻³, ρBHO ≈ 8.5–9 g cm⁻³) and confirm by ICP-OES of the mixed solution.
  • Dispersion verification by dynamic light scattering (DLS) and TEM of drop-cast films; reject solutions with DLS hydrodynamic diameter > 1.5× primary size.

Step4: Reel-to-Reel Coating and Pyrolysis
- Coating:
  • Slot-die or dip-coat reel-to-reel at 1–2 m h⁻¹ line speed; dry at 120 °C, 5 min between coats.
  • Number of coats: 10–12 passes to reach 1.5 µm final thickness.
- Pyrolysis (organics removal and BaF2 formation):
  • Ramp to 420 °C at 5 °C min⁻¹ in flowing O2 (1 bar) with 1–3% H2O (dew point ~30–40 °C); dwell 30 min.
  • Monitor exhaust for CO2 and HF; use alkaline scrubber for HF safety.
  • Outcome: dense, crack-free precursor with residual porosity < 10% (checked by SEM on witness samples).

Step5: Two-Step vs Single-Step Crystallization and Oxygenation
- Two-step crystallization (A):
  • Convert and nucleate: 785 °C for 30 min in O2 with 3–5% H2O at total pressure 1 bar; gas flow 2–5 slm across a 10–20 cm hot zone to minimize HF back-diffusion.
  • Short high-temperature finish: ramp to 790–795 °C (≤ 10 °C min⁻¹), hold 10–15 min, then cool at 10–15 °C min⁻¹ to 500 °C.
- Single-step crystallization (B):
  • 790–795 °C for 40–45 min in identical gas environment, then same cool.
- Oxygenation:
  • 450 °C in dry O2 (1 bar) for 1 h, cool to room temperature at 30 °C min⁻¹.
- Rationale and control:
  • Water vapor is required to convert BaF2 intermediates; controlled short final dwell limits nanoparticle coarsening.
  • Identical total time above 780 °C between A and B is not enforced purposely; the comparison isolates the advantage of two-step nucleation/growth separation.

Step6: Structural, Textural, and Chemical Characterization
- X-ray diffraction (XRD):
  • θ–2θ scans: confirm c-axis oriented YBCO and detect BHO reflections (cubic perovskite). Absence of BaCuO2 or Y2O3 secondary phases indicates high purity.
  • ω-rocking curve (002) and φ-scan (103) to quantify Δω and Δφ texture widths.
  • Reciprocal space mapping around (103)/(013) to assess lattice parameter and strain.
  • Williamson–Hall analysis to estimate microstrain and crystallite size.
- Transmission electron microscopy (TEM/STEM):
  • Cross-sectional lamellae via FIB (Ga+ at 30 kV, final polish at 2 kV to minimize damage).
  • HRTEM to measure nanoparticle size distribution (≥ 200 particles per sample) and number density; target mean 5.5 or 6.5 nm with σ ≤ 1 nm.
  • STEM-EDS mapping for Ba, Hf, Y, Cu, O to verify BHO composition and absence of Hf incorporation into YBCO matrix.
  • Geometric phase analysis (GPA) of HRTEM images to map local strain around BHO inclusions (quantify εxx, εyy; aim for coherent or semi-coherent interfaces).
- Surface and cross-section SEM/AFM:
  • Verify surface morphology (RMS roughness ≤ 20 nm over 10 µm); ensure no through-thickness cracks.
- Density and thickness:
  • Cross-sectional SEM and profilometry to confirm 1.5 µm ± 0.1 µm thickness; uniformity along tape length checked every 1 m.

Step7: Superconducting Properties – Magnetization-Based Jc, Angular Dependence, and Transport Checks
- Magnetization measurements:
  • Cut 4 × 4 mm squares; measure M–H loops in a Quantum Design PPMS-VSM at T = 4.2, 20, 30, 50, and 77 K; fields μ0H = 0–9 T (up to max field available).
  • Field orientations: H ∥ c (normal to tape), H ∥ ab (in plane), and variable angle θ from c-axis (0–90°, 5° steps at 30 K for 0–5 T).
  • Demagnetization correction for thin plate geometry (thickness ~1.5 µm) applied; ensure alignment accuracy within ±1°.
- Jc extraction (extended Bean model):
  • For rectangular platelet with in-plane dimensions a ≤ b and thickness t, Jc = 20 ΔM / [a (1 − a/3b)] with ΔM in emu cm⁻³ and Jc in A cm⁻²; a and b measured by optical microscopy to ±5 µm; t measured by cross-sectional SEM.
  • Cross-check a subset of samples by four-probe transport at 77 K, self-field on 2–3 mm wide bridges patterned by laser scribing; criterion 1 µV cm⁻¹. Expect agreement within ±15%.
- Flux pinning force and scaling:
  • Fp(B) = Jc(B) × μ0H; determine Fp,max, its field position B(Fp,max), and normalized scaling curves Fp/Fp,max vs b = B/Birr.
  • Estimate Birr from Kramer plots or 10³ A cm⁻² criterion at each temperature; compare to Dew-Hughes scaling for normal 3D point pins (Fp ∝ b^p (1 − b)^q; p ≈ 0.5, q ≈ 2) and track shifts with BHO content.
- Tc and resistivity:
  • Four-probe resistivity vs T to determine Tc (onset and zero) and residual resistivity ratio; target Tc ≥ 90 K and narrow transition (ΔTc ≤ 1.5 K).
- Statistics:
  • For each condition, report mean ± standard deviation across n = 3 tapes and across cut pieces; use ANOVA to assess significance of differences (p < 0.05).

Step8: Data Analysis Plan and Decision Criteria
- Primary metrics:
  • Jc(30 K, 3 T; H ∥ c and averaged over angle) and Fp,max(4.2–30 K); aim for ≥ 2.5–3× improvement over pristine.
  • Angular anisotropy ratio γJc = Jc(H ∥ ab)/Jc(H ∥ c); isotropic pinning implies γJc → 1 at low T/high B.
- Interpretation:
  • Correlate nanoparticle size dispersion and number density with Fp,max and B(Fp,max). For 3D point pins, optimal matching occurs when inter-pin spacing is comparable to vortex spacing a0 ≈ (2Φ0/(√3B))^0.5; at 3 T, a0 ≈ 28 nm, motivating higher pin densities at 15 mol% BHO.
  • Use GPA-derived strain amplitude and spatial extent to assess contribution of nano-strain to pinning; look for monotonic increase in Fp with strain amplitude at low T.
  • Compare two-step vs single-step: two-step should yield smaller mean particle size, narrower distribution, higher number density, and superior Jc particularly at low T and intermediate/high fields.
  • Compare 5.5 nm vs 6.5 nm BHO at fixed loading: if 5.5 nm shows larger coarsening (broader post-growth size distribution) and lower Jc at 0–1 T, confirm hypothesis on instability-driven growth.
- Go/no-go:
  • If texture degrades (Δφ > 3° or Δω > 2°) or self-field Jc(77 K) < 2 MA cm⁻² at 15 mol% BHO, reduce loading to 12.5 mol% and/or adjust dwell times to re-balance texture vs pinning.
  • If coarsening persists, reduce final dwell to 5–10 min or lower final temperature by 5 °C; consider dispersant optimization.

Step9: Feasibility, Timeline, and Resources
- Equipment:
  • Reel-to-reel coater with controlled atmosphere furnaces (humidified O2 at 1 bar, 500–900 °C).
  • PPMS-VSM with 9 T magnet and sample rotator; cryogenic accessories for 4.2 K.
  • SEM/FIB, HRTEM/STEM-EDS, XRD with pole figure and RSM capability; AFM.
- Personnel:
  • 1 process engineer (coating/heat treatment), 1 materials chemist (solutions/nanoparticles), 1 microscopist (TEM/XRD), 1 physicist (measurements/data analysis).
- Throughput and timeline (approximate):
  • Months 0–2: Solution/nanoparticle preparation, dispersion validation, baseline pristine runs.
  • Months 2–4: Fabricate full sample matrix (two-step and single-step across sizes/loadings).
  • Months 3–6: Structural/TEM characterization and Jc measurements; iterative tuning of dwell times and humidity.
  • Months 6–8: Complete statistics, modeling, and final optimization report.
- Consumables:
  • Precursors, BHO nanoparticles or synthesis reagents, tapes, gases (O2 with humidity control), FIB/TEM supplies.
- Expected yield:
  • >80% acceptable tapes per condition after process tuning (crack-free, textured).

Step10: Risk Assessment and Mitigation
- Nanoparticle agglomeration:
  • Risk: Aggregated BHO reduces effective pin density and disrupts texture.
  • Mitigation: Ligand exchange to short-chain carboxylates; optimize solvent polarity; use surfactant-free dispersions; DLS gate; inline 0.2 µm filtration; adjust viscosity.
- Coarsening during high-T dwell:
  • Risk: Larger particles lower pinning efficiency, especially at low fields.
  • Mitigation: Limit final dwell to 10–15 min; two-step nucleation/growth; consider slight reduction of final T by 5 °C without sacrificing phase purity; fast cool to 500 °C.
- Texture degradation at high BHO loading:
  • Risk: Excess secondary phase reduces YBCO grain alignment.

# Task: Evaluate the Executability of an Experimental Plan

Your task is to evaluate whether a given **experimental plan** has the qualities of a high-quality, implementable, executable plan.

This evaluation **only focuses on the quality of the plan itself**. It does not compare the plan with any reference plan or judge consistency with another plan.

---

## Evaluation Goal

Judge whether the experimental plan is a high-quality experimental document that is **executable, divisible into tasks, actionable, and convertible into an SOP or implementation plan**. Evaluate it strictly against the following reference template for a full-score plan.

---

## Full-Score Reference Template for Experimental-Plan Executability

A top-tier experimental plan should have the following five features:

### 1. Overall Plan Structure (clear hierarchy, closed logic)
- **Experimental overview/objective**: clearly states the core scientific or engineering problem, final goal, and key innovation.
- **Initial experimental draft/summary**: provides a high-level summary of materials, workflow, and expected outcomes.
- **Detailed experimental plan (task decomposition)**: decomposes the full experiment into logically connected, independently executable subtasks, such as Task 1: material preparation, Task 2: sample processing, Task 3: performance testing.
- **Refined experimental plan (SOP-style summary)**: summarizes key steps, parameters, and criteria in parameter tables, workflow tables, or similar forms to create a standardized document that can directly guide operations.

### 2. Task Modularity and Divisibility (clear breakdown, clear responsibility)
- **Clear subtask division**: each subtask includes its own objective, materials and instruments, steps, and expected results.
- **Connections between tasks**: clearly explains how outputs from earlier tasks become inputs for later tasks.
- **Independent operability**: each subtask is complete enough to be assigned to different team members.

### 3. SOP Level of Steps and Parameters (specific, quantitative, reproducible)
- **Detailed step breakdown**: each experimental step is decomposed into numbered concrete operations, such as 3.1 precursor preparation, 3.2 calcination, 3.3 molding.
- **Parameter tables**: key process parameters should be listed clearly in table form, including temperature, time, pressure, rate, atmosphere, concrete values, and tolerance ranges.
- **Instrument and material lists**: clearly list required material specifications, such as purity and dimensions, and key instrument performance specifications.

### 4. Risk Control and Quality Management (anticipate problems, set checkpoints)
- **Precautions**: after each key step, explicitly state possible issues and preventive measures.
- **Quality-control checkpoints**: set checkpoints after key steps, such as verifying phase by XRD or roughness by AFM.
- **Troubleshooting and contingency plans**: provide alternatives or adjustment strategies for undesirable results.

### 5. Expected Results and Feedback Loop (goal-oriented, measurable)
- **Quantified expected results**: explicitly state target performance indicators, such as Jc >= 1e4 A cm^-2 or delta-phi < 5 degrees.
- **Fabrication-characterization-feedback loop**: the workflow should reflect an iterative logic of fabrication -> characterization -> result analysis -> parameter optimization.
- **Engineering and scale-up awareness**: consider industrialization factors such as process scalability, long tape, and large-area uniformity.

---

## Score Calibration and Mandatory Defect Check (anti-inflation mechanism)

**Important instruction: to prevent inflated scores, you must strictly follow the calibration process below.**

### Step 0. Mandatory Identification of Executability Defects (deductions first)
Before calculating the score, compare the experimental plan item by item against the full-score template and explicitly list its **executability defects**.

**Defect deduction reference table (for calibrating your scoring perception):**
| Defect Category | Concrete Symptom | Suggested Deduction | Score-Band Implication |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Broken structure** | Only flat narrative description; no task decomposition and no overview-detail-summary structure. | 0.20 - 0.30 | Falls below 0.70 |
| **Parameter shell** | Mentions process names but gives **no** concrete values, such as missing temperature, time, and pressure. | 0.20 - 0.30 | Falls below 0.70 |
| **No closed loop** | Contains only fabrication steps and no characterization, testing, or validation. | 0.15 - 0.25 | Very difficult to exceed 0.75 |
| **Coarse granularity** | Steps remain slogan-level, such as "optimize process parameters", without operational details. | 0.15 - 0.20 | Ceiling is 0.80 |
| **No risk awareness** | No precautions, possible issues, or quality-control descriptions. | 0.10 - 0.15 | Ceiling is 0.85 |
| **Not quantifiable** | Expected results are only qualitative, such as "performance improves", with no concrete metrics or criteria. | 0.05 - 0.10 | Ceiling is 0.90 |

### Recalibrated Score-Band Anchors (mandatory comparison)
Before giving the final score, force-align the plan with these descriptions:

- **0.90 - 1.00 (excellent/outstanding)**: **rare**. Must satisfy: strong fit with the full-score template, tabulated parameters, complete risk and quality control. **If there is no engineering/SOP-style expression, do not give above 0.95.**
- **0.80 - 0.89 (good/strong)**: has strengths but visible flaws. Example: clear structure and concrete parameters, but missing risk prompts or troubleshooting; or some parameters are missing and would require literature lookup before execution.
- **0.70 - 0.79 (qualified/executability threshold)**: the most common floor range. The plan is coherent, has key parameters, and follows a reasonable experimental logic, but lacks detail granularity. This is the minimum passing line for executability.
- **0.55 - 0.69 (unqualified/unreliable)**: has clear defects, such as missing key parameters that prevent operation, workflow jumps, or no quality-control measures.
- **0.00 - 0.54 (very poor/unrelated)**: conceptual description that can hardly guide an experiment.

### Scoring-Logic Correction
Follow this logic:
1. **If serious defects such as "parameter shell" or "broken structure" are found** -> **cap the score at 0.69**.
2. **If key parameters are present but operational details are absent** -> **score should be in the 0.70 - 0.78 range**.
3. **Strictly control high scores**: scores above 0.85 require strict verification that the plan fully satisfies the corresponding score-band requirements, avoiding subjective score inflation.

---

## Input

Experiment:
Step1: Objectives and Hypotheses
- Objective: Establish an optimized process window (nanocrystal size, loading, and heat treatment) for MOD-derived YBa2Cu3O7−δ (YBCO) coated conductors with embedded BaHfO3 (BHO) nanocrystals that maximizes low-temperature, in-field critical current density Jc while preserving sharp biaxial texture and high self-field Jc at 77 K.
- Hypotheses:
  1) Increasing BHO content from 5 to 15 mol% (relative to Y) increases the density of three-dimensional (3D), isotropic artificial pinning centers and nano-strain fields, shifting Fp,max to higher fields and enhancing Jc at 20–30 K and 3–7 T without degrading YBCO texture if coarsening is suppressed.
  2) A two-step crystallization (pre-growth at 785 °C followed by short final growth at 785–795 °C) suppresses coarsening and preserves monodisperse BHO nanocrystals, enabling higher optimal BHO content than single-step growth.
  3) Selecting 6.5 nm BHO nanocrystals instead of 5.5 nm at otherwise identical loading reduces instability-driven coarsening and yields higher Jc at 0–1 T (4.2–30 K) without compromising high-field performance.
  4) Coherent BHO inclusions generate nano-strain that further enhances 3D pinning without introducing macroscopic residual stress that degrades the 1.5 µm-thick YBCO film.

Step2: Experimental Design – Sample Matrix, Baselines, Controls, and Ablations
- Substrate architecture: Commercial Hastelloy C-276 tape with oxide buffer stack LMO (~30 nm)/IBAD-MgO (~10 nm)/Y2O3 (~100 nm)/Al2O3 (~5 nm) ensuring biaxial texture (in-plane Δφ ≤ 3°, out-of-plane Δω ≤ 2°). Use the same spool for all samples to minimize variability.
- Film thickness target: 1.5 ± 0.1 µm for all samples. Thickness measured by cross-sectional SEM and profilometry.
- BHO nanocrystal size sets: 5.5 ± 0.5 nm and 6.5 ± 0.5 nm (TEM-verified).
- BHO loading series: 0, 5, 10, 12.5, 15 mol% (relative to Y content in YBCO precursor).
- Heat treatment routes:
  A) Two-step crystallization: pre-growth at 785 °C (30 min), final growth at 790–795 °C (10–15 min).
  B) Single-step crystallization: 790–795 °C (40–45 min) with otherwise identical conditions.
- Baselines and comparisons:
  1) Pristine YBCO (0% BHO) grown by two-step route (gold standard baseline).
  2) 5 mol% BHO (both 5.5 and 6.5 nm) by single-step route (conventional control).
  3) 10 and 15 mol% BHO (6.5 nm) by two-step vs single-step (to isolate effect of two-step).
  4) Size ablation at fixed content: 5.5 nm vs 6.5 nm at 10 and 15 mol% under identical two-step conditions.
  5) Loading ablation at fixed size: 6.5 nm at 5, 10, 12.5, 15 mol% (two-step).

- YBCO LF-MOD solution:
  • Metal–organic salts in 2-methoxyethanol/propionic acid: Y and Cu as 2-ethylhexanoates, Ba partly as trifluoroacetate (low-F formulation, F/Ba molar ratio 0.3–0.5) to minimize HF generation while forming transient BaF2 for phase-pure YBCO conversion.
  • Metal stoichiometry Y:Ba:Cu = 1:2:3 within ±1%.
  • Solids content adjusted for 120–150 nm dry-thickness per coat; viscosity 10–20 mPa·s at 25 °C.
- BHO nanoparticle incorporation:
  • Preformed cubic perovskite BaHfO3 nanocrystals of target size (5.5 or 6.5 nm), ligand-capped (e.g., short-chain carboxylates).
  • Ligand exchange to propionate or acetate to ensure compatibility and dispersion in MOD solvent. Final ligand content verified by FTIR and TGA to ensure clean burn-out.
  • Ultrasonication (100 W, 30 min) and high-shear mixing (10,000 rpm, 10 min) to break agglomerates; filtration through 0.2 µm PTFE filter.
  • Nanoparticle loading set to 5–15 mol% vs Y: compute required BHO mass using densities (ρYBCO ≈ 6.3 g cm⁻³, ρBHO ≈ 8.5–9 g cm⁻³) and confirm by ICP-OES of the mixed solution.
  • Dispersion verification by dynamic light scattering (DLS) and TEM of drop-cast films; reject solutions with DLS hydrodynamic diameter > 1.5× primary size.

- Coating:
  • Slot-die or dip-coat reel-to-reel at 1–2 m h⁻¹ line speed; dry at 120 °C, 5 min between coats.
  • Number of coats: 10–12 passes to reach 1.5 µm final thickness.
- Pyrolysis (organics removal and BaF2 formation):
  • Ramp to 420 °C at 5 °C min⁻¹ in flowing O2 (1 bar) with 1–3% H2O (dew point ~30–40 °C); dwell 30 min.
  • Monitor exhaust for CO2 and HF; use alkaline scrubber for HF safety.
  • Outcome: dense, crack-free precursor with residual porosity < 10% (checked by SEM on witness samples).

- Two-step crystallization (A):
  • Convert and nucleate: 785 °C for 30 min in O2 with 3–5% H2O at total pressure 1 bar; gas flow 2–5 slm across a 10–20 cm hot zone to minimize HF back-diffusion.
  • Short high-temperature finish: ramp to 790–795 °C (≤ 10 °C min⁻¹), hold 10–15 min, then cool at 10–15 °C min⁻¹ to 500 °C.

## Task Steps

### Step 1. Normalize and Clean
Normalize the experimental content to unify the evaluation basis:

- Standardize units and notation:
  - temperature: degrees C or K

- Ignore information that does not affect the core judgment:

### Step 2. Extract Executability Features and Defects

## Scoring Principles

1. **Defects must cause deductions**: strictly follow the defect deduction reference table. A high score without listed defects is invalid.
2. **Parameters are core**: a "parameter shell" is a fatal defect; plans with this issue should not score above 0.69.
3. **High scores require strict evidence**: for scores above 0.85, explicitly list concrete evidence in the reason showing that the plan meets "outstanding" standards, such as tabulated parameters, contingency plans, and SOP-style summaries, and confirm that there are no obvious flaws.
4. **No comparison with other plans**: this evaluation only concerns the quality of the plan itself, not whether it resembles a reference plan.
5. **Strictly avoid score inflation**: score each dimension conservatively. For scores above 0.80, repeatedly verify that the corresponding requirements are satisfied and that the score matches the plan's actual quality.

---

## Score References (calibrated, mandatory)

- **1.00 (rare)**: perfect implementation of the full-score template. Parameters are tabulated, risk and quality control are complete, and the engineering loop is clear.
- **0.90 - 0.99**: extremely strong executability; parameters are concrete, structure is clear, and only minor flaws exist, such as one missing risk note. **Verify strictly and do not give lightly.**
- **0.80 - 0.89**: strong plan quality with mostly complete parameters, but lacking engineering awareness or quality-control details. **Confirm that there are no serious defects and that parameters are sufficiently concrete.**
- **0.70 - 0.79**: **passing line**. The plan has key parameters and logic and can be implemented, but operational granularity is coarse.
- **0.55 - 0.69**: average executability. Missing key steps or parameters prevents direct execution.
- **0.35 - 0.54**: weak plan. Mostly conceptual and unable to guide an experiment.
- **0.00 - 0.34**: completely non-executable.

**Warning: most qualified plans should fall between 0.70 and 0.85. Do not give scores above 0.90 lightly; high scores must be strictly controlled.**

---

## Output Requirements
Return only a JSON object with one res field, matching the example.
Do not output True / False.
Do not output a complex nested structure.

Output format:

{"res": {
  "score": 0.00,
  "reason": "First state the main defects identified; then review performance in structural completeness, task decomposition, operational granularity, parameter specificity, risk control, quality control, and engineering loop; finally explain why this score was assigned and emphasize strict control of high scores."
}}

Experiment:
Heading: Overview and Objectives
Step 1: State the hypothesis and goals.
- Hypothesis: Oxygen post-annealing of LaMnO3−δ (LMO) buffer layers contracts the LMO pseudo-cubic lattice (≈3.92 Å → ≈3.85 Å) by reducing oxygen vacancies and oxidizing Mn3+ to Mn4+, thereby reducing lattice mismatch with YBa2Cu3O7−δ (YBCO; in-plane ≈3.85 Å). This reduces interfacial misfit strain and misfit dislocation density, suppresses a-axis oriented YBCO grains, enhances c-axis epitaxy, and improves critical current (Ic) by ~20% at 77 K self-field in second-generation coated conductors.
- Goals: (i) Quantify how LMO lattice parameter, texture, and surface topography evolve with O2 annealing; (ii) establish causal links among mismatch, defect density, a-axis grain fraction, and transport performance; (iii) demonstrate uniform enhancement on 1 m and 60 m tapes using roll-to-roll (R2R) processes.

Heading: Experimental Design
Step 2: Define architecture and fixed variables.
- Substrate architecture: Hastelloy C-276 (50–100 μm) with buffer stack Al2O3 (~10 nm)/Y2O3 (~100 nm)/IBAD-MgO (~10–12 nm)/epi-MgO (~30–50 nm)/LMO (50–150 nm).
- YBCO deposition: low-fluorine MOD, target thickness 1.2–1.5 μm across all samples; identical precursor chemistry, pyrolysis, and crystallization schedule for all experiments.
- Texture constraints: Maintain IBAD-MgO texture Δφ ~7–8°; epi-MgO Δφ ≤ 6°. Do not alter IBAD conditions during the study.
- Environmental constants during YBCO growth and oxygenation: identical gas composition and humidity; identical post-growth oxygenation to reach δ ≲ 0.1 in YBCO.

Step 3: Baseline and comparator groups.
- Baseline LMO (as-deposited): DC reactive sputtered LMO (oxygen-deficient, a_pc ≈ 3.90–3.92 Å), no post-anneal.
- Comparator A (oxygen-annealed LMO): Post-annealed in O2 (500–620 °C, 0–120 min, pO2 = 0.21–1 atm) to contract a_pc down to ≈3.85 Å.
- Comparator B (inert anneal control): Annealed in high-purity N2 at identical temperature/time cycles to rule out thermal-only effects (no oxygen uptake).
- Comparator C (over-anneal boundary): O2 anneal at upper bound (e.g., 620 °C, 120 min, 1 atm) to probe risk of over-oxidation, textural degradation, or interdiffusion.
- Thickness control: LMO thickness at 50 nm, 100 nm, 150 nm across selected anneal conditions to check thickness-dependent oxygenation and misfit relaxation.

Step 4: Experimental matrix (screening on coupons; then scale-up).
- Screening (coupon-level): 10 cm long, 12 mm wide sections across three spools; for each, prepare:
  • Temperatures: 500, 560, 590, 620 °C.
  • Dwell times: 0 (no anneal), 15, 30, 60, 120 min.
  • Atmospheres: Air (pO2 ≈ 0.21 atm) and O2 (1 atm); plus N2 (control).
  • Total unique conditions: 4 temps × 5 times × 2 O2 levels + N2 controls at 560 and 590 °C for 30 min = 40 + 2 = 42.
  • For 6 selected conditions (spanning a_pc ≈ 3.92 → 3.85 Å), add LMO thickness variation (50/100/150 nm) → 18 more.
- Scale-up (R2R): Select top 2–3 O2 anneal conditions (best Ic and microstructure) and run:
  • 1 m tapes (n = 3 per condition).
  • 60 m tape (n = 1 best condition) to assess uniformity and industrial viability.

Step 5: Sample processing sequence (to ensure comparability).
- Sequence fixed for all samples:
  1) IBAD-MgO/epi-MgO buffer completion (confirmed texture).
  2) LMO deposition by DC reactive sputtering (identical power, pressure, substrate temperature, and pO2 for the batch).
  3) Post-anneal of LMO under defined condition (only variable).
  4) YBCO low-fluorine MOD deposition under identical schedule.
  5) YBCO oxygenation to set δ.
  6) Contactless Ic mapping and four-probe validation on selected coupons.

Step 6: Ablation studies to test causal mechanisms.
- Composition tuning ablation: Compare O2-annealed vs N2-annealed LMO at same T, t → isolates oxygen chemistry from thermal effects on lattice parameter and texture.
- Interface tuning ablation: Keep LMO a_pc matched (≈3.85 Å) but introduce a thin interfacial Ca-doped CeO2 barrier (2–5 nm) on a subset to test whether reduced mismatch alone (without added interlayer) yields the same suppression of a-axis grains; if added barrier brings no further gain, mismatch reduction is the dominant mechanism. (Barrier layer optional and confined to small subset due to process complexity.)
- Texture tuning ablation: Mildly degrade LMO texture by intentionally lowering sputter substrate temperature by 50–70 °C during LMO growth (without O2 anneal), then apply the same O2 anneal to see whether restored lattice matching without good texture still suppresses a-axis grains. This separates texture from lattice parameter effects.
- Stress tuning ablation: Vary LMO thickness to modulate relaxation and residual strain; analyze sin2ψ XRD residual stress and relate to misfit dislocation spacing in cross-sectional TEM.
- Grain boundary tuning ablation: Correlate a-axis grain fraction from XRD with in-plane texture (Δφ) and Ic; intentionally promote a-axis growth by increasing YBCO crystallization heating rate by 20% in a small subset (control) to observe sensitivity of a-axis fraction to interface-mismatch condition.

Step 7: Characterization and metrics.
- LMO structure:
  • XRD θ–2θ scans for LMO (00l) peaks; extract a_pc from (001) peak near 2θ ≈ 23° (Cu Kα).
  • XRD rocking curve (ω) for LMO (00l): Δω target ≤ 2.5° (no deterioration with O2 anneal).
  • φ-scans of LMO (101) to quantify in-plane texture: Δφ target ≈ 7°.
  • Raman spectroscopy (500–650 cm−1): track Mn–O stretching modes; increased frequency and sharpening indicate shorter Mn–O bonds and reduced VO.
  • XPS (Mn 2p, Mn 3s) or XANES (optional) to quantify Mn3+/Mn4+ ratio; correlate with a_pc.
  • AFM (5 × 5 μm2): RMS roughness target ≤ 2 nm; verify no grain coarsening.
- Interface and defects:
  • Cross-sectional TEM on select samples: measure misfit dislocation spacing at LMO/YBCO; identify interfacial secondary phases; quantify thickness uniformity; measure a-axis lamellae, stacking faults.
  • XRD residual stress (sin2ψ) for LMO and YBCO; compare among anneal conditions.
- YBCO orientation and crystallinity:
  • XRD θ–2θ: quantify c-axis (00l) intensities; measure a-axis (h00) peak intensities; compute a-axis fraction Fa = ΣI(h00)/[ΣI(00l) + ΣI(h00)]. Target Fa ≤ 1–2%.
  • Rocking curve Δω(005) target ≤ 2.0°; φ-scan Δφ(103) target ≤ 7°.
- Superconducting properties:
  • Contactless Ic mapping at 77 K, self-field (magnetic induction method); calibrate with four-probe on short sections (1–5 cm) using 1 μV/cm criterion.
  • Jc(H, T) at 30–77 K and μ0H = 0–9 T; compute pinning force Fp = μ0 Jc H.
  • Tc and ρ(T) on small coupons to verify oxygenation (Tc ≈ 90 K).
- Uniformity:
  • Along-length mapping: every 5–10 m on the 60 m run, record a_pc (LMO) by XRD spot scans, texture (Δφ, Δω), surface RMS on selected locations, and Ic.

Step 8: Data analysis and evaluation criteria.
- Primary performance metric: Ic (77 K, self-field) per 12 mm width.
  • Success criterion: ≥ 20% improvement vs baseline as-deposited LMO; achieve ≥ 500 A/12 mm on 1 m tapes; demonstrate ≥ 560 A/12 mm peak and within ±5% along 60 m.
- Microstructural criteria:
  • LMO a_pc contraction to 3.85 ± 0.01 Å; Δφ ≈ 7° ± 1°; Δω ≤ 2.5°; RMS ≤ 2 nm.
  • YBCO c-axis quality: Δω(005) ≤ 2.0°; Δφ(103) ≤ 7.0°; a-axis fraction Fa ≤ 1–2%.
- Statistical treatment:
  • For screening, n ≥ 3 tapes per condition; analyze with ANOVA for Ic, Δω, Fa vs a_pc; post-hoc Tukey with α = 0.05.
  • Regression: Ic vs (lattice mismatch |f|), where f = (aLMO − aYBCO)/aYBCO. Expect monotonic improvement as |f| → 0. Fit linear or quadratic; report R2.
  • Mediation analysis: test whether reduction in Fa mediates the effect of a_pc on Ic.
- Mechanistic validation:
  • Show that O2-annealed (reduced VO, higher Mn4+) reduces a_pc and misfit dislocation density in TEM; N2-annealed samples do not replicate improvements.
  • Correlate Raman Mn–O stretching frequency shift with a_pc and Ic.
  • Demonstrate that texture (Δφ, Δω) is preserved through annealing (texture tuning objective met).

Heading: Implementation of Technologies/Methods
Step 9: LMO deposition by DC reactive magnetron sputtering.
- Target: Stoichiometric LaMnO3 ceramic; 2–3 inch for lab tool, larger for R2R.
- Conditions (typical, to be tuned for uniformity):
  • Power: 100–200 W DC; pressure: 3–5 mTorr; Ar/O2 = 90/10 to 95/5; substrate temperature: 500–600 °C to promote epitaxy on epi-MgO.
  • Film thickness: 100 nm baseline; deposition rate ≈ 0.5–1.0 nm/s.
  • Achieve as-deposited a_pc ≈ 3.90–3.92 Å (oxygen-deficient).
- Texture transfer: Ensure epitaxial cube-on-cube LMO//MgO; monitor in situ by RHEED if available (lab-scale) or ex situ XRD line scans (R2R).

Step 10: Oxygen post-annealing of LMO (composition tuning).
- Furnace/atmosphere:
  • For coupons: box furnace with high-purity O2 or air; flow 1–5 slm; ramp 10 °C/min.
  • For R2R: infrared or radiant heater zone in pure O2 (0.5–1 atm), residence times set by line speed and zone length.
- Parameters:
  • Screening: 500, 560, 590, 620 °C; dwell 0–120 min.
  • Atmosphere: O2 (1 atm) and air (0.21 atm); add N2 controls.
- Rationale (diffusion length): For D_O ~10^−10–10^−12 cm2/s at 500–600 °C in perovskites, 30–60 min suffices for 50–150 nm films (diffusion length ≫ film thickness).
- Expected signatures:
  • XRD peak shift to higher 2θ indicating lattice contraction toward ≈3.85 Å.
  • Raman Mn–O stretching mode hardening and narrowing.
  • XPS: increased Mn4+ spectral weight (e.g., Mn 3s multiplet splitting reduction).

Step 11: Interface and stress control (interface/stress tuning).
- Maintain epi-MgO and LMO surface smoothness (RMS ≤ 2 nm) to avoid step-induced a-axis nucleation.
- Optional ultrathin CeO2 cap (2–5 nm) only for interface ablation subset; standard process excludes cap to isolate LMO oxygenation effects.
- Residual stress measurement by XRD sin2ψ on LMO (00l) and YBCO (00l); reduced in-plane strain expected as mismatch |f| decreases.

Step 12: YBCO low-fluorine MOD process.
- Precursor solution: Low-F TFA-based with F:metal ratio ≲ 0.5; solution solids 0.5–1.0 M.
- Coating: Slot-die or dip-coating; target final thickness 1.2–1.5 μm via single or multiple coats with intermediate pyrolysis.
- Pyrolysis: 400–450 °C in flowing O2/N2 with 5–15% humidity to remove organics and fluorides, ramp 5–10 °C/min, dwell 30–60 min.
- Crystallization: 760–800 °C in O2 with controlled humidity (200–1000 ppm H2O), dwell 30–60 min; cool in O2 to 450 °C.
- Oxygenation: Hold at 400–450 °C in O2 for 1–2 h to achieve δ ≲ 0.1; confirm Tc ≈ 90 K on test coupons.
- Keep all YBCO steps identical across samples to isolate LMO effects.

Step 13: Texture and morphology control (texture tuning).
- Preserve IBAD-MgO and LMO biaxial texture: confirm Δφ and Δω after O2 anneal; avoid anneal conditions that induce recrystallization or grain coarsening.
- AFM screening: reject any LMO surface with RMS > 3 nm before YBCO deposition.

Step 14: Measurements and instrumentation.
- XRD: θ–2θ, ω rocking curves, φ scans; pole figures if available; spot size ~1–2 mm for along-length mapping.
- Raman: 532 nm excitation; acquire 450–750 cm−1; fit Mn–O stretching modes; monitor peak shift and FWHM.
- AFM: Tapping mode; 5 × 5 μm2 and 1 × 1 μm2 scans; extract RMS.
- XPS: Monochromatic Al Kα; Mn 2p, 3s regions; perform ion-milling carefully or angle-resolved to avoid damage; quantify Mn valence trends.
- TEM: FIB cross-sections on select best/worst; HAADF-STEM, GPA strain mapping, misfit dislocation densities at LMO/YBCO; measure a-axis lamellae density.
- Ic mapping: Contactless magnetic induction scanner; calibrate with four-probe on short sections. Use standard V–I criterion 1 μV/cm for four-probe; correct for self-field differences. For R2R, map Ic every 5–10 m.
- Jc(H, T): PPMS or 77 K variable-field setup; compute Fp = μ0 Jc H; compare Fp,max and scaling with reduced field.

Heading: Feasibility Assessment
Step 15: Resources and timeline.
- Equipment: Existing R2R DC sputter coater for LMO; R2R MOD line; tube/box furnaces with O2; XRD, AFM, Raman, XPS; access to TEM (shared facility); Ic mapping system; four-probe station; cryogenics (LN2, variable-T magnet).
- Personnel: 1 thin-film process engineer (LMO, anneal), 1 solution process engineer (MOD YBCO), 1 characterization scientist, 1 data analyst; shared TEM operator.
- Timeline:
  • Months 0–1: Process calibration (as-deposited LMO reproducibility, textural checks).
  • Months 1–3: Screening matrix on coupons; down-select best 2–3 anneal conditions.
  • Months 3–4: 1 m tapes for the top conditions; Ic and microstructure.
  • Months 4–6: 60 m demonstration for best condition; uniformity analysis and final validation.

Step 16: Risks and mitigation.
- Over-oxidation of LMO causing texture degradation or phase change.
  • Mitigation: Cap temperature ≤ 620 °C; monitor Δφ, Δω post-anneal; shorten dwell if texture worsens.
- Oxygen-induced oxidation of underlying metal.
  • Mitigation: Ensure integrity of Al2O3/Y2O3 barrier; inspect after anneal by XRD and TEM; limit O2 partial pressure to 0.21–1 atm and keep dwell minimal for full oxygenation of thin LMO.
- Mn interdiffusion into YBCO at high T.
  • Mitigation: Limit LMO anneal before YBCO deposition; avoid high-temperature (>800 °C) exposures with YBCO present; consider optional 2–5 nm CeO2 cap in ablation subset if interdiffusion is observed.
- Non-uniform oxygen uptake along length.
  • Mitigation: Uniform gas flow and line speed; real-time temperature profiling; along-length XRD spot checks.
- Measurement uncertainty in contactless Ic.
  • Mitigation: Routine calibration against four-probe on multiple segments; use consistent models (Bean strip) and geometry factors.

Heading: References to Previous Studies (pre-2025)
Step 17: Cite foundational and supporting literature.
- J. D. Jorgensen et al., Structural properties of oxygen-deficient YBa2Cu3O7−δ, Phys. Rev. B 41, 1863 (1990) — YBCO lattice and oxygenation.
- S. R. Foltyn et al., Materials science challenges for high-temperature superconducting wire, Nature Materials 6, 631–642 (2007) — Coated conductor overview, texture, Ic.
- P. N. Arendt et al., Rolling-assisted biaxially textured substrates and buffer layers for high-temperature superconductors, MRS Bulletin 29, 543–550 (2004) — IBAD templates and texture metrics.
- Y. Iijima et al., In-plane aligned YBa2Cu3O7−x thin films on polycrystalline metallic substrates, Appl. Phys. Lett. 60, 769 (1992) — Early IBAD-based coated conductor concepts.
- J. Töpfer and J. B. Goodenough, LaMnO3+δ Revisited, J. Solid State Chem. 130, 117–128 (1997) — Oxygen nonstoichiometry, Mn valence, lattice evolution in LaMnO3±δ.
- J. Mizusaki et al., Oxygen nonstoichiometry and defect structure of La1−xSrxMnO3−δ, Solid State Ionics 129, 163–177 (2000) — Oxygen transport and defect chemistry in perovskite manganites.
- M. N. Iliev et al., Raman spectroscopy of orthorhombic perovskite LaMnO3 and La1−xSrxMnO3, Phys. Rev. B 57, 2872 (1998) — Mn–O vibrational modes vs oxygen content/structure.
- J. W. Matthews and A. E. Blakeslee, Defects in epitaxial multilayers: I. Misfit dislocations, J. Cryst. Growth 27, 118–125 (1974) — Misfit dislocation and critical thickness framework.
- T. Haage et al., Growth mechanism and microstructure of a-axis oriented YBa2Cu3O7−δ thin films, Phys. Rev. B 56, 840–850 (1997) — Origins and suppression of a-axis grains.
- T. Izumi and Y. Shiohara, Development of coated conductors by the MOD method, Physica C 463–465, 510–515 (2007) — MOD/TFA process fundamentals.
- A. Xu et al., Low-fluorine solution growth of YBCO films for coated conductors, Supercond. Sci. Technol. 23, 014003 (2010) — Low-fluorine MOD chemistry and processing.
- E. H. Brandt and M. V. Indenbom, Type-II-superconductor strip with current in a perpendicular magnetic field, Phys. Rev. B 48, 12893 (1993) — Magnetization modeling relevant to contactless Ic.
- M. Oomen et al., An improved method to determine the critical current of HTS tapes by magnetic measurements, IEEE Trans. Appl. Supercond. 9, 1677–1680 (1999) — Inductive Ic measurement methodology.
- A. Goyal, Second-generation high temperature superconducting wires, MRS Bulletin 29, 552–561 (2004) — Texture transfer and coated conductor performance.
- J. H. Durrell et al., The behavior of coated conductors in magnetic fields, Supercond. Sci. Technol. 26, 093001 (2013) — Jc(H) and pinning in coated conductors.

Heading: Clarity Notes (key concepts explained)
Step 18: Explain critical concepts.
- Lattice mismatch f: The relative difference between in-plane lattice constants of film and underlying layer: f = (a_film − a_sub)/a_sub. Smaller |f| reduces misfit dislocations and interfacial strain.
- a-axis vs c-axis orientation: In YBCO, c-axis perpendicular to the substrate is desired for optimal current. a-axis grains (with a-axis out-of-plane) interrupt current paths and reduce Ic.
- Texture metrics: Δω (rocking curve FWHM) quantifies out-of-plane spread; Δφ (phi-scan FWHM) quantifies in-plane spread. Smaller values indicate better alignment.
- Oxygen vacancies (VO) in LMO: Missing oxygen increases Mn–O bond length and lattice parameter; oxygen annealing fills VO, oxidizes Mn3+ to Mn4+, shortens Mn–O bonds, and contracts the lattice.
- Inductive Ic measurement: A contactless magnetic method infers Ic from the field generated by shielding currents under an applied AC field, calibrated against transport standards.

Heading: Expected Outcomes and Decision Points
Step 19: Decision-making and scale-up.
- Select the O2 anneal condition achieving a_pc ≈ 3.85 Å, Δφ/Δω preserved, AFM RMS ≤ 2 nm, Fa ≤ 1–2%, and ≥ 20% Ic improvement vs baseline.
- If N2-annealed controls do not show improvement while O2-annealed do, oxygen chemistry is validated as the key mechanism.
- Proceed to 60 m R2R run with the best condition; accept if along-length Ic variation ≤ ±5% with peak ≥ 560 A/12 mm at 77 K self-field and microstructural metrics within targets.

# Task: Evaluate the Executability of an Experimental Plan

Your task is to evaluate whether a given **experimental plan** has the qualities of a high-quality, implementable, executable plan.

This evaluation **only focuses on the quality of the plan itself**. It does not compare the plan with any reference plan or judge consistency with another plan.

---

## Evaluation Goal

Judge whether the experimental plan is a high-quality experimental document that is **executable, divisible into tasks, actionable, and convertible into an SOP or implementation plan**. Evaluate it strictly against the following reference template for a full-score plan.

---

## Full-Score Reference Template for Experimental-Plan Executability

A top-tier experimental plan should have the following five features:

### 1. Overall Plan Structure (clear hierarchy, closed logic)
- **Experimental overview/objective**: clearly states the core scientific or engineering problem, final goal, and key innovation.
- **Initial experimental draft/summary**: provides a high-level summary of materials, workflow, and expected outcomes.
- **Detailed experimental plan (task decomposition)**: decomposes the full experiment into logically connected, independently executable subtasks, such as Task 1: material preparation, Task 2: sample processing, Task 3: performance testing.
- **Refined experimental plan (SOP-style summary)**: summarizes key steps, parameters, and criteria in parameter tables, workflow tables, or similar forms to create a standardized document that can directly guide operations.

### 2. Task Modularity and Divisibility (clear breakdown, clear responsibility)
- **Clear subtask division**: each subtask includes its own objective, materials and instruments, steps, and expected results.
- **Connections between tasks**: clearly explains how outputs from earlier tasks become inputs for later tasks.
- **Independent operability**: each subtask is complete enough to be assigned to different team members.

### 3. SOP Level of Steps and Parameters (specific, quantitative, reproducible)
- **Detailed step breakdown**: each experimental step is decomposed into numbered concrete operations, such as 3.1 precursor preparation, 3.2 calcination, 3.3 molding.
- **Parameter tables**: key process parameters should be listed clearly in table form, including temperature, time, pressure, rate, atmosphere, concrete values, and tolerance ranges.
- **Instrument and material lists**: clearly list required material specifications, such as purity and dimensions, and key instrument performance specifications.

### 4. Risk Control and Quality Management (anticipate problems, set checkpoints)
- **Precautions**: after each key step, explicitly state possible issues and preventive measures.
- **Quality-control checkpoints**: set checkpoints after key steps, such as verifying phase by XRD or roughness by AFM.
- **Troubleshooting and contingency plans**: provide alternatives or adjustment strategies for undesirable results.

### 5. Expected Results and Feedback Loop (goal-oriented, measurable)
- **Quantified expected results**: explicitly state target performance indicators, such as Jc >= 1e4 A cm^-2 or delta-phi < 5 degrees.
- **Fabrication-characterization-feedback loop**: the workflow should reflect an iterative logic of fabrication -> characterization -> result analysis -> parameter optimization.
- **Engineering and scale-up awareness**: consider industrialization factors such as process scalability, long tape, and large-area uniformity.

---

## Score Calibration and Mandatory Defect Check (anti-inflation mechanism)

**Important instruction: to prevent inflated scores, you must strictly follow the calibration process below.**

### Step 0. Mandatory Identification of Executability Defects (deductions first)
Before calculating the score, compare the experimental plan item by item against the full-score template and explicitly list its **executability defects**.

**Defect deduction reference table (for calibrating your scoring perception):**
| Defect Category | Concrete Symptom | Suggested Deduction | Score-Band Implication |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Broken structure** | Only flat narrative description; no task decomposition and no overview-detail-summary structure. | 0.20 - 0.30 | Falls below 0.70 |
| **Parameter shell** | Mentions process names but gives **no** concrete values, such as missing temperature, time, and pressure. | 0.20 - 0.30 | Falls below 0.70 |
| **No closed loop** | Contains only fabrication steps and no characterization, testing, or validation. | 0.15 - 0.25 | Very difficult to exceed 0.75 |
| **Coarse granularity** | Steps remain slogan-level, such as "optimize process parameters", without operational details. | 0.15 - 0.20 | Ceiling is 0.80 |
| **No risk awareness** | No precautions, possible issues, or quality-control descriptions. | 0.10 - 0.15 | Ceiling is 0.85 |
| **Not quantifiable** | Expected results are only qualitative, such as "performance improves", with no concrete metrics or criteria. | 0.05 - 0.10 | Ceiling is 0.90 |

### Recalibrated Score-Band Anchors (mandatory comparison)
Before giving the final score, force-align the plan with these descriptions:

- **0.90 - 1.00 (excellent/outstanding)**: **rare**. Must satisfy: strong fit with the full-score template, tabulated parameters, complete risk and quality control. **If there is no engineering/SOP-style expression, do not give above 0.95.**
- **0.80 - 0.89 (good/strong)**: has strengths but visible flaws. Example: clear structure and concrete parameters, but missing risk prompts or troubleshooting; or some parameters are missing and would require literature lookup before execution.
- **0.70 - 0.79 (qualified/executability threshold)**: the most common floor range. The plan is coherent, has key parameters, and follows a reasonable experimental logic, but lacks detail granularity. This is the minimum passing line for executability.
- **0.55 - 0.69 (unqualified/unreliable)**: has clear defects, such as missing key parameters that prevent operation, workflow jumps, or no quality-control measures.
- **0.00 - 0.54 (very poor/unrelated)**: conceptual description that can hardly guide an experiment.

### Scoring-Logic Correction
Follow this logic:
1. **If serious defects such as "parameter shell" or "broken structure" are found** -> **cap the score at 0.69**.
2. **If key parameters are present but operational details are absent** -> **score should be in the 0.70 - 0.78 range**.
3. **Strictly control high scores**: scores above 0.85 require strict verification that the plan fully satisfies the corresponding score-band requirements, avoiding subjective score inflation.

---

Step 3: Baseline and comparator groups.
- Baseline LMO (as-deposited): DC reactive sputtered LMO (oxygen-deficient, a_pc ≈ 3.90–3.92 Å), no post-anneal.
- Comparator A (oxygen-annealed LMO): Post-annealed in O2 (500–620 °C, 0–120 min, pO2 = 0.21–1 atm) to contract a_pc down to ≈3.85 Å.
- Comparator B (inert anneal control): Annealed in high-purity N2 at identical temperature/time cycles to rule out thermal-only effects (no oxygen uptake).
- Comparator C (over-anneal boundary): O2 anneal at upper bound (e.g., 620 °C, 120 min, 1 atm) to probe risk of over-oxidation, textural degradation, or interdiffusion.
- Thickness control: LMO thickness at 50 nm, 100 nm, 150 nm across selected anneal conditions to check thickness-dependent oxygenation and misfit relaxation.

Step 4: Experimental matrix (screening on coupons; then scale-up).
- Screening (coupon-level): 10 cm long, 12 mm wide sections across three spools; for each, prepare:
  • Temperatures: 500, 560, 590, 620 °C.
  • Dwell times: 0 (no anneal), 15, 30, 60, 120 min.
  • Atmospheres: Air (pO2 ≈ 0.21 atm) and O2 (1 atm); plus N2 (control).
  • Total unique conditions: 4 temps × 5 times × 2 O2 levels + N2 controls at 560 and 590 °C for 30 min = 40 + 2 = 42.
  • For 6 selected conditions (spanning a_pc ≈ 3.92 → 3.85 Å), add LMO thickness variation (50/100/150 nm) → 18 more.
- Scale-up (R2R): Select top 2–3 O2 anneal conditions (best Ic and microstructure) and run:
  • 1 m tapes (n = 3 per condition).
  • 60 m tape (n = 1 best condition) to assess uniformity and industrial viability.

Step 5: Sample processing sequence (to ensure comparability).
- Sequence fixed for all samples:
  1) IBAD-MgO/epi-MgO buffer completion (confirmed texture).
  2) LMO deposition by DC reactive sputtering (identical power, pressure, substrate temperature, and pO2 for the batch).
  3) Post-anneal of LMO under defined condition (only variable).
  4) YBCO low-fluorine MOD deposition under identical schedule.
  5) YBCO oxygenation to set δ.
  6) Contactless Ic mapping and four-probe validation on selected coupons.

Step 6: Ablation studies to test causal mechanisms.
- Composition tuning ablation: Compare O2-annealed vs N2-annealed LMO at same T, t → isolates oxygen chemistry from thermal effects on lattice parameter and texture.
- Interface tuning ablation: Keep LMO a_pc matched (≈3.85 Å) but introduce a thin interfacial Ca-doped CeO2 barrier (2–5 nm) on a subset to test whether reduced mismatch alone (without added interlayer) yields the same suppression of a-axis grains; if added barrier brings no further gain, mismatch reduction is the dominant mechanism. (Barrier layer optional and confined to small subset due to process complexity.)
- Texture tuning ablation: Mildly degrade LMO texture by intentionally lowering sputter substrate temperature by 50–70 °C during LMO growth (without O2 anneal), then apply the same O2 anneal to see whether restored lattice matching without good texture still suppresses a-axis grains. This separates texture from lattice parameter effects.
- Stress tuning ablation: Vary LMO thickness to modulate relaxation and residual strain; analyze sin2ψ XRD residual stress and relate to misfit dislocation spacing in cross-sectional TEM.
- Grain boundary tuning ablation: Correlate a-axis grain fraction from XRD with in-plane texture (Δφ) and Ic; intentionally promote a-axis growth by increasing YBCO crystallization heating rate by 20% in a small subset (control) to observe sensitivity of a-axis fraction to interface-mismatch condition.

Step 7: Characterization and metrics.
- LMO structure:
  • XRD θ–2θ scans for LMO (00l) peaks; extract a_pc from (001) peak near 2θ ≈ 23° (Cu Kα).
  • XRD rocking curve (ω) for LMO (00l): Δω target ≤ 2.5° (no deterioration with O2 anneal).
  • φ-scans of LMO (101) to quantify in-plane texture: Δφ target ≈ 7°.
  • Raman spectroscopy (500–650 cm−1): track Mn–O stretching modes; increased frequency and sharpening indicate shorter Mn–O bonds and reduced VO.
  • XPS (Mn 2p, Mn 3s) or XANES (optional) to quantify Mn3+/Mn4+ ratio; correlate with a_pc.
  • AFM (5 × 5 μm2): RMS roughness target ≤ 2 nm; verify no grain coarsening.
- Interface and defects:
  • Cross-sectional TEM on select samples: measure misfit dislocation spacing at LMO/YBCO; identify interfacial secondary phases; quantify thickness uniformity; measure a-axis lamellae, stacking faults.
  • XRD residual stress (sin2ψ) for LMO and YBCO; compare among anneal conditions.
- YBCO orientation and crystallinity:
  • XRD θ–2θ: quantify c-axis (00l) intensities; measure a-axis (h00) peak intensities; compute a-axis fraction Fa = ΣI(h00)/[ΣI(00l) + ΣI(h00)]. Target Fa ≤ 1–2%.
  • Rocking curve Δω(005) target ≤ 2.0°; φ-scan Δφ(103) target ≤ 7°.
- Superconducting properties:
  • Contactless Ic mapping at 77 K, self-field (magnetic induction method); calibrate with four-probe on short sections (1–5 cm) using 1 μV/cm criterion.
  • Jc(H, T) at 30–77 K and μ0H = 0–9 T; compute pinning force Fp = μ0 Jc H.
  • Tc and ρ(T) on small coupons to verify oxygenation (Tc ≈ 90 K).
- Uniformity:
  • Along-length mapping: every 5–10 m on the 60 m run, record a_pc (LMO) by XRD spot scans, texture (Δφ, Δω), surface RMS on selected locations, and Ic.

Step 8: Data analysis and evaluation criteria.
- Primary performance metric: Ic (77 K, self-field) per 12 mm width.
  • Success criterion: ≥ 20% improvement vs baseline as-deposited LMO; achieve ≥ 500 A/12 mm on 1 m tapes; demonstrate ≥ 560 A/12 mm peak and within ±5% along 60 m.
- Microstructural criteria:
  • LMO a_pc contraction to 3.85 ± 0.01 Å; Δφ ≈ 7° ± 1°; Δω ≤ 2.5°; RMS ≤ 2 nm.
  • YBCO c-axis quality: Δω(005) ≤ 2.0°; Δφ(103) ≤ 7.0°; a-axis fraction Fa ≤ 1–2%.
- Statistical treatment:
  • For screening, n ≥ 3 tapes per condition; analyze with ANOVA for Ic, Δω, Fa vs a_pc; post-hoc Tukey with α = 0.05.
  • Regression: Ic vs (lattice mismatch |f|), where f = (aLMO − aYBCO)/aYBCO. Expect monotonic improvement as |f| → 0. Fit linear or quadratic; report R2.
  • Mediation analysis: test whether reduction in Fa mediates the effect of a_pc on Ic.
- Mechanistic validation:
  • Show that O2-annealed (reduced VO, higher Mn4+) reduces a_pc and misfit dislocation density in TEM; N2-annealed samples do not replicate improvements.
  • Correlate Raman Mn–O stretching frequency shift with a_pc and Ic.
  • Demonstrate that texture (Δφ, Δω) is preserved through annealing (texture tuning objective met).

Heading: Implementation of Technologies/Methods
Step 9: LMO deposition by DC reactive magnetron sputtering.
- Target: Stoichiometric LaMnO3 ceramic; 2–3 inch for lab tool, larger for R2R.
- Conditions (typical, to be tuned for uniformity):
  • Power: 100–200 W DC; pressure: 3–5 mTorr; Ar/O2 = 90/10 to 95/5; substrate temperature: 500–600 °C to promote epitaxy on epi-MgO.
  • Film thickness: 100 nm baseline; deposition rate ≈ 0.5–1.0 nm/s.
  • Achieve as-deposited a_pc ≈ 3.90–3.92 Å (oxygen-deficient).
- Texture transfer: Ensure epitaxial cube-on-cube LMO//MgO; monitor in situ by RHEED if available (lab-scale) or ex situ XRD line scans (R2R).

Step 10: Oxygen post-annealing of LMO (composition tuning).
- Furnace/atmosphere:
  • For coupons: box furnace with high-purity O2 or air; flow 1–5 slm; ramp 10 °C/min.
  • For R2R: infrared or radiant heater zone in pure O2 (0.5–1 atm), residence times set by line speed and zone length.
- Parameters:
  • Screening: 500, 560, 590, 620 °C; dwell 0–120 min.
  • Atmosphere: O2 (1 atm) and air (0.21 atm); add N2 controls.
- Rationale (diffusion length): For D_O ~10^−10–10^−12 cm2/s at 500–600 °C in perovskites, 30–60 min suffices for 50–150 nm films (diffusion length ≫ film thickness).
- Expected signatures:
  • XRD peak shift to higher 2θ indicating lattice contraction toward ≈3.85 Å.
  • Raman Mn–O stretching mode hardening and narrowing.
  • XPS: increased Mn4+ spectral weight (e.g., Mn 3s multiplet splitting reduction).

Step 11: Interface and stress control (interface/stress tuning).
- Maintain epi-MgO and LMO surface smoothness (RMS ≤ 2 nm) to avoid step-induced a-axis nucleation.
- Optional ultrathin CeO2 cap (2–5 nm) only for interface ablation subset; standard process excludes cap to isolate LMO oxygenation effects.
- Residual stress measurement by XRD sin2ψ on LMO (00l) and YBCO (00l); reduced in-plane strain expected as mismatch |f| decreases.

Step 12: YBCO low-fluorine MOD process.
- Precursor solution: Low-F TFA-based with F:metal ratio ≲ 0.5; solution solids 0.5–1.0 M.
- Coating: Slot-die or dip-coating; target final thickness 1.2–1.5 μm via single or multiple coats with intermediate pyrolysis.
- Pyrolysis: 400–450 °C in flowing O2/N2 with 5–15% humidity to remove organics and fluorides, ramp 5–10 °C/min, dwell 30–60 min.
- Crystallization: 760–800 °C in O2 with controlled humidity (200–1000 ppm H2O), dwell 30–60 min; cool in O2 to 450 °C.
- Oxygenation: Hold at 400–450 °C in O2 for 1–2 h to achieve δ ≲ 0.1; confirm Tc ≈ 90 K on test coupons.
- Keep all YBCO steps identical across samples to isolate LMO effects.

Step 13: Texture and morphology control (texture tuning).
- Preserve IBAD-MgO and LMO biaxial texture: confirm Δφ and Δω after O2 anneal; avoid anneal conditions that induce recrystallization or grain coarsening.
- AFM screening: reject any LMO surface with RMS > 3 nm before YBCO deposition.

Step 14: Measurements and instrumentation.
- XRD: θ–2θ, ω rocking curves, φ scans; pole figures if available; spot size ~1–2 mm for along-length mapping.
- Raman: 532 nm excitation; acquire 450–750 cm−1; fit Mn–O stretching modes; monitor peak shift and FWHM.
- AFM: Tapping mode; 5 × 5 μm2 and 1 × 1 μm2 scans; extract RMS.
- XPS: Monochromatic Al Kα; Mn 2p, 3s regions; perform ion-milling carefully or angle-resolved to avoid damage; quantify Mn valence trends.
- TEM: FIB cross-sections on select best/worst; HAADF-STEM, GPA strain mapping, misfit dislocation densities at LMO/YBCO; measure a-axis lamellae density.
- Ic mapping: Contactless magnetic induction scanner; calibrate with four-probe on short sections. Use standard V–I criterion 1 μV/cm for four-probe; correct for self-field differences. For R2R, map Ic every 5–10 m.
- Jc(H, T): PPMS or 77 K variable-field setup; compute Fp = μ0 Jc H; compare Fp,max and scaling with reduced field.

Heading: Feasibility Assessment
Step 15: Resources and timeline.
- Equipment: Existing R2R DC sputter coater for LMO; R2R MOD line; tube/box furnaces with O2; XRD, AFM, Raman, XPS; access to TEM (shared facility); Ic mapping system; four-probe station; cryogenics (LN2, variable-T magnet).
- Personnel: 1 thin-film process engineer (LMO, anneal), 1 solution process engineer (MOD YBCO), 1 characterization scientist, 1 data analyst; shared TEM operator.
- Timeline:
  • Months 0–1: Process calibration (as-deposited LMO reproducibility, textural checks).
  • Months 1–3: Screening matrix on coupons; down-select best 2–3 anneal conditions.
  • Months 3–4: 1 m tapes for the top conditions; Ic and microstructure.
  • Months 4–6: 60 m demonstration for best condition; uniformity analysis and final validation.

Step 16: Risks and mitigation.
- Over-oxidation of LMO causing texture degradation or phase change.
  • Mitigation: Cap temperature ≤ 620 °C; monitor Δφ, Δω post-anneal; shorten dwell if texture worsens.
- Oxygen-induced oxidation of underlying metal.
  • Mitigation: Ensure integrity of Al2O3/Y2O3 barrier; inspect after anneal by XRD and TEM; limit O2 partial pressure to 0.21–1 atm and keep dwell minimal for full oxygenation of thin LMO.
- Mn interdiffusion into YBCO at high T.
  • Mitigation: Limit LMO anneal before YBCO deposition; avoid high-temperature (>800 °C) exposures with YBCO present; consider optional 2–5 nm CeO2 cap in ablation subset if interdiffusion is observed.
- Non-uniform oxygen uptake along length.
  • Mitigation: Uniform gas flow and line speed; real-time temperature profiling; along-length XRD spot checks.
- Measurement uncertainty in contactless Ic.
  • Mitigation: Routine calibration against four-probe on multiple segments; use consistent models (Bean strip) and geometry factors.

Heading: References to Previous Studies (pre-2025)
Step 17: Cite foundational and supporting literature.
- J. D. Jorgensen et al., Structural properties of oxygen-deficient YBa2Cu3O7−δ, Phys. Rev. B 41, 1863 (1990) — YBCO lattice and oxygenation.
- S. R. Foltyn et al., Materials science challenges for high-temperature superconducting wire, Nature Materials 6, 631–642 (2007) — Coated conductor overview, texture, Ic.
- P. N. Arendt et al., Rolling-assisted biaxially textured substrates and buffer layers for high-temperature superconductors, MRS Bulletin 29, 543–550 (2004) — IBAD templates and texture metrics.
- Y. Iijima et al., In-plane aligned YBa2Cu3O7−x thin films on polycrystalline metallic substrates, Appl. Phys. Lett. 60, 769 (1992) — Early IBAD-based coated conductor concepts.
- J. Töpfer and J. B. Goodenough, LaMnO3+δ Revisited, J. Solid State Chem. 130, 117–128 (1997) — Oxygen nonstoichiometry, Mn valence, lattice evolution in LaMnO3±δ.
- J. Mizusaki et al., Oxygen nonstoichiometry and defect structure of La1−xSrxMnO3−δ, Solid State Ionics 129, 163–177 (2000) — Oxygen transport and defect chemistry in perovskite manganites.
- M. N. Iliev et al., Raman spectroscopy of orthorhombic perovskite LaMnO3 and La1−xSrxMnO3, Phys. Rev. B 57, 2872 (1998) — Mn–O vibrational modes vs oxygen content/structure.
- J. W. Matthews and A. E. Blakeslee, Defects in epitaxial multilayers: I. Misfit dislocations, J. Cryst. Growth 27, 118–125 (1974) — Misfit dislocation and critical thickness framework.
- T. Haage et al., Growth mechanism and microstructure of a-axis oriented YBa2Cu3O7−δ thin films, Phys. Rev. B 56, 840–850 (1997) — Origins and suppression of a-axis grains.
- T. Izumi and Y. Shiohara, Development of coated conductors by the MOD method, Physica C 463–465, 510–515 (2007) — MOD/TFA process fundamentals.
- A. Xu et al., Low-fluorine solution growth of YBCO films for coated conductors, Supercond. Sci. Technol. 23, 014003 (2010) — Low-fluorine MOD chemistry and processing.
- E. H. Brandt and M. V. Indenbom, Type-II-superconductor strip with current in a perpendicular magnetic field, Phys. Rev. B 48, 12893 (1993) — Magnetization modeling relevant to contactless Ic.
- M. Oomen et al., An improved method to determine the critical current of HTS tapes by magnetic measurements, IEEE Trans. Appl. Supercond. 9, 1677–1680 (1999) — Inductive Ic measurement methodology.
- A. Goyal, Second-generation high temperature superconducting wires, MRS Bulletin 29, 552–561 (2004) — Texture transfer and coated conductor performance.
- J. H. Durrell et al., The behavior of coated conductors in magnetic fields, Supercond. Sci. Technol. 26, 093001 (2013) — Jc(H) and pinning in coated conductors.

Heading: Clarity Notes (key concepts explained)
Step 18: Explain critical concepts.
- Lattice mismatch f: The relative difference between in-plane lattice constants of film and underlying layer: f = (a_film − a_sub)/a_sub. Smaller |f| reduces misfit dislocations and interfacial strain.
- a-axis vs c-axis orientation: In YBCO, c-axis perpendicular to the substrate is desired for optimal current. a-axis grains (with a-axis out-of-plane) interrupt current paths and reduce Ic.
- Texture metrics: Δω (rocking curve FWHM) quantifies out-of-plane spread; Δφ (phi-scan FWHM) quantifies in-plane spread. Smaller values indicate better alignment.
- Oxygen vacancies (VO) in LMO: Missing oxygen increases Mn–O bond length and lattice parameter; oxygen annealing fills VO, oxidizes Mn3+ to Mn4+, shortens Mn–O bonds, and contracts the lattice.
- Inductive Ic measurement: A contactless magnetic method infers Ic from the field generated by shielding currents under an applied AC field, calibrated against transport standards.

Heading: Expected Outcomes and Decision Points
Step 19: Decision-making and scale-up.
- Select the O2 anneal condition achieving a_pc ≈ 3.85 Å, Δφ/Δω preserved, AFM RMS ≤ 2 nm, Fa ≤ 1–2%, and ≥ 20% Ic improvement vs baseline.
- If N2-annealed controls do not show improvement while O2-annealed do, oxygen chemistry is validated as the key mechanism.
- Proceed to 60 m R2R run with the best condition; accept if along-length Ic variation ≤ ±5% with peak ≥ 560 A/12 mm at 77 K self-field and microstructural metrics within targets.



---

## Task Steps

### Step 1. Normalize and Clean
Normalize the experimental content to unify the evaluation basis:

- Standardize units and notation:
  - temperature: degrees C or K
  - time: min / h
  - pressure: Pa / mbar / Torr
  - concentration: wt.% / mol% / at.%
  - laser parameters: wavelength in nm, fluence in J cm^-2, repetition rate in Hz
  - thickness: nm / um
- Normalize common material aliases and abbreviations, such as YBCO = YBa2Cu3O7-delta.
- Ignore information that does not affect the core judgment:
  - brands, suppliers, equipment models
  - auxiliary descriptions
  - non-core descriptive expansions

### Step 2. Extract Executability Features and Defects
Evaluate against the **Full-Score Reference Template for Experimental-Plan Executability** and forcibly identify defects:

- **Plan structure**: does it have a clear hierarchy such as overview-task decomposition-SOP summary?
- **Task decomposition**: is it broken into independent subtasks? Does each task have clear objectives, materials, steps, and expectations?
- **Step clarity**: are steps numbered and logically clear?
- **Parameter specificity**: are parameters provided in lists or tables with clear values and units?
- **Risk and quality control**: does it include precautions, quality-control checkpoints, or contingency plans?
- **Closed loop and engineering awareness**: does it reflect fabrication-characterization-feedback logic and scale-up awareness?

**Mandatory output:** in this step, identify and record at least 1-3 major defects in the experimental plan, based on the defect deduction reference table.

### Step 3. Dimension Scoring
Score the following seven dimensions separately (0.00 - 1.00), then calculate the weighted total score.

| Dimension | Weight | Scoring Focus |
| :--- | :--- | :--- |
| Structural completeness and clear hierarchy | 0.15 | Whether it has a complete structure of overall goal -> subtasks -> steps -> summary. |
| Task decomposition and collaboration assignability | 0.15 | Whether task division is clear and independently assignable. |
| Executability / operational granularity / SOP tendency | 0.25 | Whether steps are numbered, parameters are tabulated, and operations are directly executable. |
| Parameter specificity and condition sufficiency | 0.18 | Whether key process parameters, such as temperature, time, and pressure, are concrete and quantified. |
| Risk prompts, precautions, troubleshooting | 0.12 | Whether potential problems are anticipated and countermeasures are given. |
| Quality control and criteria setting | 0.09 | Whether process quality-control checkpoints and result criteria are set. |
| Fabrication-characterization-feedback-scale-up validation loop | 0.06 | Whether it reflects a fabrication-testing-optimization loop and engineering scale-up awareness. |

Total-score formula:
`score = sum(dimension score x weight)`

---

## Scoring Principles

1. **Defects must cause deductions**: strictly follow the defect deduction reference table. A high score without listed defects is invalid.
2. **Parameters are core**: a "parameter shell" is a fatal defect; plans with this issue should not score above 0.69.
3. **High scores require strict evidence**: for scores above 0.85, explicitly list concrete evidence in the reason showing that the plan meets "outstanding" standards, such as tabulated parameters, contingency plans, and SOP-style summaries, and confirm that there are no obvious flaws.
4. **No comparison with other plans**: this evaluation only concerns the quality of the plan itself, not whether it resembles a reference plan.
5. **Strictly avoid score inflation**: score each dimension conservatively. For scores above 0.80, repeatedly verify that the corresponding requirements are satisfied and that the score matches the plan's actual quality.

---

## Score References (calibrated, mandatory)

- **1.00 (rare)**: perfect implementation of the full-score template. Parameters are tabulated, risk and quality control are complete, and the engineering loop is clear.
- **0.90 - 0.99**: extremely strong executability; parameters are concrete, structure is clear, and only minor flaws exist, such as one missing risk note. **Verify strictly and do not give lightly.**
- **0.80 - 0.89**: strong plan quality with mostly complete parameters, but lacking engineering awareness or quality-control details. **Confirm that there are no serious defects and that parameters are sufficiently concrete.**
- **0.70 - 0.79**: **passing line**. The plan has key parameters and logic and can be implemented, but operational granularity is coarse.
- **0.55 - 0.69**: average executability. Missing key steps or parameters prevents direct execution.
- **0.35 - 0.54**: weak plan. Mostly conceptual and unable to guide an experiment.
- **0.00 - 0.34**: completely non-executable.

**Warning: most qualified plans should fall between 0.70 and 0.85. Do not give scores above 0.90 lightly; high scores must be strictly controlled.**

---

## Output Requirements
Return only a JSON object with one res field, matching the example.
Do not output True / False.
Do not output a complex nested structure.

Output format:

{"res": {
  "score": 0.00,
  "reason": "First state the main defects identified; then review performance in structural completeness, task decomposition, operational granularity, parameter specificity, risk control, quality control, and engineering loop; finally explain why this score was assigned and emphasize strict control of high scores."
}}

Experiment:
Step1: Objectives and Hypotheses
- Objective: Quantitatively validate that a layered precursor strategy (C-MPP), which stacks a conventional Y123+Y211 (CPP) top layer over an in-situ MPP layer (Y2O3 + Ba–Cu–O), produces single-domain YBa2Cu3O7−δ bulks with finer, more homogeneous Y211 nanoparticle dispersion, lower porosity and zero macro-cracks, resulting in higher force–volume density and lower magnetic relaxation at 77 K, without degrading epitaxial texture or mechanical robustness required for HTS Maglev service.
- Hypotheses:
  1) The C-MPP architecture increases the Y211/Y123 interfacial area via capillary-driven solute infiltration from the MPP layer into the CPP layer during TSMG, enhancing flux pinning and reducing magnetic relaxation rate R compared to CPP and MPP baselines.
  2) A CPP buffer pellet beneath a SmBCO seed mitigates seed corrosion by Ba–Cu–O liquid and maintains single-domain epitaxy with a-b plane texture comparable to CPP.
  3) C-MPP reduces oxygen porosity and eliminates macro-cracks relative to MPP by lowering internal gas pressure and balancing shrinkage, yielding higher levitation stiffness and force–volume density at 77 K.

Step2: Experimental Design (Baseline, Comparisons, Ablations, Evaluation Criteria)
- Experimental groups (all with 1 wt% CeO2 and Yb2O3 substrate barrier unless noted):
  G1 (CPP baseline): Single-layer CPP pellet (Y123 + 35 mol% Y211).
  G2 (MPP baseline): Single-layer MPP pellet (Y2O3 + Ba2Cu3Ox to form Y211 in situ) with identical geometry.
  G3 (C-MPP target): Two-layer pellet: top CPP (Y123 + 35 mol% Y211), bottom MPP (Y2O3 + Ba2Cu3Ox), with a 6 mm-diameter CPP buffer pellet under SmBCO seed.
  Ablations to deconvolve mechanisms:
  A1 (No-buffer): Same as G3 but remove the 6 mm CPP buffer pellet to test seed corrosion/texture robustness.
  A2 (No-CeO2): Same as G3 but without CeO2 to test Y211 coarsening suppression.
  A3 (No-Yb2O3 barrier): Same as G3 but remove the Yb2O3 substrate layer to quantify stray grain formation impact.
  A4 (Reverse-stack): MPP on top, CPP bottom, to test directionality of solute infiltration on Y211 distribution and texture.
  A5 (Layer-thickness scan): G3 with top:bottom thickness ratios of 30:70, 45:55, 60:40 to identify optimal architecture.
- Sample geometry and batch: Discs of 25.0 ± 0.2 mm diameter, 9.5 ± 0.1 mm thickness (a-b area ≈ 491 mm²), N = 7 per group for statistical power (minimum 5 usable per group after yield).
- Thermal history control: Process all groups per batch in the same furnace run and identical thermal schedule; arrange pellets symmetrically around the furnace hot zone to equalize thermal gradients. Use identical oxygenation protocol.
- Primary endpoints:
  1) Levitation performance at 77 K in LN2: force–volume density Fv (N mm−3) and stiffness (dF/dz) above a Halbach guideway; relaxation rate R over 180 s.
  2) Microstructure: Porosity (%) by image analysis in a–c sections; presence/size of macro-cracks; Y211 particle size distribution and spatial homogeneity; epitaxial texture quality.
- Secondary endpoints:
  1) Trapped field (field-cooled, 77 K) and magnetization-derived Jc (Bean model).
  2) Mechanical integrity: Vickers hardness and indentation fracture toughness; 3-point flexural strength; cyclic magnetic loading durability.
- Statistical analysis:
  - One-way ANOVA with Tukey HSD for group comparisons of Fv, R, porosity, crack metrics, stiffness, Jc.
  - Regression/correlation between microstructural metrics (Y211 size, porosity) and performance (R, Fv).
  - Effect sizes (Cohen’s d) and 95% confidence intervals.
- Outcome criteria aligned to Maglev targets:
  - Fv improvement ≥ 5% vs CPP baseline with equal or lower R.
  - Porosity ≤ 18% and no macro-cracks > 100 μm in a–c cross-sections.
  - Epitaxial texture: in-plane alignment comparable to CPP (e.g., (103) XRD φ-scan FWHM within ±10% of CPP; rocking-curve Δω < ~3° typical for single-domain bulks).
  - No parasitic grains observed in optical/SEM over full cross-section.

Step3: Materials and Powder Preparation
- Powders and additives:
  - CPP powder: YBa2Cu3O7−δ (Y123) + 35 mol% Y2BaCuO5 (Y211), plus 1 wt% CeO2 (relative to total mass). Grain size target: Y123 d50 ~1–3 μm; Y211 0.5–2 μm (starting), refined by CeO2 during melt processing.
  - MPP powder: Y2O3 and Ba2Cu3Ox (liquid source). Mix molar ratio to yield stoichiometric formation of Y211 plus Ba–Cu–O liquid; practical mixture: Y2O3:(BaCuO2 + CuO) chosen to achieve a Ba:Cu ≈ 2:3 to form Ba2Cu3Ox liquid near 1010–1030 °C; include 1 wt% CeO2.
  - Substrate barrier: Yb2O3 powder layer (~0.3 mm thick) on Al2O3 setter to suppress stray nucleation.
  - Binder: 2 wt% polyvinyl alcohol (PVA) aqueous solution for green strength; burnout accommodated in thermal schedule.
- Mixing:
  - Wet ball-mill each powder composition separately in isopropanol with 0.5 wt% dispersant (e.g., fish oil or commercial dispersant) for 8 h at 300 rpm using ZrO2 media; dry at 80 °C; sieve through 200 mesh.
- Granulation and pressing:
  - Add 2 wt% PVA, granulate, dry; uniaxial press top and bottom layers separately.
  - Main pellet assembly: For G3 baseline, top CPP layer 4.0 mm thickness, bottom MPP layer 5.5 mm thickness (also vary per A5). Diameter 25 mm.
  - Cold isostatic pressing (CIP) 150 MPa to consolidate the stacked pellet.
- Seed and buffer:
  - SmBCO single-crystal seed (e.g., SmBa2Cu3O7-based) oriented with a-b plane parallel to pellet top surface; four-facet lines expected post-growth.
  - 6 mm-diameter, 2–3 mm-thick CPP buffer pellet (same CPP composition) directly under the seed for G3; omitted in A1.
- Assembly:
  - Place Yb2O3 powder layer (0.3 mm) on dense Al2O3 setter; center the pellet; lightly dust pellet perimeter with Y2O3 to minimize sticking. Fix the seed and buffer by slight indentation in the top surface.

Step4: Top-Seeded Melt-Growth (TSMG) Thermal Schedule
- Furnace: Vertical high-temperature box furnace with Pt–Rh thermocouple near sample; temperature uniformity ±2 °C over 60 mm zone.
- Schedule (typical for YBCO; ensure seed safety by staying below SmBCO peritectic ~1060–1080 °C):
  1) Binder burnout: Ramp 1 °C/min to 500 °C, hold 2 h in flowing O2/air mix (50:50), then to 700 °C at 1 °C/min, hold 1 h.
